lessons.title: Two Pointers
lessons.subtitle: Two Pointers
lessons.body: Picture two people at opposite ends of a shelf of books sorted by price, looking for two books that together cost exactly your budget. If the pair is too cheap, the person at the cheap end steps inward, because even the most expensive remaining book could not lift that cheap one to the budget. If the pair is too expensive, the person at the expensive end steps inward. Each comparison rules out a whole set of pairs at once, so you never test most of the n(n-1)/2 possible pairs. In the animation, watch which cursor moves after each comparison and ask which pairs that move has ruled out. Also notice the first step: the input arrives unsorted and is sorted before the search starts, which is a separate cost.
lessons.invariant: Any pair not yet ruled out lies within the current cursor interval.
lessons.pitfall: Moving the wrong cursor. If the sum is too small and you move right inward, you throw away the partner most likely to help and can skip the answer. Too small moves left, too large moves right. On unsorted input neither move is justified, so sort first and count that cost.
code: move the pointer that improves the sum

checkpoint.question: At values 1 and 7 with target 9, which cursor moves?
checkpoint.explanation: The sum is too small. Only advancing the left value can increase it in a sorted interval.

takeaways: At every step, all discarded pairs have been ruled out by the ordering. Sorting is a prerequisite, and its cost belongs in the analysis.
Moving both pointers without comparing the sum can skip a valid pair. Repeated values still occupy different positions.
objectives: Use ordering to discard impossible pairs.

blocks.title: Sort first, then two sums
blocks.text: The input arrives as 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, so the first step sorts it into 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7. Now left = 0 points at 1 and right = 5 points at 7. Their sum is 8, below the target 9. Since 7 is the largest value left, no partner can rescue 1, so left moves to 1. The cursors now point at 2 and 7, the sum is 9, and the search stops with the pair 2 + 7. Only two sums were computed. Every pair containing 1 was ruled out by a single comparison, and right never had to move. The answer refers to positions in the sorted array, not to where 2 and 7 sat in the original input.

blocks.title: Why a discarded value never mattered
blocks.text: Before every comparison, any pair that sums to the target lies between left and right inclusive. It starts true because the cursors cover the whole sorted array. When the sum is too small, sorted[left] plus the largest remaining value is still short, so sorted[left] plus any smaller value is short too, and dropping left loses no answer. When the sum is too large, sorted[right] plus the smallest remaining value already overshoots, so dropping right is safe. Each step shrinks the interval by one and keeps the claim true. When left meets right, no pair of distinct positions remains, so returning false is correct.

blocks.title: Where the linear cost comes from
blocks.text: Each loop iteration either returns or moves one cursor one place inward, and the gap between them starts at n - 1. So the search makes at most n - 1 comparisons: O(n) time, with O(1) extra space for two indexes and a sum. That bound assumes the input is already sorted. If it is not, sorting costs O(n log n) and dominates; for one query on unsorted data, a hash set of values seen so far gives O(n) expected time without sorting, at the cost of O(n) space. Two pointers reports sorted positions, so keep each value's original index alongside it if the problem asks for indices. The sum is computed as a long so adding two large int values cannot overflow.

lessons.title: Fixed-Size Sliding Window
lessons.subtitle: Fixed-Size Sliding Window
lessons.body: Imagine a frame that holds exactly three readings. Slide it one place to the right: two readings stay inside, one leaves, and one enters. The previous sum already contains almost everything you need. Remove the outgoing reading and add the incoming one. The frame represents a contiguous interval; it cannot skip an inconvenient reading. Try changing one value before looking at the code, then predict which windows it will affect.
lessons.invariant: The running sum is exactly the sum of the current window. A fixed-size window is a different problem from a variable-length window whose validity depends on a condition.
lessons.pitfall: Updating the best answer before a full window exists gives the wrong result. Initialize the best sum below every valid sum so negative inputs work.

blocks.title: The frame and the sum agree
blocks.text: After processing index right, the running sum contains exactly the readings from max(0, right-k+1) through right. Only compare with best once the frame contains k readings. Initializing best to zero breaks all-negative inputs. Keep best unset, or at the smallest representable value, until the first full window exists.

blocks.title: What the constraint tells you
blocks.text: Recomputing each of n-k+1 sums takes O(nk). Reusing the sum takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space. This fixed-size technique works with negative readings. A variable-size window that shrinks whenever a sum is too large needs additional assumptions; negative values can break that shrinking rule.

lessons.title: Binary Search
lessons.subtitle: Binary Search
lessons.body: Think of guessing a number between 1 and 100 when someone tells you higher or lower. A good guess sits in the middle, because whichever answer comes back, half of the possibilities disappear. Binary search does the same with a sorted array: one comparison with the middle value tells you which half cannot contain the target. That turns a search through n values into about log2 n comparisons, the difference between a million checks and about twenty. In the animation, keep your eye on the interval between low and high rather than on mid. Each step should shrink it, and the search ends either on a match or when the interval is empty.
lessons.invariant: If the target exists, some occurrence remains in [low,high].
lessons.pitfall: Writing low = mid or high = mid in this inclusive version. When the interval has two elements, mid equals low, so low = mid leaves the interval unchanged and the loop never ends. Test any variant on a two-element array with the target absent.

checkpoint.question: If a[mid] is smaller than target, what is the new low in this version?
checkpoint.explanation: mid has been ruled out, so advance past it.

takeaways: If the target exists, it remains inside the inclusive interval [low, high]. The loop terminates when the interval becomes empty.
Unsorted input invalidates the argument. Use low + (high-low)/2 and make progress after each comparison. Duplicates require a modified search for first or last occurrence.
objectives: Maintain an inclusive candidate interval.
Guarantee progress and distinguish exact search from insertion boundaries.

blocks.title: Searching for a missing 5
blocks.text: The input 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 is first sorted to 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and the target is 5. The interval starts at low = 0, high = 5. The middle index is 2, holding 3. Since 3 is less than 5, the target can only be to the right, so low becomes 3. Now mid = 4 holds 6, which is too large, so high becomes 3. The interval is the single index 3, holding 4, still too small, so low becomes 4. With low = 4 and high = 3 the interval is empty, and the search returns -1. Three comparisons settled it, and the last two pinned the gap between 4 and 6, exactly where 5 would have to be.

blocks.title: The interval always holds the answer
blocks.text: If the target is in the array, some copy of it sits between low and high inclusive. At the start the interval is the whole array, so this is true. When a[mid] < target, every index up to mid holds a value no larger than a[mid], so none of them can be the target and low = mid + 1 is safe. When a[mid] > target, the same argument applies to everything from mid upward, so high = mid - 1 is safe. Because mid itself is always excluded, the interval shrinks every iteration and the loop must end. If it ends with low > high, the interval is empty, and the invariant says the target was never there.

blocks.title: Why halving gives log n
blocks.text: Each iteration removes at least half of the remaining interval, so after k steps at most n / 2^k candidates are left. The loop stops once that drops below one, which takes about log2 n iterations: O(log n) time. Space is O(1) because only low, high and mid are stored. The catch is the sorted precondition. Sorting once costs O(n log n), which pays off only when you search the same data many times; for a single lookup in unsorted data a linear scan is cheaper. Computing mid as low + (high - low) / 2 avoids int overflow on huge arrays. With duplicates, this version returns whichever match it hits first, not necessarily the first occurrence.

lessons.title: Merge Sort
lessons.subtitle: Merge Sort
lessons.body: Imagine sorting a tall stack of exam papers with a friend. You split the stack, each of you sorts half, and then you merge: look at the top paper of each sorted pile and take whichever comes first, again and again. Merge sort applies that split recursively until every pile holds one paper, which is sorted by definition. All of the real work happens in the merges. Each merge only compares the two front items, because in a sorted pile nothing behind the front can come earlier. In the animation, notice that splitting changes nothing in the array; values only move when a merge commits its buffer back. Watch the buffer fill one value at a time and count how many values each level of merging touches.
lessons.invariant: Before a merge begins, both halves are sorted. The output prefix is sorted and contains the smallest values consumed so far.
lessons.pitfall: Comparing with < instead of <= when the fronts are equal. The output is still sorted, but equal keys from the right run jump ahead of those from the left, so the sort stops being stable. Also check the two drain loops: when one run empties, the rest of the other must still be copied, or values silently disappear.
code: split a nontrivial range at mid;
merge ordered fronts into a buffer; commit the run;

takeaways: Before a merge begins, both halves are sorted. The output prefix is sorted and contains the smallest values consumed so far.
Merging needs temporary storage. Choosing the left item on equal keys preserves stability. The animation shows completed merges rather than hiding the work in a library sort.

teaching.mentalModel: Split the range in half until each piece holds one value, which is already sorted. Then merge neighbouring pieces, always taking the smaller front value.

teaching.commonMistake: Taking from the right half on equal values breaks stability. The temporary buffer costs O(n) extra space, unlike in-place quicksort.

blocks.title: From pairs to the final merge
blocks.text: The input 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 is split at mid = 2 into indexes 0 to 2 and 3 to 5, and the left part is split again until 4 and 2 stand alone. Their merge takes 2, then 4, and the array becomes 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 6. Merging 2, 4 with 7 takes all three in order and changes nothing. The right part repeats the pattern: 1 and 3 merge in order, then 1, 3 merges with 6, again unchanged. A merge still runs when values are already in order; the algorithm cannot know that without comparing. The final merge fills a buffer of 6 values from the fronts of 2, 4, 7 and 1, 3, 6, taking 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, then draining 7, and the array becomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7.

blocks.title: The buffer prefix is already final
blocks.text: During a merge, the buffer holds the smallest values consumed so far, in sorted order, and the unconsumed parts of both runs are still sorted. Each step compares only a[i] and b[j]. Every other unconsumed value sits behind one of those fronts, so it is at least as large as a front. The smaller front is therefore the smallest value left anywhere, and appending it keeps the buffer sorted. When one run empties, the rest of the other run is no smaller than anything in the buffer, so copying it in order is safe. A single value is sorted, and every merge combines two runs that smaller merges already sorted, so the top merge produces a fully sorted array.

blocks.title: Where n log n comes from
blocks.text: Halving the interval each time gives about log2 n levels of splitting. On each level the merges together touch every value once, so each level costs O(n) and the whole sort costs O(n log n). That holds for every input, sorted or reversed, which is the main reason to choose merge sort over quicksort: no bad cases. The price is the O(n) buffer each merge writes into; heapsort or quicksort sort in place instead. Taking from the left run on ties, the <= in merge, keeps equal values in their original order, so the sort is stable. For very small arrays insertion sort is often faster in practice. Merge sort also suits linked lists and data too large for memory, where sequential merging is cheap.

lessons.title: Quicksort
lessons.subtitle: Quicksort
lessons.body: Picture lining people up by height using one person as a reference. Everyone shorter or equal steps to the left, everyone taller to the right. The reference person is now standing exactly where they belong in the final line, even though neither group is sorted yet. Quicksort repeats this on each group. The step that does the work is the partition: one scan with a boundary that marks the end of the small values found so far. In the animation, watch the boundary. It advances only when a scanned value is no larger than the pivot, and a value moves only when it has to jump over a larger one. After each partition, check that the pivot never moves again.
lessons.invariant: The partition boundary separates values already classified as small from those not yet examined. The pivot reaches a valid final position after partitioning.
lessons.pitfall: Recursing on a range that still includes the placed pivot. The range may not shrink and the recursion never ends. Also expect a last-element pivot to degrade to quadratic time on input that is already sorted: every partition then places only the largest value.
lessons.timeComplexity: Average O(n log n), worst O(n²)

teaching.commonMistake: Forgetting to exclude the placed pivot from both recursive calls loops forever on equal values. A last-element pivot on already sorted input gives the O(n²) worst case.

blocks.title: Three partitions sort the row
blocks.text: With 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 the last value, 6, is the first pivot. 4 and 2 are no larger, so the boundary passes over them without moving anything. 7 is larger and stays put. Then 1 swaps with 7, giving 4, 2, 1, 7, 3, 6, and 3 swaps with 7, giving 4, 2, 1, 3, 7, 6. The pivot swaps into index 4: 4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 7. The right side holds only 7, so it is done. The left side uses pivot 3: 4 stays, 2 and then 1 swap past it, and 3 lands at index 2, giving 2, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7. Finally pivot 1 lands at index 0 and the row is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7. Each partition placed its pivot for good.

blocks.title: What the boundary guarantees
blocks.text: During a partition, every value left of the boundary is no larger than the pivot, every value between the boundary and the scan position is larger, and everything past the scan is unexamined. A small value found by the scan swaps to the boundary and the boundary advances, so both regions stay correct. When the scan reaches the pivot, swapping the pivot to the boundary puts every smaller-or-equal value on its left and every larger value on its right. That is exactly its sorted position, so it never moves again. Each recursive call works on a strictly smaller range, and a range of zero or one value is already sorted, so the process ends with every value placed.

blocks.title: Why the pivot decides the cost
blocks.text: One partition scans its range once, so it costs time proportional to the range. If pivots split ranges roughly in half, there are about log n levels and each level scans about n values in total: O(n log n) on average. If the pivot is always the largest or smallest value, as a last-element pivot is on sorted input, each partition peels off one value, giving n levels and O(n²) comparisons. Recursion depth is the space cost: O(log n) on average, up to n frames in the bad case. A random pivot makes the bad case unlikely; choose merge sort when you need a guaranteed bound or stability, since quicksort is not stable. It is often fastest in practice because it sorts in place.

lessons.title: Linked Lists
lessons.subtitle: Linked Lists
lessons.body: Think of a scavenger hunt where each clue tells you where the next one is hidden. You cannot jump to the fifth clue; you have to follow the chain from the start. A singly linked list works the same way: each node stores a value and a reference to the next node, and the list is reachable only through its head. Inserting or removing next to a node you already hold is cheap, because you only rewrite references, but reaching a position is slow. Reversing the list is the classic exercise because it forces you to rewrite every arrow without losing your grip on the rest of the chain. In the animation, watch the three markers for previous, current and next, and notice that the values never move. Only the arrows change direction.
lessons.invariant: prev heads the reversed prefix; current heads the untouched suffix.
lessons.pitfall: Writing current.next = prev before saving current.next. The moment that arrow changes, the rest of the list is unreachable and the loop stops after one node. A related slip is returning current instead of prev: when the loop ends, current is always null.
code: reverse current.next; advance previous and current;

blocks.title: Six link flips, one per node
blocks.text: The chain is 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, and previous starts as null, shown as -1. In the first step current is the node holding 4. Its next node, 2, is saved first, then the arrow from 4 is pointed at null, and the markers advance so previous is 4 and current is 2. The same three moves repeat: 2 now points back to 4, then 7 back to 2, then 1 to 7, then 3 to 1. In the sixth step current is 6, the old tail; the saved next is null, 6 is pointed at 3, and current falls off the end. previous now holds 6, which is returned as the new head, and following the arrows gives 6, 3, 1, 7, 2, 4.

blocks.title: Two lists that never overlap
blocks.text: At the top of every loop iteration the nodes form two separate lists. prev heads the part already reversed, which runs backwards from the most recent node to the original head and ends in null. current heads the untouched remainder, still linked in its original direction. No node belongs to both and none is lost. One iteration moves exactly one node from the front of the remainder to the front of the reversed part. Saving current.next before overwriting it is what keeps the remainder reachable. When current becomes null the remainder is empty, so prev heads the whole list, reversed.

blocks.title: Linear time, constant extra space
blocks.text: The loop visits each node once and does a fixed amount of work there: one read and three reference writes. That gives O(n) time. The only extra storage is the three references prev, current and next, whatever the length, so the auxiliary space is O(1). A recursive reversal is shorter to write but uses one stack frame per node, O(n) space, and can overflow on long lists. Copying values into an array and writing them back also works but costs O(n) space and surprises anyone holding a reference to a particular node. Check the edges: an empty list returns null, and a one-node list returns itself. On a list with a cycle the loop never ends.

lessons.title: Stacks
lessons.subtitle: Stacks
lessons.body: Think of a stack of plates. You add a plate to the top and take a plate from the top; the ones underneath wait until everything above them is gone. That rule, last in first out, fits every situation where the most recent unfinished thing must be finished first: undo history, matching brackets, returning from nested function calls and depth-first search. A stack never lets you look inside or reorder it, and that restriction is what makes it useful, because the top always tells you what to handle next. In the animation, the values go in one order and come out in the opposite order. Notice that the first value pushed stays at the bottom until everything above it has been popped.
lessons.invariant: The top is the most recently pushed item that has not been popped.
lessons.pitfall: Popping without checking isEmpty first. On an empty ArrayDeque, pop throws an exception, and the bug usually means an earlier step pushed too little or popped too much. In bracket matching, a closing bracket with nothing on the stack is an answer to report, not a crash.

blocks.title: Six pushes, then six pops
blocks.text: The values 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 are pushed one at a time, and the size climbs from 1 to 6 with each new value landing on top. When the last push finishes, 6 is on top and 4 is at the bottom. Popping then removes 6 first, leaving 4, 2, 7, 1, 3. The next pops remove 3, then 1, then 7, then 2, each time taking whatever is on top. The last pop removes 4, and the stack is empty with size 0. The pop order 6, 3, 1, 7, 2, 4 is the push order reversed. Nothing was sorted or compared; the order came entirely from when each value arrived.

blocks.title: The top is the newest survivor
blocks.text: At every moment the top of the stack is the value pushed most recently among those not yet popped, and the values below it are in push order from the bottom up. A push puts the new value above the old top, which keeps that true. A pop removes the top and exposes the value pushed immediately before it, which is now the newest survivor. Because each operation touches only the top, the rest of the stack is never disturbed. That is why popping everything returns the exact reverse of the push order, and why a stack can remember where you were in nested work: the innermost open item is always on top.

blocks.title: Constant work at one end
blocks.text: Each push and pop touches only the top, so it does a fixed amount of work. ArrayDeque keeps its values in a resizable array; when the array is full it copies everything into a larger one, which is occasionally O(n) but averages out to O(1) per operation. Pushing and popping n values therefore costs O(n) time, and holding them costs O(n) space. ArrayDeque behind the Deque interface is the usual choice in Java. Check isEmpty before pop, because pop on an empty ArrayDeque throws an exception rather than returning a value. If you need the oldest item first instead of the newest, you want a queue.

lessons.title: Queues and Deques
lessons.subtitle: Queues and Deques
lessons.body: A queue is the line at a ticket counter. People join at the back and are served from the front, so whoever has waited longest goes next. That first in, first out rule is what you want when order of arrival must be respected: print jobs, requests to a server, and the frontier in breadth-first search, where vertices must be processed in the order they were discovered. Java's ArrayDeque can act as a queue or a stack depending on which ends you use, so the discipline lives in your choice of methods, not in the container. In the animation, compare this with the stack lesson: the same six values go in, but they come out in the same order rather than reversed.
lessons.invariant: The front is the earliest enqueued item that has not been removed.
lessons.pitfall: Using removeLast after addLast turns a deque into a stack. BFS depends on FIFO; substituting the wrong removal changes exploration order.
lessons.timeComplexity: O(n) total; amortized O(1) per deque operation

blocks.title: First in is first out
blocks.text: The values 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 are added at the back one at a time, and the size grows from 1 to 6. The front is 4 the whole time because nothing has left yet. The first removal takes 4 from the front and leaves 2, 7, 1, 3, 6. The next removals take 2, then 7, then 1, then 3, and the final one takes 6, leaving the queue empty with size 0. The removal order 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 matches the arrival order exactly. Had the same values been taken from the back instead, they would have come out reversed, which is the stack's behaviour.

blocks.title: The front waited longest
blocks.text: At every moment the front of the queue is the earliest-added value that has not been removed, and the values behind it are in arrival order. addLast puts a new value behind everything already waiting, so it cannot overtake anyone. removeFirst takes the front, which exposes the next-oldest value. Neither operation changes the relative order of the values in between. This is why breadth-first search finds fewest-edge distances: every vertex at distance d is enqueued before any vertex at distance d + 1, so the queue hands them out layer by layer.

blocks.title: Two ends, both constant time
blocks.text: ArrayDeque keeps its values in a circular array with a head index and a tail index. Adding at the back and removing from the front each move one index, so they cost O(1); when the array fills, it is copied into a larger one, which averages out to O(1) per operation. Processing n values therefore takes O(n) time and up to O(n) space while they wait. An ArrayList used as a queue is a common slow alternative, because removing index 0 shifts every remaining element and makes each removal O(n). If items should leave by priority rather than arrival, use a priority queue. Check isEmpty before removeFirst, which throws on an empty deque.

lessons.title: Recursion and the Call Stack
lessons.subtitle: Recursion and the Call Stack
lessons.body: Picture a line of people passing a question along: each person asks the next one an easier version and waits, notes in hand, until the answer comes back. The last person can answer without asking anyone. Then the answers travel back, and each person finishes their own part using the answer they received. A recursive function works this way. Each call gets its own frame on the call stack, holding its own copy of n, and stays paused until the smaller call returns. Every recursive function needs a base case that answers directly and a call that moves toward it. In the animation, the column of frames is the call stack. Notice that it grows first with no multiplying at all, and every multiplication happens while the stack shrinks.
lessons.invariant: factorial(n) returns n times factorial(n-1), with factorial(0)=1.
lessons.pitfall: A missing base case or a call that does not reduce the problem can recurse indefinitely. The call stack consumes space even when no explicit array is allocated.

checkpoint.question: What is still pending when factorial(5) calls factorial(4)?
checkpoint.explanation: The caller frame must multiply the returned result by its own n=5.

takeaways: Each call moves closer to a base case. During unwinding, every call receives the smaller result it needs.
A missing base case or a nondecreasing argument causes runaway recursion. The experiment caps n to keep the call stack readable.

blocks.title: Five frames wait for the base case
blocks.text: The animation computes factorial(5). The first call cannot answer yet, so it pauses and calls factorial(4), which pauses and calls factorial(3), and so on. After five calls the stack holds frames for 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1, and the call for 0 is pushed on top. That call hits the base case and returns 1 without recursing. Its frame is popped, and the frame for 1 resumes: 1 times 1 is 1. Each paused frame then resumes in turn, newest first: 2 times 1 gives 2, 3 times 2 gives 6, 4 times 6 gives 24, and 5 times 24 gives 120. The stack is empty again and the result is 120.

blocks.title: Each frame trusts the smaller call
blocks.text: factorial(n) returns n times factorial(n - 1), and factorial(0) returns 1. To see that every call returns the right answer, argue by induction on n. The base case is correct by definition. If factorial(n - 1) returns (n - 1)!, then n times it is n!, so factorial(n) is correct too. Termination comes from the argument shrinking by one each call, so it must reach 0. While a call is paused, its local n is safe in its own frame; the smaller calls get their own frames and cannot overwrite it. That is why the frame for 5 still multiplies by 5 after four deeper calls have come and gone.

blocks.title: Paying for the waiting frames
blocks.text: factorial(n) makes n + 1 calls, each doing one comparison and at most one multiplication, so the time is O(n). The space is also O(n), not because of any array but because up to n + 1 frames are alive at once on the call stack. That stack is limited, and very deep recursion crashes with a stack overflow. A loop that multiplies 1 through n gives the same answer in O(1) space, and Java does not optimise tail calls, so for a simple linear recursion like this a loop is the safer choice. Recursion pays off when the problem branches, as in trees and backtracking. The Java rejects negative n, which has no base case to reach, and caps n at 10 to keep the example small.

lessons.title: Backtracking
lessons.subtitle: Backtracking
lessons.body: Imagine exploring a maze with a ball of string. At each fork you pick a corridor and keep unrolling string. When a corridor ends, you wind the string back to the last fork and try the next corridor. You never need a second ball of string, because winding back restores exactly where you were. Backtracking explores every combination of choices the same way: one shared path list, an add before exploring a branch and a remove after it. Generating all subsets is the cleanest example, since each value is either in or out. In the animation, watch the path grow and shrink like the string. Every undo should restore the path to exactly what it was before the matching choice, and every recorded subset is a copy, not the live path.
lessons.invariant: On entering visit(start), path holds chosen values in increasing index order, all from indices below start.
lessons.pitfall: Missing the undo contaminates sibling branches. Storing path itself makes every result alias one mutable list. Duplicate input values require a separate deduplication policy.
code: choose a next input position and explore;

takeaways: The current path contains precisely the choices made along the active branch. Undoing restores the state expected by the next branch.

blocks.title: Following the path through the trace
blocks.text: The trace begins by recording the empty path. It then chooses values in input order and records each path on the way down: 4, then 4, 2, then 4, 2, 7, then 4, 2, 7, 1, then 4, 2, 7, 1, 3. Nothing is left to add, so it undoes 3 and then 1, returning to 4, 2, 7, and records 4, 2, 7, 3. Undoing 3 and 7 brings it back to 4, 2, which leads to 4, 2, 1, then 4, 2, 1, 3, then 4, 2, 3. Removing 2 leaves 4, and the next branch is 4, 7. A long stretch continues the same way. Near the end the path visits 7, 3, then 1 and 1, 3, then 3 alone, and the final undo leaves it empty. This trace uses only the first five values, so 6 never joins the path.

blocks.title: Undo restores the parent exactly
blocks.text: Whenever a call starts, the shared path holds exactly the choices made on the way from the root of the decision tree to this call, and nothing else. Each call that adds a value removes that same value before it returns, so the path is handed back to its caller unchanged. That is what lets siblings share one list: the second branch starts from the same path the first branch started from. In the Java, visit(i) is entered with path holding the chosen values among indices below i, so when i reaches a.length the path is one complete subset and a copy goes into out. Each subset matches one root-to-leaf route, so none is missed or repeated.

blocks.title: Exponential output, linear working space
blocks.text: With n distinct values there are 2^n subsets, because each value is independently in or out. You cannot do better than producing all of them, and copying each one costs up to n, so the time is O(n × 2^n). The working space is small: the path holds at most n values and the recursion is at most n + 1 calls deep, so O(n) auxiliary space. The output itself is O(n × 2^n). That growth is why backtracking suits only small n; at 30 values there are over a billion subsets. If you need only a count or the best subset, look for pruning or dynamic programming instead. With duplicate values this code produces repeated subsets, so sort and skip equal siblings when that matters.

lessons.title: AVL Trees
lessons.subtitle: AVL Trees
lessons.body: A plain binary search tree is only as good as its shape. Feed it keys in sorted or nearly sorted order and it turns into a long chain, so a search walks past almost every key. An AVL tree keeps the ordering rule of a search tree and adds one duty: every node remembers its height, and after each insertion the nodes on the way back to the root check whether their two subtrees differ in height by more than one. When one does, a rotation, a small relinking of two or three nodes, lowers the taller side without disturbing the sorted order. In the animation, watch where each repair happens: it is anchored at the lowest node on the insertion path that went out of balance, and a double rotation first turns that node's child.
lessons.invariant: For every node, the subtree heights differ by at most one. Rotations preserve the in-order sequence of keys.
lessons.pitfall: A single rotation does not fix a zig-zag. When the new key went left and then right (or right and then left) below the unbalanced node, rotating only at that node moves the imbalance to the other side. Check which way the child leans first and rotate the child before the node. After any rotation, recompute the lower node's height before the upper one, because the upper height is built from it.

blocks.title: One single rotation, two double ones
blocks.text: The keys arrive as 30, 20, 10, 25, 28, 27. After 30 and 20 the tree is a two-node chain of height 2. Inserting 10 makes the chain three long, and 30 sees a balance of 2: its left side is two levels taller. One right rotation at 30 lifts 20 to the root with 10 and 30 as children. 25 then settles as the left child of 30, and the height becomes 3. Inserting 28 as the right child of 25 unbalances 30 again, but now the extra height sits in the inner grandchild, so two rotations are needed: left at 25, then right at 30, leaving 28 above 25 and 30. Last, 27 goes under 25 and the root 20 is too heavy on the right. A right rotation at 28 and a left rotation at 20 make 25 the new root. The final tree has 25 on top, 20 with 10 on the left, 28 with 27 and 30 on the right, and height 3.

blocks.title: Balanced heights, unchanged order
blocks.text: Two facts hold after every insertion. First, the search-tree order: every key in a left subtree is smaller than its ancestor and every key in a right subtree is larger, so an in-order walk lists the keys sorted. A rotation only changes which of the nodes involved is the parent, and the middle subtree is reattached on the other side, so the in-order sequence is the same before and after. Second, the balance rule: at every node the two subtree heights differ by at most one. An insertion changes heights only along its own path, by at most one each, so the lowest node that reaches a difference of two is the only place that needs repair. After the rotation that subtree is back to its height before the insertion, so nothing above it needs work.

blocks.title: Logarithmic height for a little bookkeeping
blocks.text: Because subtree heights differ by at most one everywhere, the sparsest AVL tree of a given height grows like the Fibonacci numbers, which keeps the height below about 1.44 log2 n. Search, insert and delete therefore cost O(log n) in the worst case, not only on friendly inputs. Each node stores one extra integer, and an insertion needs at most one single or double rotation plus height updates along its path. The cost is code: four rotation cases, careful height updates, and deletions that may rotate at several levels. Red-black trees accept looser balance, up to about 2 log2 n, and need only a constant number of rotations even on deletion; Java's TreeMap is one. If the data never changes after loading, a sorted array with binary search is simpler still.

lessons.title: Binary Trees and Traversal
lessons.subtitle: Binary Trees and Traversal
lessons.body: A family tree has a person at the top and branches below, and there is no single obvious order to read it in. Tree traversal gives you rules for that order. The recursive shape is always the same: handle the left subtree, the node itself and the right subtree, and the three classic orders differ only in where the node goes. Preorder visits the node first, inorder in the middle, postorder last. Inorder matters most for binary search trees, where it reads values in sorted order, but the rule itself knows nothing about values; it only follows links. In the animation, watch frames open and close. A node is emitted only after its whole left subtree has finished, and its frame stays open until its right subtree is done too.

blocks.title: Left, node, right on this tree
blocks.text: The input 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 is read as level-order slots: 4 is the root, 2 and 7 are its children, 1 and 3 hang under 2, and 6 is the left child of 7. The walk enters 4, then 2, then 1. Node 1 has no left child, so it emits 1 and returns. Back in 2, the left side is done, so it emits 2, then enters 3, emits 3 and returns. Node 2 returns to 4, which emits 4 and turns right. It enters 7, then 6, emits 6 and returns. Node 7 emits 7, has no right child, and returns, and finally 4 returns. The output is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7. It is sorted because this tree happens to satisfy the search-tree ordering, not because inorder sorts anything.

blocks.title: A subtree finishes before moving on
blocks.text: When walk returns from a node, out has gained exactly the values of that node's subtree, in inorder, and nothing else. For an empty subtree this holds trivially, because walk returns at once. For a real node, the first recursive call adds its whole left subtree in order, then out.add places the node, then the second call adds the right subtree. Each subtree is smaller, so the claim follows by induction from the leaves up, and calling walk on the root lists every node exactly once. The order depends only on the shape of the links. If the tree also has the search-tree property, that order is sorted.

blocks.title: Linear time, height-deep stack
blocks.text: walk is called once for each node and once for each null child, and a tree with n nodes has n + 1 null links, so there are 2n + 1 calls doing constant work each: O(n) time. The space that matters is the call stack, which holds one frame per node on the current root-to-leaf path, so O(h) where h is the height. For a balanced tree h is about log n; for a tree that degenerates into a chain h is n, and a deep enough chain can overflow the stack. An explicit stack in a loop avoids that limit, and level order needs a queue instead. The output list adds O(n). height uses the same pattern and counts nodes, so the empty tree has height 0.

lessons.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
lessons.subtitle: Heaps and Priority Queues
lessons.body: Think of a company org chart where every manager earns more than the people who report directly to them. You can see the top earner at a glance, but nothing tells you whether someone in one department earns more than someone in another. A max-heap keeps exactly that weak order: every parent is at least as large as its children, so the maximum is always at the root. Because the tree is complete, it packs into an array with no gaps. That partial order is cheaper to maintain than full sorting, which is why heaps power priority queues. In the animation, follow the newly inserted value. It only ever moves up its own path toward the root, and it stops at the first parent that is at least as large.

blocks.title: Six insertions, three swaps
blocks.text: Inserting 4 makes it the root. 2 lands at index 1; its parent at index 0 holds 4, which is larger, so nothing moves. 7 lands at index 2, its parent 4 is smaller, so they swap and the array is 7, 2, 4 with 7 at the root. 1 lands at index 3 under 2 and stays. 3 lands at index 4, beats its parent 2 at index 1 and swaps up, giving 7, 3, 4, 1, 2; the next comparison with 7 stops it. Finally 6 lands at index 5, beats its parent 4 at index 2 and swaps, giving 7, 3, 6, 1, 2, 4, and 7 stops it again. The root is the maximum, but the array is not sorted in either direction.

blocks.title: Only one path can break
blocks.text: Before each insertion, every parent in the array is at least as large as its children. Adding a value at the end can break that rule in one place only: between the new value and its parent. If the parent is at least as large, the heap is valid and the loop breaks. If not, swapping fixes that pair, and the value that moves down was already the parent of that position, so it is still at least as large as anything below it. The only possible violation has moved one level up the same path. Repeating this ends at a large-enough parent or at index 0, and either way the whole array is a valid heap again, with the maximum at the root.

blocks.title: Height bounds every insertion
blocks.text: A complete tree with n nodes has height about log2 n, and an inserted value climbs at most that many levels, comparing and maybe swapping once per level. So one insertion costs O(log n), and inserting n values one by one costs O(n log n). The array holds every value once, O(n) space, with no child references because index arithmetic replaces them. Use a heap when you repeatedly need the current maximum while values keep arriving. If you need everything in order once, sort instead; searching a heap for an arbitrary value is O(n). Building a heap bottom-up from a full array is O(n), faster than repeated insertion. Equal values are fine: the >= check stops the climb.

lessons.title: Breadth-First Search
lessons.subtitle: Breadth-First Search
lessons.body: Imagine ripples moving out from a starting room. Breadth-first search explores the nearest discovered rooms before moving farther away. Its queue is the boundary between what has been discovered and what still needs processing. In this small directed network we start at vertex 0; each input value helps derive an edge weight, but BFS ignores weights and follows discovery order.

lessons.title: Depth-First Search
lessons.subtitle: Depth-First Search
lessons.body: Picture exploring a cave with a ball of string. You follow one passage as far as it goes, and only when it dead-ends do you wind the string back to the last fork and try the next opening. Depth-first search does the same on a graph: the call stack is the string, recording the path from the start to where you stand. It answers questions such as which vertices can I reach, is there a cycle, or what belongs to one connected piece. In the animation, watch the list of open frames grow by one vertex each time the search goes deeper, and shrink by one each time a vertex is finished. The order in which vertices are entered and the order in which they finish are both useful later, for example in topological sorting.
lessons.invariant: Every active frame represents a discovered vertex whose outgoing neighbours are not yet fully explored.
lessons.pitfall: Do not expect DFS to find shortest routes. It follows the first neighbour as deep as it goes, so a target one edge away can be reached through a long detour first. Also mark a vertex when you enter it, not when you finish it. If the mark comes late, a cycle sends the search back into a vertex that is still on the path, and the recursion never ends.

blocks.title: One long dive, then unwind
blocks.text: The search starts at vertex 0 and marks it entered. From 0 it descends to neighbour 1 before looking at any other neighbour of 0, and the same thing repeats: 1 descends to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4, and 4 to 5. At that moment six frames are open, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], which is the exact path from the source. Vertex 5 has nothing new to explore, so it finishes and returns. Then 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 finish in turn. None of them finds another unvisited neighbour on the way back, so the stack empties without a second dive. The final state reports 6 visited vertices, and the entry order 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is what dfs returns in its out list.

blocks.title: The open frames are the path
blocks.text: At every moment, the open frames form a path of discovered vertices from the source to the vertex being explored, and each of them may still have neighbours left to check. A vertex is marked in seen the moment explore is called on it, before any of its neighbours are tried. That early mark keeps the search finite: if a cycle leads back to a vertex already marked, the check fails and the search does not enter it again. When a frame returns, every vertex reachable from it through still-unmarked vertices has been entered. So no vertex is entered twice, and every vertex reachable from the source is entered once.

blocks.title: Each edge is checked once
blocks.text: Each vertex is entered once because seen blocks a second entry, and each vertex's neighbour list is scanned once while its frame is open. Across the whole graph that is V entries plus E neighbour checks, so the time is O(V+E) with adjacency lists. The space is O(V): the seen array has one slot per vertex, and in the worst case, a long chain like the one in this trace, the call stack holds every vertex at once. On a large graph shaped like a long line, recursion can overflow Java's stack, so switch to an explicit stack. If you need the fewest edges to a target, use BFS instead. The outer loop in dfs restarts from every unmarked vertex, so disconnected parts are covered too.

lessons.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
lessons.subtitle: Dijkstra's Algorithm
lessons.body: Breadth-first search finds the fewest edges, but road maps, networks and schedules put a cost on each edge, and the cheapest route can use more edges than the shortest one. Dijkstra's algorithm handles nonnegative costs. It keeps a tentative distance for every vertex, 0 at the source and infinity elsewhere, and grows a set of settled vertices whose distances are final. Each round it settles the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance, then relaxes that vertex's outgoing edges: if going through it gives a neighbour a cheaper route, the neighbour's estimate drops and its parent changes. In the animation, watch the distance row. A number can shrink while its vertex is unsettled, but once the vertex is settled the number never changes again.
lessons.invariant: With nonnegative edge weights, a settled distance cannot later improve. This is the reason greedy finalization is valid.
lessons.pitfall: Do not finalise a vertex the moment it is first reached. A first estimate is only an upper bound: a route with more edges but lighter weights can still beat it, and only the smallest-estimate rule guarantees nothing cheaper is on the way. Keep weights nonnegative too; a single negative edge can leave a settled distance wrong without any error being raised.
code: choose the smallest unsettled tentative cost;
finalize the vertex and relax its outgoing edges;
repeat until no reachable unsettled vertex remains;

blocks.title: Settling six vertices in order
blocks.text: The source is vertex 0 at distance 0. Its edges reach 1 with weight 5 and 2 with weight 6, so those estimates become 5 and 6, and 0 is settled. The smallest unsettled estimate is 5, so 1 is settled next. Its edge to 3 gives 5 + 4 = 9, while its edge to 2 would give 5 + 3 = 8, which does not beat 6. Vertex 2 is settled at 6, and its edge to 4 gives 6 + 4 = 10; reaching 3 through 2 would cost 6 + 8, worse than 9. Vertex 3 is settled at 9 and offers 5 a route of 9 + 3 = 12, while 9 + 2 does not beat the 10 already held by 4. Then 4 is settled at 10 and 5 at 12. The final distances are [0, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12], and following parents back from 5 gives the route 0, 1, 3, 5.

blocks.title: Settled means final
blocks.text: When a vertex is settled, its tentative distance is its true shortest distance from the source. Suppose a cheaper route to it existed. That route starts in the settled set, so let u be its first unsettled vertex, reached by an edge from a settled one. Relaxing that edge already gave u an estimate no larger than the route's cost up to u, and with nonnegative weights the rest of the route can only add cost. So u's estimate would be smaller than the picked vertex's, contradicting the choice of the minimum. That argument is why the greedy choice is safe, and it is exactly where a negative edge breaks things: a later edge could subtract cost and make a settled distance wrong.

blocks.title: Scanning versus a heap
blocks.text: This version finds the next vertex by scanning every unsettled estimate, which costs O(V) per round and O(V²) overall, plus O(E) relaxations. On a dense graph, where E is close to V², that is as good as it gets and the code stays short. On a sparse graph, a binary heap keyed by tentative distance finds the minimum in O(log V) and brings the total to O((V + E) log V); stale heap entries are simply skipped when popped. Space is O(V) for distances and parents, plus the graph itself. If every edge has the same weight, plain BFS gives the same answer more cheaply. If weights can be negative, use Bellman-Ford, which is slower but also detects negative cycles.

lessons.title: Maximum Flow: Edmonds–Karp
lessons.subtitle: Maximum Flow: Edmonds–Karp
lessons.body: Picture pipes from a reservoir to a city, each with a limit on how much water it can carry per second. How much can arrive in total? A flow network models this with directed edges that have capacities, a source, a sink, and the rule that every inner vertex passes on exactly what it receives. Edmonds-Karp builds the answer in rounds. Each round runs a breadth-first search in the residual network, the edges that still have spare capacity plus reverse edges that allow earlier flow to be cancelled, and pushes as much as the narrowest edge on the found path allows. When no path from source to sink remains, the flow is maximum. In the animation, watch reverse edges appear after each augmentation, and the reachable set at the end, which marks a minimum cut.
lessons.invariant: Flow respects capacity and conservation. Residual capacity records what can still be added or reversed.
lessons.pitfall: Do not leave out the reverse edges. Without them, a path chosen early can block a better arrangement, and the search stops while more flow is still possible. Also take the bottleneck over residual capacities, not the original ones: an edge that already carries flow has less room left than its label says.

blocks.title: Two paths, then a cut
blocks.text: The source is vertex 0 and the sink is vertex 5. The first search finds the path 0, 1, 3, 5 with capacities 5, 4 and 3. The narrowest is 3, so 3 units flow and the total is 3, and each of those edges gains a reverse residual edge of 3. The second search finds 0, 2, 4, 5 with capacities 6, 4 and 4, which carries 4 more units, so the total becomes 7. Now the edges from 3 to 5 and from 4 to 5 are both full. From the source the residual network still reaches 1, 2, 3 and 4, but not 5, so the search fails and the algorithm stops at 7. The edges leaving that reachable set are exactly those two full edges into the sink, with capacities 3 + 4 = 7, matching the flow: a minimum cut. This run never needed a reverse edge, but they are what lets other inputs reroute earlier choices.

blocks.title: Capacity, conservation, residuals
blocks.text: Throughout the run, the flow on each edge stays between zero and its capacity, and every vertex other than the source and sink sends out exactly what comes in. An augmentation keeps both facts. It adds the same amount along one path, so every inner vertex on it gains equal inflow and outflow, and that amount is the smallest residual capacity on the path, so no edge overflows. The residual network records for each edge how much more can be pushed forward and how much already sent could be pushed back. When the sink is unreachable, the vertices the source can still reach form a cut whose outgoing edges are full and whose incoming edges carry nothing, so the flow equals the cut's capacity and no flow can be larger.

blocks.title: Shortest paths bound the rounds
blocks.text: Any augmenting path keeps the answer correct, but careless choices can need a huge number of tiny augmentations. Choosing the path with the fewest edges, via BFS, guarantees at most O(VE) rounds, each costing O(E) for the search, so Edmonds-Karp runs in O(VE²) time. This lesson keeps capacities in a V by V matrix, which costs O(V²) space and suits small dense graphs; adjacency lists with paired reverse edges suit large sparse ones. Dinic's algorithm pushes many shortest paths per phase and is often much faster in practice. Whichever you use, the final failed search also hands you a minimum cut, which answers bottleneck questions directly.

lessons.title: Memoization
lessons.subtitle: Memoization
lessons.body: Suppose a friend asks you for 37 times 43 and you work it out on paper. If they ask again five minutes later, you read your answer off the paper instead of redoing the multiplication. Memoization gives a recursive function that same notepad. Plain recursive Fibonacci calls F(n-1) and F(n-2), and those two calls share almost all of their work, so the number of calls explodes as n grows. Storing each answer the first time it is finished collapses that tree of calls into one computation per value of n. In the animation, watch two things: the chain of frames that dives down to the base cases once, and the cache hits on the way back up, where a call returns at once without opening any deeper frames.
lessons.invariant: A cached state is correct once all dependencies have been computed correctly. The recursive structure remains visible.
lessons.pitfall: Check the cache before recursing and store the result before returning. If the two recursive calls still run on every visit and memo is only written afterwards, the table fills up but nothing is saved. A quick test: every repeated n should show a cache hit with no new frames under it. Also keep not computed apart from a computed zero; memo uses Integer and null for that reason.

store the result and return to the caller;

blocks.title: Dive once, then reuse
blocks.text: The trace computes F(8). The first call opens frames for 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and finally 1, always taking the n minus one branch first. F(1) returns 1 and F(0) returns 0 as base cases, so F(2) is stored as 1. Back in F(3), its second call F(1) is another base case, and F(3) is stored as 2. Now the reuse starts. F(4) needs F(2), which is already in the table: a cache hit returns 1 with no new frames, and F(4) is stored as 3. The same pattern repeats at every level. F(5) reuses F(3) and becomes 5, F(6) reuses F(4) and becomes 8, F(7) reuses F(5) and becomes 13, and F(8) reuses F(6) and becomes 21. The finished table is [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21], and the answer read from it is 21.

blocks.title: A stored value is final
blocks.text: Once memo holds a value for n, that value is the true F(n) and never changes. It is written only after both recursive calls have returned, and those calls return correct values by the same argument applied to smaller n, with F(0) and F(1) returned directly as base cases. So a cache hit is safe: reading memo[n] gives exactly what recomputing would give. The table in the trace fills strictly left to right, because an entry can only be written after the entries it depends on. The bottom-up fibTable relies on the same fact in loop form: when it writes dp[i], the two entries before it are already final.

blocks.title: Calls drop from exponential to linear
blocks.text: Without the cache, F(n) makes two calls that each make two more, and the shared work is redone again and again, so the call count grows exponentially, roughly like the Fibonacci numbers themselves. With memo, each n from 2 up to the target is computed once, and every other call is a base case or a cache hit that does constant work. That gives O(n) time. Space is O(n) for the memo array, plus O(n) for the recursion stack, which in the trace is deepest with 8 frames open. fibTable has the same O(n) time and table with no recursion, so it cannot overflow the stack. If you only need the final value, keep the last two numbers and the space drops to O(1). Note that int overflows after F(46); use long for larger n.

lessons.title: Tabulation
lessons.subtitle: Tabulation
lessons.body: Imagine a row of small solved questions. A later cell can depend on earlier cells, but never on a value that has not been computed. For Fibonacci, each cell is the sum of its two predecessors. Tabulation chooses an order that makes these dependencies available. Start by changing n and tracing the dependency arrows; the table is a record of reusable results, not a formula to memorize without understanding its base cases.

blocks.title: Build the answer from the beginning
blocks.text: Set F(0)=0 and F(1)=1. Then F(2)=1, F(3)=2, F(4)=3, and F(5)=5. Computing F(7) reads 5 and 8 from the two preceding cells and stores 13. Each write highlights both dependencies and the destination so you can see why that computation is valid.

lessons.title: Tries
lessons.subtitle: Tries
lessons.body: Autocomplete keeps asking one question: which stored words begin with what has been typed so far? Keeping the words in a list means comparing the prefix with every one of them. A trie spreads the words over a tree instead, one character per edge, so all words that start the same way share the same opening path. Looking up a prefix of length L follows at most L edges, however many words are stored, and every word below the node you reach is a completion. A flag on each node records whether a word actually ends there, because a path can be a stored word, a prefix of longer words, or both. In the animation, notice how later words reuse the edges earlier words created and only branch off where they first differ.
lessons.invariant: Each root-to-node path spells a prefix. A terminal marker distinguishes a complete word from a prefix that is not itself a word.
lessons.pitfall: Reaching a node is not the same as finding a word. Walking t, r, y proves that some stored word starts with try, not that try itself was inserted; only the word-end flag says that. The opposite slip also happens: forgetting to set the flag on a word that is a prefix of a longer one, such as adding car after cart, makes car invisible to exact lookups.
code: follow or create one prefix edge;
mark the endpoint as a complete word;
return to root for the next word;

checkpoint.question: Which statement captures the key idea?
checkpoint.explanation: A word-ending marker. Each root-to-node path spells a prefix. A terminal marker distinguishes a complete word from a prefix that is not itself a word.

takeaways: Each root-to-node path spells a prefix. A terminal marker distinguishes a complete word from a prefix that is not itself a word.
Prefix lookup cost and result enumeration cost are different. Returning many completions costs at least as much as writing those results.

An unsorted list scanned on every keystroke
challenges.explanation: Each keystroke extends the prefix by one edge, and every completion lies in the subtree below. A hash set only answers exact matches.

challenges.prompt: Insert tree, trie, try, track. Fill the table at the step where inserting track creates its first new node.
challenges.explanation: Your entries agree with the actual Java trace for this input.
challenges.hint: Every earlier word shares t and r; find where track first leaves the existing paths. Type text without quotes.

blocks.title: Four words, one shared stem
blocks.text: The words are tree, trie, try and track. Inserting tree starts at the empty root, creates one node each for t, r, e and e, and marks the last one as a word end: 1 word stored. Inserting trie follows the existing t and r edges, so the only new nodes are i and e, and the count becomes 2. try follows t and r again and creates just y, giving 3 words. track follows t and r, branches at a, and creates a, c and k, so the count reaches 4. The trie holds only 10 nodes below the root, fewer than the letters in the four words, because the stem tr is stored once and shared by every word. A query for the prefix tr would stop at that shared node and find all four words beneath it.

blocks.title: Every path spells one prefix
blocks.text: Each node stands for exactly one string: the characters on the edges from the root down to it. No two nodes stand for the same string, because insertion follows an existing edge whenever one matches and creates a new edge only where the stored paths stop. That is why a lookup can be a plain walk. If the walk for a prefix falls off the tree, no stored word starts with that prefix; if it reaches a node, every stored word with that prefix lies in the subtree below. The word-end flag records what the shape cannot: here a node for tr exists, yet tr was never inserted, so its flag stays off and an exact lookup for tr answers false.

blocks.title: Fast prefixes, many small nodes
blocks.text: With constant-time child lookup, insert and lookup cost O(L) for a word or prefix of length L, independent of how many words are stored. Listing completions costs extra, in proportion to the subtree you walk, so a short prefix over a large dictionary can still produce a lot of output. Space is the weak point: every node carries a map or array of children, which is heavy next to the characters themselves. A sorted list with binary search answers the same prefix questions in O(L log n) time with far less memory, and a hash set answers exact membership with less memory. A trie earns its memory when prefix queries are frequent and the stored words share long stems.

objectives: Insert words so that shared prefixes reuse existing edges.
Separate prefix lookup from exact-word lookup with the word-end flag.

lessons.title: Greedy Set Cover
lessons.subtitle: Greedy Set Cover
lessons.body: Suppose you want a short study plan that touches every topic on your list, and each practice question covers a few topics. Finding the smallest set of questions that covers everything is hard in general: no known method solves large cases exactly in reasonable time. The greedy rule is a practical compromise. In each round, score every candidate by how many still-uncovered topics it would add, take the best one, and repeat until everything is covered or no candidate adds anything. It never revisits a choice. In the animation, watch the scores change from round to round: a candidate's value depends on what is already covered, not on how many topics it lists.
lessons.invariant: The covered set grows after every useful choice. The algorithm stops with complete coverage or identifies topics no remaining question can cover.
lessons.pitfall: Do not score a candidate by how many topics it lists. Its value is only what it adds now: in the second round, candidate 3 still lists two topics but adds one, because Arrays is already covered. And do not read the greedy result as proof that no smaller plan exists.
code: define goals and candidate topic sets;
choose the largest gain; remove those goals;
stop if no positive gain exists;
report selected sets and uncovered goals;

checkpoint.question: Which statement captures the key idea?
options: It is an approximation, not always optimal
It always finds the exact minimum
checkpoint.explanation: It is an approximation, not always optimal. The covered set grows after every useful choice. The algorithm stops with complete coverage or identifies topics no remaining question can cover.

takeaways: The covered set grows after every useful choice. The algorithm stops with complete coverage or identifies topics no remaining question can cover.
The result is not guaranteed to use the fewest questions. Under unit costs and feasible coverage, the standard greedy bound is harmonic in the number of topics.

challenges.hint: Picture a left-to-right scan that replaces its best choice only on a strictly larger gain.

options: Greedy set cover: repeatedly open the site serving the most unserved districts
Open sites in listed order until every district is served

challenges.explanation: This is set cover; greedy is fast and has a proven approximation bound, while listed order ignores how much each site adds.
challenges.hint: Which rule looks at what is still uncovered?

challenges.prompt: Goals Arrays, Hashing, Trees, Graphs, DP. Fill the table when candidate 3 (Arrays, DP) is scored in the second round.
challenges.explanation: Your entries agree with the actual Java trace for this input.

blocks.title: Three rounds to cover five topics
blocks.text: The goals are Arrays, Hashing, Trees, Graphs and DP, so 5 topics start uncovered. Candidate 1 covers Arrays and Hashing, candidate 2 covers Graphs and Trees, candidate 3 covers Arrays and DP, and candidate 4 covers only Trees. In the first round candidates 1, 2 and 3 each add 2 topics and candidate 4 adds 1; the tie goes to the first, so candidate 1 is chosen and Trees, Graphs and DP remain. In the second round candidate 1 adds nothing, candidate 2 still adds 2, and candidates 3 and 4 add 1 each, so candidate 2 is chosen and only DP remains. In the third round only candidate 3 adds anything, and it covers DP. Three candidates were chosen and nothing is left uncovered. Here three is also the true minimum, since no two candidates together cover all five topics.

blocks.title: Coverage only grows
blocks.text: After each round, the covered set is exactly the union of the chosen candidates, and the remaining set is the goals minus that union. A candidate is chosen only when its gain is positive, so every round strictly shrinks what remains, and the loop runs at most once per goal. When it stops there are two honest outcomes: everything is covered, or the leftover goals appear in no candidate at all, and the algorithm reports them instead of hiding them. What this invariant does not promise is minimality. Gains are measured against the current remaining set only, so a choice that looked best early can force extra picks later.

blocks.title: A guarantee, not an optimum
blocks.text: Each round scores every candidate against the remaining goals. With P candidates and T goals, a straightforward version spends up to O(P·T) per round over at most min(P, T) rounds. Finding the exact minimum cover is NP-hard, so for large inputs a fast heuristic is the realistic option. Greedy comes with a proven bound: with equal costs it uses at most H(T) times as many sets as the optimum, where the harmonic number H(T) is below ln T + 1. On small inputs like this one, trying every subset of candidates is affordable and gives the true minimum. When candidates have different costs, score by uncovered topics per unit of cost instead.

objectives: Score each candidate by the uncovered goals it adds and pick the largest gain.
Explain why a greedy cover can be larger than the optimum.

lessons.title: Randomized Quickselect
lessons.subtitle: Randomized Quickselect
lessons.body: Sometimes you need one value by rank, such as the median or the third smallest, not a fully sorted list, and sorting does more work than the question asks for. Quickselect borrows the partition step from quicksort: choose a pivot, move the values not larger than it to its left and the larger ones to its right, and the pivot lands exactly where it would sit after sorting. If that position is the requested rank, you are done. Otherwise only one side can contain the answer, and the other side is dropped for good. Choosing the pivot at random makes it unlikely that the split is lopsided round after round. In the animation, watch the range of interest shrink, and notice the values outside it that are never put in order.
lessons.invariant: After partitioning, the pivot’s position tells us which interval can contain the requested rank. Random pivots make repeatedly bad splits unlikely.
lessons.pitfall: Mixing up ranks and indexes is the classic bug: rank 3 means index 2. The expected bound also depends on the pivots being random; a fixed first or last pivot on sorted input discards only one value per round. With many repeated values a two-way partition can degrade as well, which is why many implementations, including this app's own Quickselect class, split into less, equal and greater.
code: stop at a trivial candidate range;
compare values and partition at the boundary;
place pivot; continue in the appropriate subranges;
selection returns when the requested rank is fixed;

checkpoint.question: Which statement captures the key idea?
options: Only the side containing the requested rank
Both sides must be fully sorted
checkpoint.explanation: Only the side containing the requested rank. After partitioning, the pivot’s position tells us which interval can contain the requested rank. Random pivots make repeatedly bad splits unlikely.

takeaways: After partitioning, the pivot’s position tells us which interval can contain the requested rank. Random pivots make repeatedly bad splits unlikely.
Expected linear time is not a worst-case guarantee. The production selector uses three-way partitioning to handle duplicates efficiently; this small lesson shows pivot movement explicitly.

options: Indices 0 to 4, left of the pivot

challenges.explanation: The pivot sits at its sorted position 5; index 2 is smaller, so only the left part can hold the answer.
challenges.hint: Compare the target index with the pivot's final index.

challenges.title: Spot the pattern
challenges.prompt: You need the 100 largest of 10 million scores, in any order, as fast as possible on average. Which approach fits?
options: Sort all scores and take the last 100: O(n log n)
Quickselect the 100th largest, then keep it and everything on its larger side: expected O(n)
Binary search the unsorted scores for the cutoff
challenges.explanation: After the selection the partition has already put the 100 largest values on one side, and their order was never required. Binary search needs sorted input.
challenges.hint: The output does not have to be sorted.

challenges.title: Dry-run the state
challenges.prompt: Rank 3 in 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6. The third partition uses pivot 3 on indices 1 to 4. Fill the table when the pivot is placed.
challenges.explanation: Your entries agree with the actual Java trace for this input.
challenges.hint: Count the values in the range that are at most the pivot, starting from the low index.

blocks.title: Finding the third smallest
blocks.text: The input is 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 and the requested rank is 3, which is index 2 once sorted. The first random pivot is 7. It is moved to the end, every other value is at most 7, so the boundary advances past all of them and 7 is placed at index 5. Index 2 lies to its left, so the search continues on indices 0 to 4. The second pivot is 1, the smallest value: no scanned value is at most 1, so the pivot lands at index 0, giving 1, 2, 6, 3, 4, 7. The range is now indices 1 to 4. The third pivot is 3. Only 2 is at most 3, so the boundary moves once and 3 is placed at index 2. That is the requested position, and the answer is 3. The values 4 and 6 were never compared with each other; that they end up in order is luck.

blocks.title: The pivot's index is its rank
blocks.text: After a partition of the range from low to high, the pivot sits at some index p, every value from low up to p minus one is at most the pivot, and every value after p up to high is larger. So the pivot is exactly the value that would sit at index p in sorted order. The requested index always stays inside the current range: if it equals p the search stops, if it is smaller only the left part can hold the answer, and if it is larger only the right part can. Each round removes at least the pivot from the range, so the loop must end. Values outside the range are already on the correct side of the answer, which is why they never need sorting.

blocks.title: Expected linear, worst quadratic
blocks.text: Each partition is one pass over the current range. With random pivots the range shrinks by a constant fraction on average, so the passes add up like n + n/2 + n/4 and the expected time is O(n). A run that keeps drawing the largest or smallest value, as the first two pivots here did, costs O(n²), but over many runs that is very unlikely. If a worst-case bound is required, the median-of-medians pivot rule guarantees O(n) at the price of a much larger constant. Sorting first costs O(n log n) and pays off only when you need many ranks from the same data. This version works on a copy of the input, using O(n) space, so the caller's array is left untouched.

objectives: Partition around a random pivot and continue only into the side that holds the rank.
Distinguish quickselect's expected O(n) time from its O(n²) worst case.

lessons.title: Bloom Filters
lessons.subtitle: Bloom Filters
lessons.body: Before an expensive lookup on disk or across a network, it helps to learn cheaply that an item is definitely not there. A Bloom filter does this with a fixed array of bits and a few hash functions. Inserting an item sets the bits its hashes point to. A query checks those same bits: if any is zero, the item was never inserted; if all are one, it might have been, because other items may have set the same bits. The filter never stores the items, so it is far smaller than a set, but it cannot list its contents or delete safely. In the animation, watch bits turn on as words arrive, and notice that a later word can land entirely on bits that are already set.
lessons.invariant: With insert-only operation, a previously inserted identifier has all its bits set. Collisions can create false positives, not false negatives.
lessons.pitfall: Do not act on a positive answer as if it were exact: in this trace sheep was never inserted, yet both of its bits are set. Do not size the filter for today's data only, either. As more items arrive, more bits turn on and the false-positive rate climbs until almost every query says possibly present.
code: query bits; verify positives with an exact set;

checkpoint.question: Which statement captures the key idea?
options: Possibly present; confirm exactly when needed
checkpoint.explanation: Possibly present; confirm exactly when needed. With insert-only operation, a previously inserted identifier has all its bits set. Collisions can create false positives, not false negatives.

takeaways: With insert-only operation, a previously inserted identifier has all its bits set. Collisions can create false positives, not false negatives.
A positive result cannot justify discarding an item when exact membership matters. Confirm it against authoritative storage. Ordinary bit clearing is not a safe deletion operation.

challenges.hint: With insert-only operation, a previously inserted identifier has all its bits set. Collisions can create false positives, not false negatives.

options: No bit changes; only the exact set grows
The filter rejects graph as a duplicate
challenges.explanation: Setting a bit that is already one leaves it one, so the bit array is unchanged; the filter cannot tell that a different word arrived.
challenges.hint: Each position holds a single bit.
