challenges.prompt: A crawler tracks billions of visited URLs in little memory. Occasionally skipping a page it never visited is acceptable, but it must never fetch the same page twice. Which structure fits?
options: A Bloom filter of visited URLs
A hash set of every URL string
A sorted list of URLs with binary search
challenges.explanation: The filter never forgets an inserted URL, so nothing is fetched twice; its false positives cause only the acceptable skips. Exact structures need far more memory.
challenges.hint: Which kind of error can a Bloom filter make, and which can it never make?

challenges.title: Dry-run the state
challenges.prompt: Insert tree, graph, heap, then query sheep. Fill the table at the query step.
challenges.explanation: Your entries agree with the actual Java trace for this input.
challenges.hint: sheep hashes to bits 11 and 12. Check which insertion set those bits, and whether sheep was ever inserted.

blocks.title: A false positive for sheep
blocks.text: The filter starts with every bit at zero, and each word sets two positions. tree hashes to bits 14 and 9, so those turn on. graph happens to hash to the same two bits, 14 and 9, so the bit array does not change at all, even though the exact set now holds 2 words. heap hashes to 12 and 11, which turns those bits on; 4 bits are now set and the exact count is 3. The query sheep hashes to 11 and 12. Both are already one, set by heap, so the filter answers possibly present. The exact set shows that sheep was never inserted: this is a false positive. A query whose bits had included any position that is still zero would have been rejected at once, with certainty.

blocks.title: No false negatives
blocks.text: Bits are only ever switched on, never off. So once an item has been inserted, every bit its hashes name stays one for the rest of the filter's life, and a query for it always answers possibly present. That is the guarantee a Bloom filter sells: a no is always right. A yes is weaker; it only says that each of the item's bits was set by some insertion, not necessarily by this item. The exact set kept beside the filter in this lesson exists to show that difference. In real use the confirmation comes from the authoritative store the filter protects. Clearing a bit to delete an item would break the guarantee, because the same bit may belong to other items.

blocks.title: Tiny, fast and approximate
blocks.text: Insert and query each compute k hashes and touch k bits, so both cost O(k), however many items are stored. Space is m bits, about 9.6 bits per item for a one percent false-positive rate with the best k, far less than storing the items. The price is that rate, which rises as bits fill: with n items and well-mixed hashes a bit is still zero with probability about e^(-kn/m), so an absent item passes all k checks with probability about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, which is lowest near k = (m/n) ln 2. A filter cannot shrink, list its items or delete; a counting Bloom filter swaps bits for small counters to allow deletion, at several times the space. Put one in front of a slow lookup, never in place of exact membership.

objectives: Explain why a zero bit proves absence while all-ones only suggests presence.
Relate filter size, hash count and item count to the false-positive rate.

lessons.body: Timing code with a stopwatch tells you about one machine on one day. Complexity asks a sturdier question: if the input doubles, how much more work does the code do? To answer it, pick one basic operation, here one pass through a loop body, and count how many times it runs as a formula in n. Think of counting steps instead of minutes: a walker's speed changes from day to day, the number of steps does not. In the animation the same n drives three loops. Notice how differently their counters grow. One ticks once per position, one adds a whole row at a time, and one stops after a handful of visits because its variable is halved each time.
lessons.invariant: The operation counter increases once for each visit of the selected loop body.
lessons.pitfall: Do not read complexity off the shape of the code. Two nested loops are quadratic only when both run about n times. If the inner loop runs a fixed 3 times, or halves its range, the count is very different. Write down how many times the inner body runs for each outer value and add those numbers up.
lessons.timeComplexity: O(n), O(n²), O(log n) for the three loops
code: if (n < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("n must be nonnegative");
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) scan++;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) square++;
for (int x = n; x > 0; x /= 2) halves++;

blocks.title: Three counters for n = 8
blocks.text: With n = 8, the scan loop visits positions 0 through 7, and its counter climbs one step at a time until it reads 8. The nested loop counts ordered pairs. Each outer row contributes a full inner loop of 8 visits, so the counter jumps to 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56 and ends at 64 after row 7. The halving loop starts with x at 8 and divides by two: it visits 8, 4, 2 and 1, and when x becomes 0 the loop stops, giving 4 visits. The final comparison is 8, 64 and 4 for the same input size. Try predicting n = 16 before you run it: the scan doubles, the pair count grows fourfold, and the halving count grows by one.

blocks.title: Count what the body does
blocks.text: Each counter in counts goes up by exactly one every time its loop body runs, so when a loop finishes, its counter equals the number of times that body executed. That is the whole method: choose the operation you care about, write down how many times it runs, and keep the term that grows fastest. For the scan the count is n. For the square loop the inner body runs n times for each of n outer values, so n times n. For halving, x takes the values n, n/2, n/4 and so on down to 1, which is about log2(n) plus one values. Big-O then drops constant factors and smaller terms, because they stop mattering as n grows.

blocks.title: Why growth beats milliseconds
blocks.text: The three loops cost O(n), O(n²) and O(log n) time because those are the formulas their counters follow. Space is O(1) auxiliary: however large n is, counts keeps three long counters and a loop variable or two, and nothing grows with n. Growth rate matters more than constant factors once inputs get large. At n = 1000 the scan does a thousand visits and the square loop a million, so a quadratic method that was fine on a small test can stall on real data. Counting has limits too. It ignores memory effects and fixed overhead, so for small n a plain O(n²) loop can beat a cleverer method. Treat Big-O as a guide to how cost scales, then measure when the constants matter.

lessons.body: Think of an array as a row of numbered lockers. Each locker has a fixed position, and you can open locker 2 directly without walking past lockers 0 and 1. That direct jump is why arrays are the default container for ordered data: reading or writing any slot by its index costs the same, however long the row is. The index names a place, not what is stored there, so two lockers can hold the same value and still be different slots. In the animation, watch the index move left to right while a running total absorbs one slot at a time. That pattern, a loop plus a variable that summarises everything seen so far, is the shape of most array algorithms you will meet next.

lessons.pitfall: The last valid index is length-1. Iterating with i <= length reads beyond the array. Integer sums may overflow; use long for the accumulator.

blocks.title: Summing [2, 1, 5] slot by slot
blocks.text: Before the loop starts, total is 0 because nothing has been read yet. At index 0 the loop reads 2, and total becomes 2. At index 1 it reads 1, and total becomes 3. At index 2 it reads 5, and total becomes 8. The condition i < a.length now fails, since the length is 3, and sum returns 8. Notice that each step adds only the value in the current slot. The earlier slots are never read again, because total already stands for them. If the array were empty, the loop body would never run and the method would return the starting value 0.

blocks.title: Total covers the slots behind i
blocks.text: Each time the loop is about to read index i, total equals the sum of every slot before i and none after it. At the start i is 0 and no slots are behind it, so total must be 0, which is how it is initialised. Each iteration adds a[i] and then moves i forward by one, so the statement is true again for the new i. When the loop ends, i equals a.length, and every slot before i means the whole array. That is why the returned value is the full sum. This style of reasoning, true at the start, kept by each step, useful at the end, is how you check any loop.

blocks.title: One visit per slot
blocks.text: The loop body runs once per slot and does constant work each time, so summing takes O(n) time. You cannot do better for a sum, because every value must be read at least once. Auxiliary space is O(1): one long and one int index, whatever the length. The accumulator is long rather than int because adding many large ints can pass the int limit of about 2.1 billion and wrap silently to a negative number. Arrays are the right tool for indexed reads and scans, but their size is fixed when they are created, and inserting into the middle means shifting every later slot. When the size changes often, a growable list or a linked structure fits better.

lessons.body: A string is a fixed line of characters, each at a numbered position, like letters stamped on a strip of metal. In Java you can read any position, but you cannot change the strip itself: String is immutable. To produce changed text, you copy characters into a new buffer and turn that buffer into a fresh string at the end. This matters for cost. Gluing strings together with + inside a loop copies the whole growing result each time, while a StringBuilder appends in place. In the animation, keep two things apart: the read index, which walks backwards through the source, and the output, which grows forwards one character at a time. The source never changes.
lessons.invariant: After k iterations, the buffer contains the final k characters in reverse order.
lessons.pitfall: Java char indexes UTF-16 code units, not all user-perceived characters. This introductory example is restricted to ASCII; it is not a Unicode grapheme reverser.
code: for (int i = s.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) out.append(s.charAt(i));

blocks.title: Reversing "cat" into a buffer
blocks.text: The source is "cat", with c at index 0, a at index 1 and t at index 2. The output buffer starts empty. The loop begins at the last index, 2, and appends t, so the output is "t". Next it reads index 1 and appends a, giving "ta". Then it reads index 0 and appends c, giving "tac". The index would now be negative, the condition i >= 0 fails, and reverse returns "tac". The source is still "cat", because every step only read from it. Notice that the read index goes 2, 1, 0 while the output length goes 1, 2, 3. That is why the two must be tracked separately.

blocks.title: The buffer holds a reversed suffix
blocks.text: After k characters have been appended, the buffer holds the last k characters of the source in reverse order. Before the loop, k is 0 and the buffer is empty, which matches. Each step reads the next character further left and appends it to the right end of the buffer, so the reversed suffix grows by one and stays in the right order. When i passes index 0, k equals the length of the source, the suffix is the whole string, and the buffer is its full reverse. Because nothing is ever written to s, any other code holding a reference to it still sees the original text.

blocks.title: Why the builder keeps it linear
blocks.text: The loop runs once per character, and each append adds one character to the end of the builder, which is amortised constant work. So the reversal costs O(n) time. Space is O(n) because the output is a new string of the same length, which you cannot avoid since the original cannot be changed. Concatenating onto a String with + inside the loop would copy the partial result on every step, 1 + 2 + ... + n characters in total, which is O(n²). For one or two concatenations + is fine. One caution: charAt reads UTF-16 code units, so reversing text with emoji or combined accents can split a character in two.

lessons.body: Think of a coat check. You hand over a coat, get a ticket number, and later the attendant goes straight to the right hook instead of searching every coat. A hash set does that for values: it turns a key into a bucket number, goes to that bucket, and compares only the few keys stored there. A hash map adds a value to each key, such as a count or an earlier index. This turns questions like have I seen this before, or how many times did this appear, from a scan of everything seen so far into one lookup that takes expected constant time. In the animation, notice that two different keys can land in the same bucket. The bucket only narrows the search; an equality check decides whether the key is really there.
lessons.invariant: Before reading position i, seen contains exactly the values at earlier positions.
lessons.pitfall: Do not treat the bucket as the answer. Keys 2 and 6 share a bucket in the trace but are different keys; only equality settles membership. For your own key classes, define equality and hashing together, or equal objects will be stored twice and lookups will miss. And remember the speed is expected, not guaranteed: many colliding keys make lookups slow.

blocks.title: Counting [2, 1, 6, 2, 5]
blocks.text: The trace follows frequencies on [2, 1, 6, 2, 5], using an illustrative bucket rule of key mod 4. Key 2 goes to bucket 2, is not found, and enters with count 1. Key 1 goes to bucket 1 and enters with count 1. Key 6 also lands in bucket 2, but equality shows it is not 2, so it becomes a separate entry: 3 unique keys now. The second 2 goes to bucket 2, matches the existing key, and its count rises to 2 without a new entry. Finally 5 shares bucket 1 with key 1 and enters as the fourth unique key. The map ends with 2 counted twice and 1, 6 and 5 once each. With duplicate, the second 2 is where seen.add returns false and the method returns true.

blocks.title: The table mirrors what came before
blocks.text: Before position i is read, the set or map contains exactly the distinct values from positions before i, and in frequencies each count equals how often that value has appeared so far. It starts empty, which is correct for an empty prefix. Each step either finds the key and updates it, or inserts it, so the statement holds again for the next position. For duplicate this gives a clean proof: seen.add fails exactly when the current value already appeared earlier, so the first false means a repeat, and finishing the loop means every value was new. Correctness also rests on equality and hashing agreeing: equal keys must hash to the same bucket, or a lookup searches the wrong place.

blocks.title: Expected constant, not guaranteed
blocks.text: Each element costs one lookup plus one insert or update. With a good hash function and a table that resizes as it fills, buckets stay short, so each operation takes expected constant time and the whole pass is expected O(n). The worst case is worse: if many keys collide, a bucket grows long and lookups slow down, which is why the bound says expected. Space is O(n) because, when all values are distinct, every one gets an entry. Compare the alternatives. Checking each value against all earlier ones is O(n²) with no extra memory, and sorting first is O(n log n) and puts repeats next to each other. Use a LinkedHashMap, as frequencies does, when you also need the insertion order back.

lessons.body: Imagine a long road with a milestone at every kilometre, each showing the distance from the start. To find the length of any stretch you do not walk it: you read two milestones and subtract. A prefix-sum table puts those milestones on an array. Entry i holds the total of everything before boundary i, so the sum of any contiguous range is one subtraction. This pays off when you need many range sums from the same data. You pay one pass to build the table, then each question is answered in constant time instead of by adding up the slots again. In the animation, watch the table gain one boundary per step, then watch the query use only two of its entries.
lessons.invariant: prefix[i] equals the sum of the first i values; prefix[0] is zero.
lessons.pitfall: Mixing inclusive and exclusive endpoints causes off-by-one errors. Prefix sums work with negative values; a positive-only shrinking window is a different technique.
lessons.timeComplexity: O(n) build; O(1) per range query

blocks.title: Building [0, 2, 3, 8]
blocks.text: The input is [2, 1, 5]. Boundary 0 stores 0, since nothing has been added yet. Boundary 1 stores 0 + 2 = 2, the sum of the first value. Boundary 2 stores 2 + 1 = 3. Boundary 3 stores 3 + 5 = 8, the sum of the whole array. The table has 4 entries for 3 values, one per boundary. The query asks for the half-open range from 1 to 3, which covers the values 1 and 5. The method reads the entry at the right boundary, 8, and subtracts the entry at the left boundary, 2, giving 6. Check by hand: 1 + 5 is 6.

blocks.title: Each entry sums everything before it
blocks.text: p[i] always equals the sum of the first i values of a, and p[0] is 0 because zero values add to nothing. The loop keeps this true: p[i + 1] is p[i] plus a[i], so it covers exactly one more value. Given that, a range from left to right, including left and excluding right, is the first right values with the first left values taken away. That is p[right] minus p[left], and nothing else is needed. The half-open convention is what keeps the formula clean: the range length is right minus left, and an empty range, where left equals right, correctly sums to 0.

blocks.title: One pass now, constant time later
blocks.text: Building the table touches each value once, so it costs O(n) time, and the table takes O(n) space for its n plus one entries. Each range query then reads two entries and subtracts, which is O(1) however wide the range is. For a single query this is no win, since summing the range directly is also O(n). The payoff comes with many queries: q questions cost O(n + q) instead of up to O(n times q). Prefix sums work with negative values too. They handle updates badly: changing one value forces every later entry to change, so for frequent updates use a Fenwick tree or a segment tree. The entries are long so that sums of many values do not overflow.

lessons.body: Think of reading a sentence through a stretchable frame that must never show the same letter twice. You keep pulling the right edge forward to see more. When a new letter would repeat one already inside, you slide the left edge forward until the old copy drops out, then carry on. Each edge only ever moves right. That one-way movement is what makes the technique fast: instead of checking every substring, you find the longest valid one in a single sweep. Unlike a fixed window, the width here changes. In the animation, watch left jump forward in a burst when a repeat arrives, and notice that the frame may have to drop more than one character before it is valid again.
lessons.invariant: After shrinking, all characters in the current frame are distinct.
lessons.pitfall: Writing if instead of while removes only one character per repeat. On "abba" the buggy version leaves the frame bb after the second b, then lets a in and reports 3, while the correct answer is 2. Test any window code on an input where the repeated character is not the leftmost one.

blocks.title: Why "abba" needs a loop
blocks.text: Take "abba". With right at 0 the frame is a and best becomes 1. With right at 1 the frame is ab and best becomes 2. At right 2 the incoming b is already inside. Removing the leftmost character, a, moves left to 1, but the old b is still there, so shrinking continues: removing b moves left to 2. Now the frame is the single b at index 2 and best stays 2. At right 3 the incoming a is no longer in the set, because it left during the shrink, so the frame becomes ba from index 2 to 3, length 2. The answer is best = 2. A single if in place of the while would have stopped after removing a and left two b characters in the frame.

blocks.title: Distinct after every shrink
blocks.text: After the while loop ends and incoming is added, window holds exactly the characters from index left through index right, all distinct. The loop runs until incoming is absent, so adding it cannot create a repeat. Why is it safe to drop characters from the left for good? Any frame that starts before the new left and ends at right would contain the repeated character twice, and extending such a frame further right keeps that repeat. So no frame the method skips can be valid and longer than one it measured, and best ends as the true maximum.

blocks.title: Each character enters and leaves once
blocks.text: The right edge moves n times in total, and the left edge moves at most n times across the whole run, since it never moves back. Each move does one set operation in expected constant time, so the total is expected O(n), even though there is a loop inside a loop. Space is O(min(n, alphabet size)) because the set holds only distinct characters: at most the length of the string, and at most the size of the alphabet. A brute-force check of every substring costs O(n²) or more. Use this pattern only when shrinking from the left always helps restore validity. For sums with negative numbers that property fails, and prefix sums with a hash map are the usual alternative.

lessons.body: Picture bookings for a shared meeting room, written as time ranges on a whiteboard in no particular order. To see when the room is actually busy, you would first line the bookings up by start time, then sweep left to right, joining any booking that starts before the current busy block ends. That is interval merging. Sorting is the step that makes it work: once starts are in order, a new interval can only overlap the most recent merged block, so you never look further back. The same sort-then-sweep idea shows up in calendar conflicts and total covered length. In the animation, notice that each interval causes exactly one of two outcomes: extend the last block, or start a new one.
lessons.invariant: Output segments are disjoint and cover exactly the processed input intervals.
lessons.pitfall: For closed intervals [1,2] and [2,3], equality means overlap. Half-open intervals need a different convention. Never mutate caller intervals accidentally while merging.

checkpoint.question: With closed endpoints, do [1,2] and [2,3] merge?
checkpoint.explanation: Both contain 2, so the merged interval is [1,3].

blocks.title: Merging three segments
blocks.text: The input pairs are [1, 3], [2, 6] and [8, 10], so there are 3 intervals. Sorting by start leaves them in the same order, since 1, 2, 8 is already ascending. The output is empty, so [1, 3] is appended and there is 1 merged block. Next, [2, 6] starts at 2, which is not past the block's end of 3, so the two overlap and the block's end grows to the larger end, 6. The count stays at 1 and the block is now [1, 6]. Finally [8, 10] starts at 8, past the end 6, so it is appended as a separate block. The result is [1, 6] and [8, 10]: 2 blocks.

blocks.title: Only the last block can overlap
blocks.text: After each interval is processed, the output blocks are in order, do not overlap, and together cover exactly the intervals seen so far. Sorting is what lets the loop compare only with the last block. Every earlier block ends before the last block starts, and every new interval starts at or after the last block's start, so a new interval cannot reach back to an earlier block. If the new start is at most the last end, the two share at least one point and joining them keeps coverage exact. If the start is greater, there is a real gap, and a new block keeps the output disjoint. Taking the larger of the two ends matters when one interval sits inside another.

blocks.title: Sorting dominates the cost
blocks.text: The sweep visits each interval once and does constant work, so it is O(n). The sort before it is O(n log n), and that term dominates, so the whole method is O(n log n). If the intervals already arrive sorted by start, you can skip the sort and merge in O(n). Space is O(n): mergeIntervals clones every pair so the caller's arrays are not changed, and the output can hold up to n blocks when nothing overlaps. Decide edge cases up front. Touching endpoints such as [1, 2] and [2, 3] merge here because the intervals are closed, while half-open ranges would keep them apart. An empty input returns an empty array.

lessons.body: A matrix is a grid, like a spreadsheet or a seating chart. Every cell has two coordinates: which row it is in and which column. In Java a matrix is an array of row arrays, so a[r][c] means pick row r first, then column c inside it. Grids appear everywhere: images, game boards, distance tables, and the adjacency matrix of a graph. The transpose is a good first exercise because it forces you to keep the two dimensions apart. Rows become columns, so a wide grid turns tall. In the animation, follow one source cell to its new home and notice that its two coordinates trade places, while the row and column counts of the output trade places too.
lessons.invariant: Every copied source cell a[r][c] appears at out[c][r].
lessons.pitfall: Using row count for both dimensions only works for square inputs. Reject ragged rows for this rectangular operation.

for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++) for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++) out[c][r] = a[r][c];

blocks.title: From 2 × 3 to 3 × 2
blocks.text: The input values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 form 2 rows of 3: row 0 is 1, 2, 3 and row 1 is 4, 5, 6. So out is created with 3 rows and 2 columns. The loop walks the source row by row. Cell (0,0) goes to (0,0), (0,1) goes to (1,0) and (0,2) goes to (2,0). The first source row becomes the first output column, which now reads 1, 2, 3 from top to bottom. Then (1,0) goes to (0,1), (1,1) to (1,1) and (1,2) to (2,1), filling column 1 with 4, 5, 6. The result is [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]. Cells on the diagonal, (0,0) and (1,1), keep their coordinates.

blocks.title: Cell (r, c) lands at (c, r)
blocks.text: Every source cell a[r][c] is written to out[c][r], and each output cell receives exactly one source cell. That one rule makes the whole result correct: row r of the input becomes column r of the output, and column c becomes row c. The output shape follows from it. Source row numbers now index output columns, so out needs cols rows and rows columns. The nested loop visits every (r, c) pair once, so no cell is missed or copied twice. The ragged check before the loop guarantees that a[r][c] exists for every r and c the loop will touch.

blocks.title: Every cell is copied once
blocks.text: The nested loop runs cols times for each of rows, and each pass copies one value, so the time is O(rows × columns). You cannot do better, because every cell must move. Space is also O(rows × columns), since the result is a new grid with the same number of cells. A square matrix can be transposed in place by swapping a[r][c] with a[c][r] for the cells above the diagonal, which needs O(1) extra space, but a non-square grid cannot, because its shape changes. Edge cases: zero rows give an empty result, and a ragged input, where rows have different lengths, is rejected with an exception instead of producing a wrong grid.

lessons.body: A graph is a set of things and the connections between them: cities and roads, people and friendships, web pages and links. The things are vertices and the connections are edges. Before any search can run, you need to store the connections so that you can quickly ask what is next to this vertex. An adjacency list gives each vertex its own row listing where its edges lead. It is like one contacts page per person: you open a page and see only that person's links, not the whole network. In the animation, watch the rows get created first, one per vertex even if nothing connects to it, and then watch each edge drop its endpoint into the row of the vertex it leaves from.

lessons.pitfall: Forgetting isolated vertices changes n. A matrix costs O(V²) storage, while a list stores O(V+E). Parallel edges and self loops require an explicit policy.

blocks.title: Four rows, three edges
blocks.text: The trace uses 4 vertices and the edges 0 to 1, 0 to 2 and 2 to 3. First, adjacency creates 4 empty rows, numbered 0 to 3, before reading any edge, so a vertex with no edges still has a row. Edge 0 to 1 adds 1 to row 0. Edge 0 to 2 adds 2 to row 0, which now reads [1, 2]. Edge 2 to 3 adds 3 to row 2. After 3 edges the graph is [[1, 2], [], [3], []]. Rows 1 and 3 stay empty: those vertices have no outgoing edges, even though edges point into them. Because the edges are directed, asking for the neighbours of 1 returns nothing, not 0.

blocks.title: Each edge lands in one row
blocks.text: Every edge u to v that has been read appears as v in row u, once, and nowhere else. The rows are created for all n vertices before any edge is read, so every valid u has a row waiting. The validity check rejects an edge whose endpoint is outside 0 to n minus one, so a bad edge cannot slip into the wrong row or cause a crash later. With this property, the neighbours of u are exactly row u, which is what BFS and DFS rely on. For an undirected graph, add each edge twice, u to v and v to u. Repeated edges and self loops are kept as given, so decide whether your problem allows them.

blocks.title: Lists versus a matrix
blocks.text: Building takes O(V+E) time: one pass creates V rows and a second pass appends each of the E edges in amortised constant time. Space is O(V+E) for the same reason, one row per vertex plus one entry per edge. An adjacency matrix uses V × V cells, so it costs O(V²) space even when there are few edges, but it answers whether an edge u to v exists in O(1). Lists are the usual choice for sparse graphs, where E is far smaller than V², and they let you loop over a vertex's neighbours in time proportional to how many it has. When vertex names are strings rather than 0 to n minus one, map each name to an index first with a hash map.

problems.title: Silent sensors
problems.description: Count readings equal to zero.
problems.constraints: One nonempty line of 1–1000 integers, each between -10000 and 10000.
problems.inputFormat: Read the sequence until end of input; there is no leading length.
problems.outputFormat: Print the requested result. Separate sequence elements with spaces.
problems.editorial: Walk through the readings once, keeping a counter of how many equal zero. The invariant is simple: after looking at the first i readings, the counter holds exactly the number of zeros among them, so after the last reading it holds the answer. Each reading is inspected once, so the time is O(n) and, apart from storing the input, the extra space is O(1). There is nothing to sort or remember. Edge cases: a sequence with no zeros at all prints 0 (not an empty line), a single reading of 0 prints 1, and a run where every reading is zero prints n. Negative readings are never zero, however close to it.
hints: Only one property of each reading matters here: whether it is exactly zero. Its sign and size are irrelevant.
Keep a single running counter. Each reading either adds one to it or leaves it unchanged.
Scan the readings once and increment the counter on every value equal to 0. Negative numbers are not zero, and a line with no zeros must still print 0.

problems.title: Reverse route
problems.description: Print the readings in reverse input order.
problems.constraints: One nonempty line of 1–1000 integers, each between -10000 and 10000.
problems.inputFormat: Read the sequence until end of input; there is no leading length.
problems.outputFormat: Print the requested result. Separate sequence elements with spaces.
problems.editorial: Read every token, then output them from the last index down to the first. This is the stack idea in its simplest form: the first item in is the last item out. Correctness is direct, since position i of the output holds input position n-1-i, which is exactly the reversed order. The tokens never need to be parsed as numbers because reversing does not depend on their values, so printing them unchanged keeps signs such as -10000 intact. Time is O(n) for one pass and space is O(n) for the stored list (an in-place two-pointer swap would also work). Edge cases: a single reading prints itself, repeated values stay in their mirrored positions, and the output has no trailing separator.
hints: There is no leading count: every token on the input line is a reading, so read the whole input and split it on whitespace.
The last reading must be printed first. A stack does exactly this: push in input order, pop in reverse order. Walking an array backwards is the same idea.
Iterate the index from the last position down to 0 and join the values with single spaces. A single reading is its own reverse, and negative values must keep their minus sign.

# Walk the list from the back to the front.

problems.description: Print the input in nondecreasing order.
problems.constraints: One nonempty line of 1–1000 integers, each between -10000 and 10000.
problems.inputFormat: Read the sequence until end of input; there is no leading length.
problems.outputFormat: Print the requested result. Separate sequence elements with spaces.
problems.editorial: Read every token, convert it to an integer and sort the list with the language's built-in sort, then print it separated by single spaces. The built-in sort is a comparison sort, so after it finishes every adjacent pair satisfies a[i] <= a[i+1], which is exactly the nondecreasing order requested. It runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space. A hand-written insertion sort (O(n^2)) would also pass for n <= 1000, and because values lie in [-10000, 10000] a counting sort over 20001 buckets would run in linear time. Edge cases: a single value, many duplicates, and negative numbers, which must be compared numerically rather than as strings.
hints: There is no length prefix: every whitespace-separated token on the line is a value, and duplicates and negatives must all be kept.
Nondecreasing order means equal values simply sit next to each other; you only need a comparison sort on whole integers, not on their text.
Parse every token as an integer (so -10 sorts before -9 and 10 after 9), sort once, then print the values joined by single spaces.

problems.constraints: One nonempty line of 1–1000 integers, each between -10000 and 10000.
problems.inputFormat: Read the sequence until end of input; there is no leading length.
problems.outputFormat: Print the requested result. Separate sequence elements with spaces.
problems.editorial: Scan the readings once while keeping a running total. When you reach position i, add a[i] to the total and output it. The invariant is that before processing position i the total equals a[0] + ... + a[i-1], so after adding a[i] it is precisely the prefix sum ending at i. A naive version recomputes each prefix from scratch in O(n^2); the running total makes it O(n) time and O(1) extra space beyond the output. Edge cases: a single value prints itself, all-negative input produces a strictly decreasing sequence, and zeros repeat the previous total. With at most 1000 values of magnitude 10000 the totals stay well within normal integer range.
hints: Each output value depends only on the values up to and including the same position, so you can produce the answer while scanning left to right.
Keep one running total. After adding the current value, that total is exactly the prefix sum for this position.
Add first, then print, so the first output equals the first input. Negative values simply pull the total down; it can dip below zero and come back.

    prefix.append(running)

problems.editorial: Insert every reading into a hash set and print the size of the set. A set stores each value at most once, so the invariant after processing i readings is that the set contains exactly the distinct values among them. Insertion is expected O(1), giving O(n) expected time and O(n) space. A slower but equally valid alternative is to sort the readings and count positions where a value differs from its predecessor, which costs O(n log n) time and no hashing. Edge cases: a single reading gives 1, all-equal readings give 1, and a value and its negation (for example 10000 and -10000) are counted separately.

references.python:
import sys


def sort_and_count(a):
    """Return (sorted copy of a, number of pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j])."""
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a, 0
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, left_count = sort_and_count(a[:mid])
    right, right_count = sort_and_count(a[mid:])
    merged = []
    count = left_count + right_count
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            merged.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            # right[j] is smaller than every remaining left value
            count += len(left) - i
            merged.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    merged.extend(left[i:])
    merged.extend(right[j:])
    return merged, count


values = [int(x) for x in sys.stdin.read().split()]
print(sort_and_count(values)[1])

import sys
a = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
nodes = []
for value in a:
    if not nodes:
        nodes.append([value, None, None])
        continue
    at = 0
    while nodes[at][0] != value:
        side = 1 if value < nodes[at][0] else 2
        if nodes[at][side] is None:
            nodes[at][side] = len(nodes)
            nodes.append([value, None, None])
            break
        at = nodes[at][side]
stack = [(0, 1)]
height = 0
while stack:
    at, depth = stack.pop()
    height = max(height, depth)
    for child in nodes[at][1:]:
        if child is not None:
            stack.append((child, depth + 1))
print(height)

        parent[v] = parent[parent[v]]  # path halving keeps trees shallow

Count in-degrees, put every vertex with in-degree 0 in a min-heap, then repeatedly remove the smallest, append it to the order and decrement the in-degree of each successor, pushing those that reach 0. Greedy choice is safe: the smallest ready vertex can go first in some valid order, and putting any larger vertex first would make the sequence lexicographically bigger. If the order ends with fewer than n vertices, the rest lie on or behind a cycle, so print CYCLE. Time is O((n + m) log n) and space O(n + m). import sys
import heapq

numbers = [int(token) for token in sys.stdin.read().split()]
n = numbers[0]
graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
indegree = [0] * n
for i in range(2, len(numbers), 2):
    u, v = numbers[i], numbers[i + 1]
    graph[u].append(v)  # parallel edges are kept, so they are also removed one at a time
    indegree[v] += 1

ready = [v for v in range(n) if indegree[v] == 0]
heapq.heapify(ready)
order = []
while ready:
    u = heapq.heappop(ready)  # always take the smallest available vertex
    order.append(u)
    for v in graph[u]:
        indegree[v] -= 1
        if indegree[v] == 0:
            heapq.heappush(ready, v)

if len(order) != n:
    print('CYCLE')
else:
    print(' '.join(str(v) for v in order))

problems.title: Outgoing links
problems.description: The input begins n m, followed by m directed edges u v. Print each vertex’s outdegree in vertex order.
problems.constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 100; 0 ≤ m ≤ 1000; vertex identifiers are 0..n-1. Self loops and parallel edges are allowed.
problems.inputFormat: Read one line.
problems.outputFormat: Print the requested result. Separate sequence elements with spaces.
problems.editorial: Create an array of n zeros. For each directed edge u v, increment the counter for u. Then print the counters in vertex order. This is correct because the outdegree of a vertex is by definition the number of edges whose source is that vertex, and every edge is visited once. Building a full adjacency list first and taking list sizes also works but uses more memory than needed. Time is O(n + m) and space O(n). Edge cases: m = 0 prints all zeros, a self loop u u counts once toward u, parallel edges are each counted, and vertices with no outgoing edges still appear in the output.
hints: Outdegree counts edges leaving a vertex, so for each edge u v only u matters.
One counter per vertex is enough: no adjacency list is needed to answer this question.
Read n, skip m, then step through the edge pairs adding one to the source counter. Self loops count once for their vertex, parallel edges count every time, and isolated vertices print 0.

references.python:
import sys

numbers = [int(x) for x in sys.stdin.read().split()]
n = numbers[0]
outdegree = [0] * n
# edges start at index 2 and come in (u, v) pairs; only the source u matters
for u in numbers[2::2]:
    outdegree[u] += 1
print(" ".join(map(str, outdegree)))

guides.title: Percentages
guides.summary: Percentages are fractions out of 100, and most questions come down to picking the right base and handling successive changes correctly.

sections.title: What a percentage really is
sections.text:
Per cent means per hundred, so p% is just the fraction p/100. Finding p% of a number N is therefore N × p ÷ 100. For example, 35% of 260 is 260 × 35 ÷ 100 = 91.

It pays to know a few fraction equivalents, because they turn long multiplication into quick division: 50% = 1/2, 25% = 1/4, 20% = 1/5, 12.5% = 1/8, 33.33% = 1/3, 16.67% = 1/6, 11.11% = 1/9 and 9.09% = 1/11. So 12.5% of 64 is simply 64 ÷ 8 = 8.

Percentage change always compares the change with the original value, not the new one:

Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100

If a bus fare goes from ₹240 to ₹282, the change is ₹42 and the increase is 42 ÷ 240 × 100 = 17.5%. Dividing by the new value (282) is the most common slip, and it gives a wrong answer of about 14.9%.

sections.title: Comparing two quantities
sections.text:
Questions often say 'A is r% more than B' and then ask how much less B is than A. The two answers are not equal, because each percentage is measured against a different base.

If A is r% more than B, then B is less than A by r ÷ (100 + r) × 100 percent.
If A is r% less than B, then B is more than A by r ÷ (100 − r) × 100 percent.

Picture it with numbers. If X earns 60% more than Y, let Y earn 100, so X earns 160. The gap is 60, but measured against X's 160 it is only 37.5%. Y earns 37.5% less than X, not 60% less.

The same idea answers price and consumption questions. If the price of an item rises by r% and a family wants its total spending to stay the same, it must cut consumption by r ÷ (100 + r) × 100 percent. If the price falls by r%, it can raise consumption by r ÷ (100 − r) × 100 percent and still spend the same amount.

sections.title: Successive changes and percentage points
sections.text:
When a value changes by a% and then by b%, you cannot just add the two. The second change acts on the already changed value. The net effect is

Net change = a + b + (a × b) ÷ 100 percent

Use a negative sign for a decrease. A rise of 12% followed by a rise of 25% is 12 + 25 + 300 ÷ 100 = 40%, not 37%. A useful special case: a rise of x% followed by a fall of x% (in either order) always leaves a net fall of x² ÷ 100 percent. The value never returns to where it started.

Be careful when the quantity being changed is itself a percentage, such as an interest rate or a pass rate. If a rate moves from 6% to 9%, it has risen by 3 percentage points, but by 3 ÷ 6 × 100 = 50 percent. Both statements are true; they simply measure different things. Read the question to see which one it wants, and do not mix them up in the options.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. A phone costs ₹18,400. Its price is raised by 15% and later the new price is cut by 15%. Find the final price and the net percentage change.

Step 1: After the rise, price = 18,400 × 115 ÷ 100 = ₹21,160.
Step 2: The cut is 15% of 21,160, which is ₹3,174, so the final price = 21,160 − 3,174 = ₹17,986.
Step 3: Net change = (17,986 − 18,400) ÷ 18,400 × 100 = −414 ÷ 18,400 × 100 = −2.25%.
Shortcut check: 15 − 15 + (15 × −15) ÷ 100 = −2.25%, so the price does not return to where it started.

Example 2. The price of rice rises by 28%. By what percentage must a household reduce its consumption to keep its monthly spending on rice unchanged?

Step 1: Required cut = r ÷ (100 + r) × 100 = 28 ÷ 128 × 100 = 21.875%.
Step 2: Check with figures. 40 kg at ₹50 per kg costs ₹2,000. The new price is 50 × 1.28 = ₹64 per kg.
Step 3: ₹2,000 now buys 2,000 ÷ 64 = 31.25 kg, a drop of 8.75 kg, and 8.75 ÷ 40 × 100 = 21.875%. Both methods agree.

keyPoints: p% of N is N × p ÷ 100; learn the common fraction equivalents such as 12.5% = 1/8.
Percentage change is always measured against the original value.
If A is r% more than B, B is r ÷ (100 + r) × 100 percent less than A.
Successive changes combine as a + b + ab ÷ 100, never by simple addition.
A change from 6% to 9% is 3 percentage points but a 50 percent increase.

challenges.title: Two years of growth
challenges.prompt: A town has 48,000 residents. Its population grows by 15% in the first year and by 25% in the second year. What is the population after two years?
challenges.explanation: 48,000 × 1.15 = 55,200, then 55,200 × 1.25 = 69,000. The net change is 15 + 25 + (15 × 25) ÷ 100 = 43.75%. Adding the rates to get 40% gives 67,200, which ignores that the second year's growth acts on the larger population.
challenges.hint: The second year's growth is calculated on the population at the end of the first year.

challenges.title: Less than by how much
challenges.prompt: A delivery van carries 40% more parcels a day than a scooter rider. By what percentage does the scooter rider carry fewer parcels than the van?
challenges.explanation: Let the rider carry 100 parcels, so the van carries 140. The gap of 40 is measured against the van's 140: 40 ÷ 140 × 100 ≈ 28.57%. Answering 40% uses the rider's load as the base, but this question compares against the van. 71.43% is the rider's load as a percentage of the van's (100 ÷ 140), not how much smaller it is.
challenges.hint: Ask whose load the comparison is measured against.

challenges.title: Points versus percent
challenges.prompt: A college's placement rate climbs from 55% one year to 66% the next. By what percentage has the placement rate increased?
challenges.explanation: The rate rose by 11 percentage points. As a percentage of the old rate, that is 11 ÷ 55 × 100 = 20%. Answering 11% confuses percentage points with percent, and 16.67% divides by the new rate (11 ÷ 66) instead of the old one.
challenges.hint: Percentage change is always measured against the starting value.

challenges.title: Down then up
challenges.prompt: The price of a jacket is reduced by 30%, and the reduced price is then increased by 40%. What is the net effect on the original price?
challenges.explanation: Net change = −30 + 40 + (−30 × 40) ÷ 100 = 10 − 12 = −2%. On ₹100: 100 → 70 → 70 × 1.4 = 98, a 2% decrease. Saying 10% increase just adds the two rates and forgets that the 40% acts on the smaller, reduced price.
challenges.hint: Try it on a starting price of ₹100.

challenges.title: Finding the income
challenges.prompt: A person spends 35% of monthly income on rent and 40% of what remains on food. If ₹11,700 is left after both, what is the monthly income?
challenges.explanation: After rent, 65% of the income remains. Food takes 40% of that, leaving 60% of 65% = 39% of the income. So income = 11,700 ÷ 0.39 = ₹30,000. Adding 35% and 40% to get 75% spent (25% left) gives ₹46,800, but the 40% is a share of the remainder, not of the full income.
challenges.hint: Work out what fraction of the whole income is left, one step at a time.

guides.title: Profit and loss
guides.summary: Profit and loss questions turn on one rule: gain and loss percentages are measured on the cost price, while discounts are measured on the marked price.

sections.title: Cost price, selling price and the base
sections.text:
The cost price (CP) is what the seller paid. The selling price (SP) is what the buyer pays. If SP is higher, the difference is profit; if it is lower, the difference is a loss.

Profit = SP − CP and Loss = CP − SP
Profit% = Profit ÷ CP × 100 and Loss% = Loss ÷ CP × 100

The base is always the cost price unless a question clearly says otherwise. That single fact settles most traps.

Rearranged forms save time:

SP = CP × (100 + p) ÷ 100 for a gain of p%
SP = CP × (100 − l) ÷ 100 for a loss of l%
CP = SP × 100 ÷ (100 + p) when you know SP and the gain

For instance, an item bought for ₹1,600 and sold at a 12.5% gain fetches 1,600 × 112.5 ÷ 100 = ₹1,800. If instead an item sold for ₹1,380 at a 15% gain, its cost was 1,380 × 100 ÷ 115 = ₹1,200. Taking 15% off ₹1,380 gives ₹1,173, which is wrong because the 15% was calculated on CP, not on SP.

sections.title: Marked price and discounts
sections.text:
Shops often print a marked price (MP), also called the list price, and then offer a discount on it. A discount is always a percentage of MP:

SP = MP × (100 − d) ÷ 100

Two discounts in a row do not add. After the first discount, the second is taken on a smaller price, so the single equivalent discount is

Equivalent discount = d1 + d2 − (d1 × d2) ÷ 100

For example, discounts of 10% and 30% equal 10 + 30 − 3 = 37%, not 40%. The order of the two discounts makes no difference.

When a trader marks goods m% above cost and then allows a d% discount, the overall profit percentage is

Profit% = m − d − (m × d) ÷ 100

This is the successive-percentage rule from the percentages guide with the discount written as a negative change. Marking up by 50% and then giving 20% off leaves 50 − 20 − 10 = 20% profit. If the result is negative, the trader has made a loss.

sections.title: Three classic traps
sections.text:
Same selling price, equal gain and loss. If two articles are each sold for the same price, one at x% profit and the other at x% loss, the seller always makes an overall loss of x² ÷ 100 percent. The loss happens because the article sold at a loss had a higher cost price, so its loss in rupees outweighs the other article's profit. The common selling price does not affect the percentage.

False weights. A dealer who claims to sell at cost but hands over less than the stated weight gains on every sale:

Gain% = (true weight − weight given) ÷ weight given × 100

The denominator is the weight actually given, because that is what the dealer really paid for. A dealer who gives 950 g for every kilogram gains 50 ÷ 950 × 100 ≈ 5.26%, not 5%.

Articles for the price of others. If the cost price of a articles equals the selling price of b articles, the result is (a − b) ÷ b × 100 percent. A positive answer is a gain and a negative one is a loss.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. A shopkeeper buys a lamp for ₹1,250, marks it 40% above cost and then offers a 15% discount. Find the selling price and the profit percentage.

Step 1: Marked price = 1,250 × 140 ÷ 100 = ₹1,750.
Step 2: Discount = 15% of 1,750 = ₹262.50, so SP = 1,750 − 262.50 = ₹1,487.50.
Step 3: Profit = 1,487.50 − 1,250 = ₹237.50, and profit% = 237.50 ÷ 1,250 × 100 = 19%.
Shortcut check: m − d − md ÷ 100 = 40 − 15 − 6 = 19%.

Example 2. A trader sells two used bicycles for ₹9,240 each. On one he gains 12% and on the other he loses 12%. Find his overall gain or loss.

Step 1: CP of the first = 9,240 × 100 ÷ 112 = ₹8,250.
Step 2: CP of the second = 9,240 × 100 ÷ 88 = ₹10,500.
Step 3: Total CP = 8,250 + 10,500 = ₹18,750. Total SP = 2 × 9,240 = ₹18,480.
Step 4: Loss = 18,750 − 18,480 = ₹270, and loss% = 270 ÷ 18,750 × 100 = 1.44%.
Shortcut check: x² ÷ 100 = 144 ÷ 100 = 1.44% loss. The gain and the loss do not cancel.

keyPoints: Profit and loss percentages are calculated on the cost price.
Discounts are calculated on the marked price.
Two discounts d1 and d2 equal one discount of d1 + d2 − d1d2 ÷ 100.
Equal gain and loss of x% on the same selling price always means a net loss of x² ÷ 100 percent.
With false weights, divide the shortfall by the weight actually given.

challenges.title: Profit on cost
challenges.prompt: A trader buys a chair for ₹840 and sells it for ₹966. What is the profit percentage?
challenges.explanation: Profit = 966 − 840 = ₹126. Profit% = 126 ÷ 840 × 100 = 15%. The option 13.04% divides by the selling price (126 ÷ 966), but profit percent is measured on the cost price.
challenges.hint: Decide which price is the base for a profit percentage.

challenges.title: From loss to gain
challenges.prompt: Selling a mixer for ₹2,412 causes a 10% loss. At what price should it be sold to make a 15% profit?
challenges.explanation: First recover the cost: CP = 2,412 × 100 ÷ 90 = ₹2,680. Then SP for a 15% gain = 2,680 × 115 ÷ 100 = ₹3,082. ₹3,015 adds 25% to ₹2,412, and ₹2,773.80 adds 15% to ₹2,412; both treat the old selling price as the base, but both percentages belong to the cost price.
challenges.hint: Find the cost price before applying the new percentage.

challenges.title: Two discounts
challenges.prompt: A store offers a 25% discount followed by a further 12% discount on the reduced price. What single discount is equivalent?
challenges.explanation: Equivalent discount = 25 + 12 − (25 × 12) ÷ 100 = 37 − 3 = 34%. Check on ₹100: 100 → 75 → 75 × 0.88 = 66, which is 34% off. Answering 37% adds the discounts, but the 12% is taken on ₹75, not on ₹100.
challenges.hint: Apply both discounts, one after the other, to a ₹100 item.

challenges.title: Light weights
challenges.prompt: A dealer claims to sell rice at cost price but gives only 920 g when a customer pays for 1 kg. What is his gain percentage?
challenges.explanation: He pays for 920 g and charges for 1,000 g. Gain% = (1,000 − 920) ÷ 920 × 100 = 80 ÷ 920 × 100 ≈ 8.70%. The option 8% divides by 1,000, but the gain must be compared with what the dealer actually spent, which is the cost of 920 g.
challenges.hint: The base is the quantity the dealer actually hands over.

challenges.title: Same price, equal rates
challenges.prompt: Two lamps are sold for ₹7,820 each. One is sold at a 15% profit and the other at a 15% loss. What is the overall result?
challenges.explanation: CP of the first = 7,820 × 100 ÷ 115 = ₹6,800 and CP of the second = 7,820 × 100 ÷ 85 = ₹9,200. Total CP = ₹16,000 and total SP = ₹15,640, a loss of ₹360, which is 360 ÷ 16,000 × 100 = 2.25%. Shortcut: 15² ÷ 100 = 2.25% loss. Assuming no profit, no loss ignores that the lamp sold at a loss cost more to begin with.
challenges.hint: Find each lamp's cost price separately before comparing totals.

guides.title: Ratio and proportion
guides.summary: A ratio compares quantities by division, and most questions reduce to finding the value of one part and scaling it.

sections.title: Ratios as parts
sections.text:
A ratio a : b says that for every a units of the first quantity there are b units of the second. It is a comparison, not an amount, so 6 : 9, 2 : 3 and 20 : 30 are the same ratio. Simplify by dividing both terms by their HCF, after putting both quantities in the same unit: 40 minutes to 2 hours is 40 : 120, which is 1 : 3, not 40 : 2.

Think of a ratio in parts. If ₹4,500 is split in the ratio 4 : 5, there are 9 parts in all. One part is 4,500 ÷ 9 = ₹500, so the shares are ₹2,000 and ₹2,500.

To combine two ratios that share a term, make the shared term equal. Given A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, B is 3 in one and 4 in the other. Scale both to 12: A : B = 8 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 15, so A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15. A quick route is A : B : C = (2 × 4) : (3 × 4) : (3 × 5).

sections.title: Proportion and its special terms
sections.text:
Four numbers a, b, c and d are in proportion when a : b = c : d, written a : b :: c : d. The key property is that the product of the outer terms equals the product of the inner terms:

a × d = b × c

Cross-multiplying in this way gives three named terms that come up often.

Fourth proportional to a, b and c: the d with a : b = c : d, so d = (b × c) ÷ a.
Third proportional to a and b: the c with a : b = b : c, so c = b² ÷ a.
Mean proportional between a and b: the x with a : x = x : b, so x = √(a × b).

For example, the third proportional to 4 and 10 is 100 ÷ 4 = 25, because 4 : 10 = 10 : 25. The mean proportional between 8 and 18 is √144 = 12, because 8 : 12 = 12 : 18. Note that the mean proportional is a geometric mean, not the ordinary average. For 8 and 18 the ordinary average would be 13, and 8 : 13 is not equal to 13 : 18.

sections.title: Partnership and changing ratios
sections.text:
In a business partnership, profit is shared in proportion to each partner's capital multiplied by the time it was invested:

Share ratio = (capital of A × months of A) : (capital of B × months of B)

If one partner puts in ₹20,000 for a full year and another puts in ₹30,000 but joins after four months, the ratio (working in thousands) is 20 × 12 : 30 × 8 = 240 : 240, or 1 : 1. Using the capital alone, 2 : 3, is a common mistake.

Another frequent pattern adds or subtracts the same number from both terms of a ratio. Write the original quantities as ax and bx, apply the change, set the result equal to the new ratio and cross-multiply to find x.

There is a built-in sanity check. Adding the same positive number to both terms always moves a ratio towards 1 : 1. So a ratio below 1 should rise and a ratio above 1 should fall. If your answer moves the other way, recheck the algebra.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. A : B = 3 : 5 and B : C = 4 : 7. Divide ₹6,030 among A, B and C in this combined ratio.

Step 1: Make B equal to 20 in both: A : B = 12 : 20 and B : C = 20 : 35, so A : B : C = 12 : 20 : 35.
Step 2: That is 12 + 20 + 35 = 67 parts, and one part = 6,030 ÷ 67 = ₹90.
Step 3: A = 12 × 90 = ₹1,080, B = 20 × 90 = ₹1,800 and C = 35 × 90 = ₹3,150, which total ₹6,030.

Example 2. Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 8. If 9 is added to each, the ratio becomes 2 : 3. Find the numbers.

Step 1: Let the numbers be 5x and 8x, so (5x + 9) ÷ (8x + 9) = 2 ÷ 3.
Step 2: Cross-multiply: 3(5x + 9) = 2(8x + 9), so 15x + 27 = 16x + 18.
Step 3: x = 27 − 18 = 9, so the numbers are 45 and 72.
Check: 54 : 81 = 2 : 3, and the ratio rose towards 1, as expected.

keyPoints: Think of a ratio as parts: find the value of one part, then scale.
Combine A : B and B : C by making the shared term B equal in both.
In a proportion a : b = c : d, the outer product equals the inner product.
The mean proportional of a and b is √(ab), not their average.
Partnership profit is shared in the ratio of capital × time.

challenges.title: Fourth proportional
challenges.prompt: What is the fourth proportional to 6, 15 and 14?
challenges.explanation: We need d with 6 : 15 = 14 : d. Cross-multiplying, 6d = 15 × 14 = 210, so d = 35. The option 23 treats the ratio as a difference (15 − 6 = 9, then 14 + 9), but proportion is about multiplying, not adding.
challenges.hint: Write the proportion out and cross-multiply.

challenges.title: Mean proportional
challenges.prompt: What is the mean proportional between 12 and 75?
challenges.explanation: The mean proportional x satisfies 12 : x = x : 75, so x² = 12 × 75 = 900 and x = 30. Check: 12 : 30 = 2 : 5 and 30 : 75 = 2 : 5. The option 43.5 is the ordinary average of 12 and 75, which does not keep the two ratios equal.
challenges.hint: The middle term multiplied by itself equals the product of the outer two.

challenges.title: Capital and time
challenges.prompt: P invests ₹40,000 for 12 months and Q invests ₹60,000 for 7 months. Out of a total profit of ₹27,000, what is Q's share?
challenges.explanation: Weight each investment by time (in thousands): P = 40 × 12 = 480 and Q = 60 × 7 = 420, so the ratio is 8 : 7. Q's share = 27,000 × 7 ÷ 15 = ₹12,600. ₹16,200 uses capital alone (2 : 3) and forgets that Q's money was in the business for only 7 months; ₹14,400 swaps the two shares.
challenges.hint: Profit shares depend on how much was invested and for how long.

challenges.title: Chain of ratios
challenges.prompt: If A : B = 2 : 3, B : C = 5 : 4 and C : D = 6 : 7, what is A : D?
challenges.explanation: A : D = (A/B) × (B/C) × (C/D) = (2 × 5 × 6) : (3 × 4 × 7) = 60 : 84 = 5 : 7. The option 2 : 7 joins the first term of the first ratio to the last term of the last ratio, ignoring the links in between.
challenges.hint: Multiply the ratios together so that B and C cancel out.

challenges.title: After a raise
challenges.prompt: The monthly salaries of Asha and Bina are in the ratio 4 : 7. If each gets a raise of ₹3,000, the ratio becomes 7 : 11. What was Asha's salary before the raise?
challenges.explanation: Let the salaries be 4x and 7x. Then (4x + 3,000) ÷ (7x + 3,000) = 7 ÷ 11, so 44x + 33,000 = 49x + 21,000, giving 5x = 12,000 and x = 2,400. Asha earned 4 × 2,400 = ₹9,600. Check: 12,600 : 19,800 = 7 : 11. ₹16,800 is Bina's salary, and ₹12,000 is 5x, one step short of the answer.
challenges.hint: Write both salaries in terms of one unknown and cross-multiply.

guides.title: Averages
guides.summary: An average is the total shared out equally, so almost every question is solved by working with totals rather than with the averages directly.

sections.title: Average means total divided by count
sections.text:
The average (arithmetic mean) of a set of values is their sum divided by how many there are:

Average = Sum of values ÷ Number of values, so Sum = Average × Number

The second form is the one that solves problems. Whenever an average changes, convert both the old and the new averages into totals and look at the difference.

A handy shortcut when the numbers are close together is the assumed-mean method. Pick a convenient value near the middle, find how far each value is above or below it, average those deviations and add the result back. For 47, 52, 49, 55 and 51, assume 50. The deviations are −3, +2, −1, +5 and +1, which sum to 4. Their average is 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8, so the average is 50.8.

An average always lies between the smallest and the largest value. If your answer falls outside that range, something has gone wrong.

sections.title: Adding, removing and replacing
sections.text:
When one value joins a group of n and the average changes by c, the newcomer differs from the old average by (n + 1) × c:

New value = old average + (n + 1) × change in average

The logic: the newcomer must bring the old average for itself, plus enough extra to lift each of the n + 1 members by c. If the average falls, c is negative.

When one member leaves a group of n and the average of the rest changes by c, the person who left equals old average − (n − 1) × c.

Replacement is different because the group size stays at n. If one member is swapped for another and the average rises by c, the total rose by n × c, so

New member = member replaced + n × change in average

For example, if replacing a 40 kg child in a group of 6 raises the average by 0.5 kg, the newcomer weighs 40 + 6 × 0.5 = 43 kg. Using n + 1 instead of n here is a frequent slip.

sections.title: Weighted averages and evenly spaced numbers
sections.text:
When groups of different sizes are combined, you cannot simply average their averages. Each group's average must be weighted by its size:

Combined average = (n1 × a1 + n2 × a2) ÷ (n1 + n2)

The combined average always lies between a1 and a2, and closer to the average of the larger group.

For numbers in an arithmetic progression, where each term differs from the previous one by the same amount, the average is simply

Average = (first term + last term) ÷ 2

So the average of all multiples of 4 from 12 to 60 is (12 + 60) ÷ 2 = 36. With an odd count the average is the middle term; with an even count it is the mean of the two middle terms.

Two useful consequences: the average of the first n natural numbers is (n + 1) ÷ 2, and the average of the first n odd numbers is n.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. The average weight of 14 students is 52 kg. When their teacher's weight is included, the average rises by 1.5 kg. Find the teacher's weight.

Step 1: Total for the students = 14 × 52 = 728 kg.
Step 2: The new average is 52 + 1.5 = 53.5 kg across 15 people, so the new total = 15 × 53.5 = 802.5 kg.
Step 3: Teacher's weight = 802.5 − 728 = 74.5 kg.
Shortcut check: old average + (n + 1) × change = 52 + 15 × 1.5 = 74.5 kg.

Example 2. Section A has 32 students with an average score of 68, and Section B has 48 students with an average score of 73. Find the average of all 80 students.

Step 1: Total for A = 32 × 68 = 2,176.
Step 2: Total for B = 48 × 73 = 3,504.
Step 3: Combined average = (2,176 + 3,504) ÷ 80 = 5,680 ÷ 80 = 71.
Check: the simple mean of 68 and 73 is 70.5, but the true answer is pulled towards 73 because Section B is the larger group.

keyPoints: Turn averages into totals: Sum = Average × Number.
A newcomer who shifts the average by c differs from the old average by (n + 1) × c.
In a replacement the group size stays n, so the total changes by n × c.
Combine groups with a weighted average, never by averaging the averages.
For evenly spaced numbers, average = (first + last) ÷ 2.

challenges.title: Evenly spaced
challenges.prompt: What is the average of all multiples of 7 from 21 to 98, inclusive?
challenges.explanation: The multiples of 7 form an arithmetic progression, so the average is (21 + 98) ÷ 2 = 119 ÷ 2 = 59.5. Check: there are 12 terms (7 × 3 up to 7 × 14) with a total of 714, and 714 ÷ 12 = 59.5. The option 59 drops the half; the average of evenly spaced whole numbers need not be a whole number.
challenges.hint: For evenly spaced numbers, only the first and last terms matter.

challenges.title: One value swapped
challenges.prompt: The average of 9 numbers is 46. If one of them, 58, is replaced by 31, what is the new average?
challenges.explanation: The total drops by 58 − 31 = 27. Spread over 9 numbers, the average drops by 27 ÷ 9 = 3, giving 46 − 3 = 43. Check: 9 × 46 = 414 and 414 − 27 = 387 = 9 × 43. The option 43.3 divides the drop by 10, but a swap leaves the group at 9 numbers.
challenges.hint: Find how much the total changes, then share that change among the numbers.

challenges.title: A big innings
challenges.prompt: Scoring 126 runs in her 21st match lifts a batter's average by 3 runs. What is her average after the 21st match?
challenges.explanation: Let the average after 20 matches be a. Then 20a + 126 = 21(a + 3), so 20a + 126 = 21a + 63 and a = 63. The new average is 63 + 3 = 66. Check: 20 × 63 = 1,260 and (1,260 + 126) ÷ 21 = 1,386 ÷ 21 = 66. The option 63 is the average before the 21st match, not after it.
challenges.hint: Write the total runs before and after the 21st match using one unknown.

challenges.title: Replacement
challenges.prompt: In a group of 8 workers, one worker weighing 61 kg is replaced by a new worker, and the group's average weight goes up by 2.5 kg. What does the new worker weigh?
challenges.explanation: The group still has 8 people, so the total went up by 8 × 2.5 = 20 kg, and the new worker weighs 61 + 20 = 81 kg. The option 83.5 kg uses 9 × 2.5 = 22.5, which applies only when someone joins without anyone leaving; 63.5 kg adds the change in average just once.
challenges.hint: The number of people stays the same, but the total does not.

challenges.title: The middle number
challenges.prompt: The average of 21 numbers is 32. The average of the first 11 is 30 and the average of the last 11 is 36. What is the 11th number?
challenges.explanation: The first 11 total 11 × 30 = 330 and the last 11 total 11 × 36 = 396. Together that is 726, but the 11th number is counted in both groups. All 21 numbers total 21 × 32 = 672, so the 11th number = 726 − 672 = 54. The option 33 is just the mean of 30 and 36, which ignores the totals.
challenges.hint: Add the two partial totals and compare them with the overall total.

guides.title: Simple and compound interest
guides.summary: Simple interest adds the same amount every year, while compound interest earns interest on interest, and the gap between them follows neat formulas.

sections.title: Simple interest
sections.text:
Under simple interest (SI), interest is calculated only on the original principal, so the same amount is added every year.

SI = P × R × T ÷ 100 and Amount A = P + SI

Here P is the principal in rupees, R is the rate per cent per annum and T is the time in years. If time is given in months, divide by 12: 9 months is 0.75 years.

Rearranging gives the other unknowns: P = SI × 100 ÷ (R × T), R = SI × 100 ÷ (P × T) and T = SI × 100 ÷ (P × R).

Because SI grows by a fixed amount each year, two amounts at different times reveal it directly. If a sum grows to ₹5,600 in 2 years and to ₹6,200 in 4 years, the yearly interest is (6,200 − 5,600) ÷ 2 = ₹300. Working backwards, P = 5,600 − 2 × 300 = ₹5,000, and the rate is 300 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 6%.

A sum doubles under SI when the total interest equals P, that is, when R × T = 100.

sections.title: Compound interest
sections.text:
Under compound interest (CI), each year's interest is added to the principal and itself earns interest in later years.

A = P × (1 + R ÷ 100)^T and CI = A − P

The growth factor (1 + R ÷ 100) is the same multiplier used for successive percentage increases. Over two years the effective rate is 2R + R² ÷ 100 percent, which is exactly the a + b + ab ÷ 100 rule with a = b = R. At 10% per annum, two years of compounding give 21%, not 20%.

When interest is compounded more often than once a year, divide the rate and multiply the number of periods:

Half-yearly: rate R ÷ 2 per half-year, for 2T periods.
Quarterly: rate R ÷ 4 per quarter, for 4T periods.

So 12% per annum compounded quarterly for one year means 3% per quarter for 4 quarters, a factor of 1.03⁴ ≈ 1.1255, slightly better than 12%.

If the rate differs from year to year, multiply the separate factors: 5% and then 8% gives 1.05 × 1.08 = 1.134.

sections.title: CI minus SI, and growth patterns
sections.text:
For the same principal, rate and whole number of years, compound interest is never less than simple interest. With yearly compounding the two are equal for the first year, and after that the gap has closed forms:

For 2 years: CI − SI = P × (R ÷ 100)²
For 3 years: CI − SI = P × (R ÷ 100)² × (3 + R ÷ 100)

The 2-year gap is simply the interest earned in year two on year one's interest.

Compound growth also follows a multiplying pattern. If a sum doubles in n years at a fixed compound rate, it becomes 4 times in 2n years and 8 times in 3n years, because each block of n years multiplies the money by 2 again. Simple interest behaves differently: if a sum doubles in n years under SI, it becomes 3 times in 2n years and 4 times in 3n years, since only the original principal earns interest.

Finally, when compound amounts are given for two consecutive years, the rate comes from their ratio: A2 ÷ A1 = 1 + R ÷ 100.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. Find the simple interest and the amount on ₹18,500 at 7.5% per annum for 4 years.

Step 1: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100 = 18,500 × 7.5 × 4 ÷ 100.
Step 2: R × T = 7.5 × 4 = 30, so SI = 18,500 × 30 ÷ 100 = ₹5,550.
Step 3: Amount = 18,500 + 5,550 = ₹24,050.

Example 2. Find the compound interest on ₹25,000 at 8% per annum, compounded annually, for 3 years, and compare it with the simple interest.

Step 1: The growth factor is 1.08, so A = 25,000 × 1.08³.
Step 2: Year by year: 25,000 × 1.08 = 27,000; 27,000 × 1.08 = 29,160; 29,160 × 1.08 = 31,492.80.
Step 3: CI = 31,492.80 − 25,000 = ₹6,492.80.
Step 4: SI on the same terms = 25,000 × 8 × 3 ÷ 100 = ₹6,000, so CI − SI = ₹492.80.
Shortcut check: P × (R ÷ 100)² × (3 + R ÷ 100) = 25,000 × 0.0064 × 3.08 = 492.80.

keyPoints: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, and it adds the same amount every year.
Compound amount A = P × (1 + R ÷ 100)^T.
For half-yearly compounding, halve the rate and double the number of periods.
For 2 years, CI − SI = P × (R ÷ 100)².
Under CI, if money doubles in n years it becomes 8 times in 3n years.

challenges.title: Two amounts at simple interest
challenges.prompt: At simple interest, a sum grows to ₹15,200 in 3 years and to ₹16,800 in 5 years. What is the principal?
challenges.explanation: The extra 2 years add 16,800 − 15,200 = ₹1,600, so SI is ₹800 a year. Three years of interest is ₹2,400, so P = 15,200 − 2,400 = ₹12,800 (and the rate is 800 ÷ 12,800 × 100 = 6.25%). ₹11,200 subtracts 5 years of interest from the 3-year amount.
challenges.hint: Use the difference between the two amounts to find one year's interest.

challenges.title: The two-year gap
challenges.prompt: What is the difference between compound interest and simple interest on ₹15,000 at 12% per annum for 2 years, compounded annually?
challenges.explanation: CI − SI for 2 years = P × (R ÷ 100)² = 15,000 × 0.12 × 0.12 = ₹216. Directly: A = 15,000 × 1.12² = 18,816, so CI = 3,816, while SI = 15,000 × 12 × 2 ÷ 100 = 3,600, and 3,816 − 3,600 = 216. ₹3,600 is the simple interest itself, not the difference.
challenges.hint: The gap comes only from interest earned on the first year's interest.

challenges.title: Half-yearly compounding
challenges.prompt: What is the compound interest on ₹20,000 at 10% per annum for 1 year, compounded half-yearly?
challenges.explanation: Half-yearly means 5% per half-year for 2 half-years. A = 20,000 × 1.05² = 20,000 × 1.1025 = ₹22,050, so CI = ₹2,050. ₹2,000 compounds only once in the year, which for a single year is the same as simple interest.
challenges.hint: Halve the rate and double the number of periods.

challenges.title: From double to eight times
challenges.prompt: An investment earning a fixed rate of compound interest is worth 3 times its starting value after 4 years. After how many years will it be worth 81 times its starting value?
challenges.explanation: Each 4-year block multiplies the money by 3. Eighty-one times is 3 × 3 × 3 × 3, so it takes four blocks: 4 × 4 = 16 years. 108 years scales the time in proportion to the multiple (81 ÷ 3 × 4), and 160 years is the simple-interest answer (80 lots of P at 2P per 4 years); 12 years reaches only 27 times.
challenges.hint: Ask what each 4-year block does to the money.

challenges.title: Finding the rate
challenges.prompt: ₹6,250 grows to ₹7,290 in 2 years at compound interest, compounded annually. What is the rate per annum?
challenges.explanation: 7,290 ÷ 6,250 = 1.1664 = 1.08², so 1 + R ÷ 100 = 1.08 and R = 8%. Check: 6,250 × 1.08 = 6,750 and 6,750 × 1.08 = 7,290. The option 8.32% treats the gain as simple interest (1,040 ÷ 6,250 ÷ 2 × 100), which overstates the rate because it ignores interest on interest.
challenges.hint: Divide the amount by the principal and look for a perfect square.

guides.title: Time and work
guides.summary: Time and work problems become simple once you think in terms of work done per day and give the whole job a convenient number of units.

sections.title: Work as a rate
sections.text:
If a person can finish a job in n days, they do 1/n of it each day. When people work together their rates add; their times do not:

If A takes a days and B takes b days, together they do 1/a + 1/b of the job per day, and the time together = (a × b) ÷ (a + b) days.

Fractions get messy with three or more workers, so a cleaner method is to set the total work equal to the LCM of the individual times. Suppose P takes 8 days and Q takes 12 days. Call the job 24 units. P does 24 ÷ 8 = 3 units a day and Q does 24 ÷ 12 = 2 units a day. Together they do 5 units a day and finish in 24 ÷ 5 = 4.8 days.

Never average the times. Working together must be faster than the faster worker alone, so 4.8 days, less than P's 8 days, passes the sanity check, while the average of 10 days does not.

If one worker is k times as efficient as another, they take 1/k of the time.

sections.title: Efficiency and the worker-days rule
sections.text:
Efficiency and time are inversely proportional. If the efficiencies of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 2, their times for the same job are in the ratio 2 : 3.

When many workers of equal ability share a job, the total effort can be measured in worker-days or worker-hours. More workers, more days or longer hours all produce more work, which gives the rule

(M1 × D1 × H1) ÷ W1 = (M2 × D2 × H2) ÷ W2

where M is the number of workers, D the days, H the hours per day and W the amount of work. Leave out any factor that does not change between the two situations.

The same idea handles workers joining or leaving midway. Find the total worker-days the job needs, subtract the worker-days already done, and divide the rest by the new number of workers. For example, if 10 workers would take 9 days (90 worker-days) and 4 more join after 2 days, then 90 − 20 = 70 worker-days remain, which 14 workers finish in 5 more days, 7 days in all.

sections.title: Pipes and cisterns
sections.text:
Pipes and cisterns are time-and-work questions in disguise. A pipe that fills a tank in n hours does 1/n of the job per hour, and a pipe or leak that empties it in m hours does −1/m of the job per hour. Add the rates of whatever is open:

Net rate = sum of filling rates − sum of emptying rates

The LCM method works here too. Say an inlet fills a tank in 6 hours and an outlet empties it in 9 hours. Take the tank as 18 units. The inlet adds 3 units an hour and the outlet removes 2, so with both open the tank gains 1 unit an hour and fills in 18 hours.

Watch the sign. Treating the outlet as a helper and adding 3 + 2 would give 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6 hours, which is faster than the inlet alone and so cannot be right when something is draining the tank.

If the net rate is negative, a full tank empties instead, and the same arithmetic tells you how quickly.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. They start together, but A leaves after 4 days. How many days does the whole job take?

Step 1: Take the job as LCM(12, 18) = 36 units, so A does 3 units a day and B does 2.
Step 2: In 4 days together they complete 4 × 5 = 20 units.
Step 3: B does the remaining 36 − 20 = 16 units alone in 16 ÷ 2 = 8 days, so the job takes 4 + 8 = 12 days.

Example 2. 18 workers, working 8 hours a day, lay 540 m of pipe in 15 days. How many days will 24 workers, working 6 hours a day, take to lay 720 m?

Step 1: Use (M1 × D1 × H1) ÷ W1 = (M2 × D2 × H2) ÷ W2.
Step 2: Left side = 18 × 15 × 8 ÷ 540 = 2,160 ÷ 540 = 4.
Step 3: Right side = 24 × D × 6 ÷ 720 = D ÷ 5, so D ÷ 5 = 4 and D = 20 days.
Sense check: more pipe and shorter hours push the time up, more workers push it down.

keyPoints: Rates add, times do not: together, A and B take ab ÷ (a + b) days.
Set the total work to the LCM of the individual times to avoid fractions.
Efficiency is inversely proportional to time.
Use (M1 × D1 × H1) ÷ W1 = (M2 × D2 × H2) ÷ W2 for groups of equal workers.
In pipes and cisterns, emptying rates are subtracted.

challenges.title: Working together
challenges.prompt: X can finish a task in 20 days and Y in 30 days. How long will they take working together?
challenges.explanation: Take the task as 60 units. X does 3 units a day and Y does 2, so together they do 5 units a day and finish in 60 ÷ 5 = 12 days. Equivalently, 20 × 30 ÷ (20 + 30) = 600 ÷ 50 = 12. The option 25 days averages the times, but two people working together must finish faster than either alone.
challenges.hint: Add the daily rates, not the numbers of days.

challenges.title: Twice as efficient
challenges.prompt: A is twice as efficient as B. Working together, they finish a job in 14 days. How long would A take alone?
