challenges.hint: Recall which referential action standard SQL applies when you declare none, and what it does.

challenges.title: Where NULL is allowed
challenges.prompt: Which of these columns can legally contain NULL?
options: One column of a composite primary key
No column in a table that has a primary key
A foreign key column declared without NOT NULL
challenges.explanation: Entity integrity bans NULL in every part of a primary key, single or composite. Other columns in a keyed table can be NULL, so the third option is too strict. A foreign key without NOT NULL may be NULL, which simply means the row references nothing.
challenges.hint: Entity integrity applies to one kind of key only.

guides.subject: DBMS
guides.title: Normalization (1NF to BCNF)
guides.summary: Use functional dependencies to spot redundancy and decompose tables step by step through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF.

sections.title: Why normalize: the three anomalies
sections.text:
Imagine one table Enrollment(roll_no, student_name, course_id, course_title, grade). It works, but it repeats a lot. Every student's name appears once per course they take, and every course title appears once per student enrolled.

That repetition causes three classic problems. An update anomaly: if a course is renamed, you must change many rows, and missing one leaves the data contradicting itself. An insertion anomaly: you cannot record a new course until some student enrolls, because there is no row to put it in. A deletion anomaly: if the last student drops a course, deleting that row also erases the only record of the course title.

Normalization is the process of splitting such tables so each fact is stored once. The normal forms are checkpoints that tell you how much of this redundancy is left.

sections.title: Functional dependencies
sections.text:
A functional dependency X -> Y means that whenever two rows agree on X, they must agree on Y. In the Enrollment table, course_id -> course_title, because one course has one title, and (roll_no, course_id) -> grade.

To find keys, compute the closure of a set of attributes: start with the set and keep adding anything the dependencies let you derive. If the closure of X contains every attribute, X is a super key. Here the closure of (roll_no, course_id) reaches every column, so it is a key.

Two shapes of dependency cause trouble. A partial dependency is when a non prime attribute depends on only part of a candidate key, like course_title depending on course_id alone. A transitive dependency is when a non prime attribute depends on the key through another non key attribute, as in emp_id -> dept_id -> dept_name. 2NF removes the first pattern and 3NF removes the second.

sections.title: First and second normal form
sections.text:
A table is in first normal form (1NF) when every cell holds a single atomic value and there are no repeating groups. A phones column holding '98200, 99300' breaks 1NF; you fix it by moving phones to their own table with one phone per row.

A table is in second normal form (2NF) when it is in 1NF and no non prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key. In plain words, every non key column must depend on the whole key, not just part of it.

Our Enrollment table fails 2NF, since course_title depends on course_id alone and student_name depends on roll_no alone. Split it into Student(roll_no, student_name), Course(course_id, course_title) and Enrollment(roll_no, course_id, grade). Notice that partial dependency needs a composite key. A table whose candidate keys are all single columns, and which is in 1NF, is automatically in 2NF.

sections.title: Third normal form and BCNF
sections.text:
A table is in third normal form (3NF) if, for every non trivial dependency X -> A, either X is a super key or A is a prime attribute. This removes transitive dependencies of non prime attributes on the key. Employee(emp_id, dept_id, dept_name) fails, because dept_id -> dept_name, dept_id is not a super key, and dept_name is not prime. Move dept_name into a Department table.

Boyce Codd normal form (BCNF) drops the escape clause: for every non trivial X -> A, X must be a super key. Every BCNF table is in 3NF, but not the other way round.

The classic gap: Teaching(student, subject, teacher), where each teacher teaches one subject, so teacher -> subject, and (student, subject) -> teacher. Candidate keys are (student, subject) and (student, teacher), so all three columns are prime. teacher -> subject is allowed in 3NF because subject is prime, but it breaks BCNF because teacher is not a super key.

sections.title: Good decompositions
sections.text:
Splitting a table is only safe if you can put it back together. A decomposition is lossless if joining the pieces gives exactly the original rows, with no extra rows. For a split into two tables, a simple test works: the shared columns must be a super key of at least one of the pieces. Splitting R(A, B, C) with A -> B into (A, B) and (A, C) is lossless, because A is a key of (A, B).

A decomposition is dependency preserving if every original dependency can still be checked inside a single table, without joins.

Here is the trade-off interviewers like. You can always reach 3NF with a decomposition that is both lossless and dependency preserving. BCNF can always be reached losslessly, but sometimes only by losing a dependency, as in the Teaching example. In practice, many systems stop at 3NF, and some read heavy systems deliberately denormalize to avoid joins.

keyPoints: Redundancy causes update, insertion and deletion anomalies.
2NF: no non prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key.
3NF: for every non trivial X -> A, X is a super key or A is prime.
BCNF: for every non trivial X -> A, X is a super key.
3NF is always reachable losslessly with dependencies preserved; BCNF may lose a dependency.

challenges.title: Composite key with a partial dependency
challenges.prompt: R(A, B, C, D) has candidate key (A, B) and dependencies AB -> C and B -> D. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
challenges.explanation: D is non prime and depends on B alone, which is only part of the key (A, B). That is a partial dependency, so R fails 2NF and therefore also 3NF and BCNF. Assuming atomic values, it is in 1NF only.
challenges.hint: Does every non key column depend on the whole key?

challenges.title: A chain through a non key column
challenges.prompt: R(A, B, C) has key A and dependencies A -> B and B -> C. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
challenges.explanation: The key is a single attribute, so there can be no partial dependency and R is in 2NF. But B -> C has a left side that is not a super key and a right side, C, that is not prime, which is a transitive dependency. So R fails 3NF, and with it BCNF.
challenges.hint: With a single column key, 2NF is easy. Check B -> C against the 3NF rule.

challenges.title: 3NF but not BCNF
challenges.prompt: In Teaching(student, subject, teacher), teacher -> subject and (student, subject) -> teacher. The table is in 3NF but not BCNF. Why?
options: Because subject depends on part of the key (student, subject)
Because there are no candidate keys with two columns
Because teacher -> subject has a left side that is not a super key, but subject is prime
Because the table has a transitive dependency on a non prime attribute
challenges.explanation: 3NF allows X -> A when A is prime, and subject belongs to the candidate key (student, subject), so 3NF holds. BCNF has no such exception and requires teacher to be a super key, which it is not. There is no non prime attribute here at all, so neither partial nor transitive dependency of a non prime attribute applies.
challenges.hint: Which escape clause does 3NF have that BCNF lacks?

challenges.title: Is the split lossless
challenges.prompt: R(A, B, C) has the dependency A -> B. You split it into R1(A, B) and R2(A, C). Is the decomposition lossless?
options: Lossy, because C does not appear in R1
Lossless only if B -> C also holds
You cannot tell without looking at the data
Lossless, because the shared column A is a key of R1
challenges.explanation: The shared attribute is A, and A -> B makes A a key of R1(A, B). Each row of R2 then joins with exactly one row of R1, so no extra rows appear. Not every column needs to be in every piece, B -> C is irrelevant to this test, and the dependency guarantees the result for any valid data.
challenges.hint: Check whether the common columns determine everything in one of the pieces.

challenges.title: Naming the anomaly
challenges.prompt: In an unnormalized Enrollment table, the last student taking 'Compilers' drops it. Deleting that row also wipes out the course's title. Which anomaly is this?
challenges.explanation: Removing one fact, the enrollment, unintentionally removed another fact, the course title. That is a deletion anomaly. An insertion anomaly is being unable to add a fact without an unrelated one, and an update anomaly is having to change the same fact in many rows.
challenges.hint: Which operation caused the loss?

guides.subject: DBMS
guides.title: Transactions and ACID
guides.summary: See how a database groups work into transactions and keeps the ACID promises, including the isolation levels and the anomalies each one allows.

sections.title: What a transaction is
sections.text:
A transaction is a group of operations the database treats as one unit of work. The usual example is moving 500 rupees from account A to account B: subtract 500 from A, then add 500 to B. If the system stops between those two steps, money has vanished. A transaction makes sure that cannot be the final state.

You start a transaction with BEGIN, do your reads and writes, then end with COMMIT to make the changes permanent or ROLLBACK to throw them away.

A transaction moves through states. It is active while running, partially committed after its last statement, and committed once the commit is safely recorded. If something goes wrong it becomes failed, and after rollback it is aborted. The four promises a database makes about transactions are summed up as ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.

sections.title: Atomicity and durability
sections.text:
Atomicity means all or nothing. Either every change in the transaction takes effect or none does. If the transfer fails after debiting A, the database undoes that debit.

Durability means that once the database says committed, the change survives crashes, power cuts and restarts.

Both are usually built on a log. With write ahead logging, the database writes a description of each change to the log before the changed data page reaches disk. A transaction counts as committed once its commit record is flushed to stable storage, even if the data pages are still only in memory.

After a crash, recovery reads the log. It redoes the changes of committed transactions whose pages never reached disk, which gives durability, and undoes changes of transactions that never committed, which gives atomicity. This is why committing can be fast: only the log must be flushed, not every page.

sections.title: Consistency and isolation
sections.text:
Consistency means a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another. Valid means all declared rules hold: keys, foreign keys, CHECK constraints, and business rules like the total money across accounts staying the same during a transfer. The database enforces the rules you declare, but the application must write transactions that make sense. That is why consistency is often called the property the application shares responsibility for.

Isolation means concurrent transactions should not see each other's half finished work. The gold standard is serializability: running transactions together gives the same result as running them one after another in some order.

Full serializability costs performance, so databases offer weaker isolation levels. Each level allows certain anomalies in exchange for more concurrency, which is the topic of the next section.

sections.title: Isolation levels and their anomalies
sections.text:
The SQL standard names three read anomalies. A dirty read is reading data another transaction wrote but has not committed, which might be rolled back. A non repeatable read is reading the same row twice and getting different values because another transaction updated it and committed in between. A phantom read is running the same query twice and getting a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows.

Read uncommitted allows all three. Read committed prevents dirty reads only. Repeatable read prevents dirty and non repeatable reads, but the standard still allows phantoms. Serializable prevents all three and behaves like some serial order.

Real systems differ in detail. PostgreSQL and Oracle default to read committed, and MySQL InnoDB defaults to repeatable read, where snapshot reads avoid most phantoms. In an interview, state the standard table first, then mention that engines may be stricter.

keyPoints: A transaction is one unit of work that ends in COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
Atomicity is all or nothing; durability means committed changes survive crashes.
Write ahead logging supports both: undo for atomicity, redo for durability.
Read committed stops dirty reads, repeatable read also stops non repeatable reads, serializable also stops phantoms.
Consistency depends on both declared constraints and correct application logic.

challenges.title: Reading a value that disappears
challenges.prompt: T1 updates a row's price to 90 but has not committed. T2 reads the row and sees 90. Then T1 rolls back. What anomaly did T2 experience?
challenges.explanation: T2 read a value written by a transaction that never committed, which is the definition of a dirty read. A non repeatable read involves committed changes between two reads of the same row, a phantom involves a changing set of rows, and a lost update involves two writers overwriting each other.
challenges.hint: Was the value T2 saw ever committed?

challenges.title: Lowest level that fixes it
challenges.prompt: Under the SQL standard, what is the lowest isolation level that prevents non repeatable reads?
challenges.explanation: Read committed only stops dirty reads, so a row can still change between your two reads. Repeatable read is the first level that guarantees rows you read stay the same. Serializable also prevents it but is not the lowest such level.
challenges.hint: List what each level prevents beyond the one below it.

challenges.title: Crash right after commit
challenges.prompt: A transaction commits and the database confirms success. The power fails before the changed data pages are written to disk, but the commit record was flushed to the log. What do you see after restart?
options: The change is lost, because the data pages never reached disk
The change is present, because recovery redoes it from the log
The database keeps half the change and flags the row as corrupt
challenges.explanation: Durability is guaranteed by the log, not by the data pages. Because the commit record and change records were flushed, recovery replays them, so the committed change reappears. Losing it would break durability, and a half applied change would break atomicity.
challenges.hint: What exactly must be on disk for a commit to count?

challenges.title: Which property is shared
challenges.prompt: A transfer running alone debits A by 500 but, due to a coding bug, credits B by 50, then commits. No constraint is violated. Which ACID property did the application break?
challenges.explanation: All the steps ran and committed together, so atomicity held, no concurrency was involved, so isolation is not the issue, and the result was saved, so durability held. The broken business rule, that total money is unchanged, is a consistency problem, which depends on the application writing correct transactions.
challenges.hint: The database did everything it was told to do.

challenges.title: The count changed
challenges.prompt: T1 counts employees with salary over 50000 and gets 10. T2 inserts a new employee with salary 60000 and commits. T1 runs the same count again and gets 11. What anomaly is this?
challenges.explanation: No existing row changed; a new row appeared in the set matching T1's condition. That is a phantom read. It is not dirty, because T2 committed first, and it is not a non repeatable read, which is about an existing row's values changing.
challenges.hint: Did a row change, or did the set of rows change?

guides.subject: DBMS
guides.title: Indexing
guides.summary: Learn how indexes speed up lookups, how B+ trees work, and the difference between clustered, non-clustered, dense and sparse indexes.

sections.title: Why indexes exist
sections.text:
Without an index, finding a row means reading the whole table and checking each row, which is a full table scan. For ten rows that is fine. For ten million it is painfully slow.

An index is a separate structure that maps values of a column, the search key, to where the matching rows live. It works like the index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page to find 'deadlock', you look it up and jump to the right page.

Indexes are not free. Each one takes disk space, and every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE that touches the indexed column must also update the index. So a table with many indexes reads fast but writes slower. The art is to index the columns your queries actually filter, join or sort on, and not every column just in case.

sections.title: B+ trees and hash indexes
sections.text:
Most database indexes are B+ trees. A B+ tree is balanced, so every leaf is at the same depth, and each node holds many keys, often hundreds, because a node fills a disk page. That high fanout keeps the tree shallow: three or four levels can cover millions of rows, so a lookup reads only a handful of pages.

Internal nodes only guide the search. All actual entries sit in the leaves, which are kept in key order and linked to their neighbours. That link is what makes range queries fast: find the first key, then walk sideways along the leaves.

A hash index instead hashes the key to a bucket. It is excellent for equality, like WHERE id = 42, with roughly constant cost. But hashing scatters neighbouring values, so it cannot help with ranges, sorting or prefix searches. That is why B+ trees are the default.

sections.title: Clustered and non-clustered indexes
sections.text:
A clustered index decides the physical order in which rows are stored. In engines like MySQL InnoDB, the table itself is the B+ tree of the primary key, with full rows in the leaves. Because rows can be stored in only one order, a table has at most one clustered index.

A non-clustered, or secondary, index is a separate structure. Its leaves hold the key plus a pointer to the row, either a physical row address or the row's primary key value. A table can have many of these.

The difference shows up in cost. A range query on the clustered key reads rows that sit next to each other. A lookup through a secondary index finds the pointer first, then makes a second trip to fetch the row, and a wide range can mean many scattered trips.

If a secondary index already contains every column a query needs, the second trip is skipped. That is called a covering index.

sections.title: Dense, sparse and multilevel indexes
sections.text:
Textbooks also classify indexes by how many entries they keep.

A dense index has an entry for every search key value in the data file. You can answer 'does key 57 exist?' from the index alone.

A sparse index has entries for only some values, typically one per data block, holding the first key in that block. To find key 57, you locate the largest index entry not greater than 57 and scan that block. This only works if the data file is sorted on the search key, so a sparse index must be on the ordering column. A secondary index on an unsorted column has to be dense.

When an index itself grows too large to search quickly, you can build a sparse index on top of it, and another on top of that. That is a multilevel index, and a B+ tree is essentially a self balancing version of this idea.

sections.title: Composite indexes and when indexes do not help
sections.text:
A composite index covers several columns in a fixed order, such as (city, age). Entries are sorted by city first and by age within each city.

This gives the leftmost prefix rule. The index helps WHERE city = 'Pune', and WHERE city = 'Pune' AND age > 25. In general it does not help a seek on WHERE age = 30 alone, just as a phone book sorted by surname then first name cannot find everyone named Ravi quickly. Some engines, such as Oracle, MySQL 8.0 and PostgreSQL 18, can do a skip scan, one seek per distinct city, but that only pays off when the leading column has few distinct values.

Indexes also go unused in other common cases. Wrapping the column in a function, like WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024, hides the raw values the index is sorted on, unless you build an expression (function based) index on that exact expression. A pattern with a leading wildcard, like LIKE '%son', cannot use the sorted order. And when a condition matches a large share of rows, such as a status column with two values, the optimizer may decide a full scan is cheaper than thousands of index lookups.

keyPoints: Indexes trade extra storage and slower writes for faster reads.
B+ trees keep entries in sorted, linked leaves, so they handle equality and range queries.
Hash indexes handle equality only.
A table has at most one clustered index; it can have many non-clustered ones.
Sparse indexes need the data sorted on the key; composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule.

challenges.title: How many clustered indexes
challenges.prompt: How many clustered indexes can a single table have?
challenges.explanation: A clustered index defines the physical order of the rows, and rows can only be stored in one order at a time. Additional indexes must be non-clustered structures that point back to the rows.
challenges.hint: Think about what a clustered index controls.

challenges.title: Leftmost prefix
challenges.prompt: A table has a composite B+ tree index on (city, age). Which query can use the index to seek directly to matching rows?
challenges.explanation: The index is sorted by city first, then age within each city. Fixing city lets the engine jump to the Pune section and then use the age order inside it. Conditions on age alone skip the leading column, and ages are scattered across every city, so there is no single place to seek to.
challenges.hint: Entries are sorted by the first column before the second.

challenges.title: Range on a hash index
challenges.prompt: You need to run WHERE price BETWEEN 100 AND 200 frequently. Which index type suits this best?
options: A hash index, because lookups are constant time
Either one, they perform the same on ranges
Neither; ranges always need a full scan
A B+ tree, because its leaves are in key order and linked
challenges.explanation: A B+ tree finds 100 and then walks along the linked leaves until it passes 200. A hash index scatters nearby prices into unrelated buckets, so it only helps exact matches. A full scan is not required when a sorted index exists.
challenges.hint: Which structure keeps neighbouring values next to each other?

challenges.title: Requirement for a sparse index
challenges.prompt: What must be true for a sparse index on column K to work?
options: The index must fit entirely in memory
Every value of K must be unique
The data file must be sorted on K
Column K must not contain NULLs
challenges.explanation: A sparse index stores one entry per block and relies on scanning forward inside that block. That only finds the right rows if they are physically ordered by K. Uniqueness, NULLs and memory size do not change how the lookup works.
challenges.hint: How do you find a key that has no entry of its own in the index?

challenges.title: Index everything
challenges.prompt: A teammate proposes adding an index on every column of a busy orders table that receives thousands of inserts per second. What is the main problem?
options: Queries would get slower because the optimizer gets confused
Every insert must also update every index, slowing writes and using more storage
Databases forbid more than one index per table
Indexes stop working once a table has many rows
challenges.explanation: Each index is a structure that must be kept in sync, so every insert does extra work per index, and each takes disk space. Optimizers handle many indexes fine, databases allow many non-clustered indexes, and indexes matter most on large tables.
challenges.hint: What has to happen to each index when a row is added?

guides.subject: DBMS
guides.title: Concurrency control
guides.summary: Understand how databases run transactions at the same time safely, using serializability, locks, two-phase locking, deadlock handling and MVCC.

sections.title: Why interleaving goes wrong
sections.text:
A database runs many transactions at once to stay fast. The order in which their operations interleave is called a schedule. A serial schedule runs one transaction fully before the next, which is always safe but slow.

Interleaving can break things. Suppose a balance is 100. T1 reads 100 and plans to add 10. T2 also reads 100 and plans to add 20. T1 writes 110, then T2 writes 120. The final value is 120, but it should be 130. T1's update has been lost.

The goal of concurrency control is to allow interleaving while guaranteeing the result matches some serial order. A schedule with that property is called serializable. The rest of this guide covers how databases check for it and enforce it: conflict analysis, locking, and versioning.

sections.title: Conflict serializability
sections.text:
Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, touch the same data item, and at least one of them is a write. Read and read never conflict. Read and write, write and read, and write and write do.

A schedule is conflict serializable if you can swap neighbouring non conflicting operations until it becomes a serial schedule. The practical test is the precedence graph. Draw one node per transaction. Whenever an operation of Ti conflicts with a later operation of Tj, draw an edge from Ti to Tj, meaning Ti must come first.

If the graph has no cycle, the schedule is conflict serializable, and any topological order of the graph is an equivalent serial order. If there is a cycle, such as T1 -> T2 -> T1, no serial order can satisfy both edges, so the schedule is not conflict serializable. In the lost update example, both reads come before both writes, giving edges in both directions.

sections.title: Locks and two-phase locking
sections.text:
Locks are the most common way to enforce serializability. A shared (S) lock lets a transaction read an item, and several transactions can hold shared locks together. An exclusive (X) lock lets a transaction write, and no other lock of either kind can coexist with it. A request that is not compatible waits.

Locking alone is not enough; you also need a rule about when locks are taken and released. Two-phase locking (2PL) splits each transaction into a growing phase, where it may acquire locks but not release any, and a shrinking phase, which starts at the first release, where it may release locks but not acquire new ones. 2PL guarantees conflict serializable schedules.

Basic 2PL still allows cascading aborts: if T1 releases an X lock early and T2 reads that value, T1 aborting forces T2 to abort too. Strict 2PL fixes this by holding all exclusive locks until commit or abort. Rigorous 2PL holds every lock until then. Neither prevents deadlocks.

sections.title: Deadlocks
sections.text:
A deadlock happens when transactions wait for each other in a circle. T1 holds a lock on A and wants B, while T2 holds B and wants A. Neither can move.

Databases usually detect deadlocks with a wait-for graph, where an edge from T1 to T2 means T1 is waiting on a lock T2 holds. A cycle means deadlock, and the system aborts one transaction, the victim, so the others can continue. Timeouts are a cruder alternative.

Prevention schemes use transaction timestamps, where an older transaction has a smaller timestamp. In wait-die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one, but a younger transaction that requests a lock held by an older one is aborted, or dies, and restarts later with its original timestamp. In wound-wait, an older transaction that requests a lock held by a younger one wounds it, forcing the younger to abort, while a younger requester simply waits. Keeping the original timestamp means a restarted transaction eventually becomes the oldest and cannot starve.

sections.title: Timestamps, optimistic control and MVCC
sections.text:
Locking is pessimistic: it blocks in case a conflict happens. Other approaches exist.

Timestamp ordering gives each transaction a timestamp and forces conflicting operations to happen in timestamp order. If a transaction tries to read an item a younger transaction has already written, or write an item a younger transaction has already read or written, it is aborted and restarted with a new timestamp rather than made to wait. Thomas's write rule relaxes the last case: an outdated write over a younger write is simply ignored.

Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions run freely on private copies, then validates at commit time that nothing they read was changed by others. It works well when conflicts are rare.

Multiversion concurrency control (MVCC) keeps several versions of each row. A reader sees a consistent snapshot of committed data as of some point, while writers create new versions. The big win is that readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers. PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL InnoDB all use MVCC, usually combined with locks for write-write conflicts.

keyPoints: Two operations conflict when they are from different transactions, on the same item, and at least one writes.
A schedule is conflict serializable if its precedence graph has no cycle.
2PL: a growing phase then a shrinking phase; it guarantees conflict serializability but not freedom from deadlock.
Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit or abort, which avoids cascading aborts.
Wait-die and wound-wait prevent deadlocks using timestamps; MVCC lets readers and writers avoid blocking each other.

challenges.title: Shared then exclusive
challenges.prompt: T1 holds a shared lock on row R. T2 requests an exclusive lock on R. What happens under standard locking?
options: T2 waits until T1 releases its lock
T1's lock is silently upgraded to exclusive
T1 is always aborted to make room
challenges.explanation: An exclusive lock is incompatible with any other lock, including shared, so T2 must wait. Shared locks only coexist with other shared locks. No upgrade happens to T1 unless T1 asks for it, and aborting is a deadlock or prevention decision, not the default response to a conflict.
challenges.hint: Check the lock compatibility rules.

challenges.title: Locking after a release
challenges.prompt: Under basic two-phase locking, transaction T has locked A and B, then released its lock on A. Can T now acquire a lock on C?
options: Yes, because C is unrelated to A
Yes, but only a shared lock
No, because releasing A started its shrinking phase
challenges.explanation: The first release ends the growing phase. From then on, 2PL allows releases only, whatever the item or lock mode. That rule is exactly what produces the serializability guarantee.
challenges.hint: What marks the boundary between the two phases?

challenges.title: What strict 2PL adds
challenges.prompt: What does strict two-phase locking add on top of basic two-phase locking?
options: Exclusive locks are held until commit or abort, so no one reads uncommitted writes and cascading aborts are avoided
It allows new locks after the first release
It removes the need for shared locks
challenges.explanation: Holding exclusive locks until the end means other transactions cannot read data that might still be rolled back, so one abort never forces others to abort. Strict 2PL can still deadlock, it is stricter rather than looser about acquiring locks, and it still uses shared locks for reads.
challenges.hint: Think about when the write locks are released.

challenges.title: Reading a precedence graph
challenges.prompt: A schedule's precedence graph has edges T1 -> T2, T2 -> T3 and T3 -> T1. What can you conclude?
options: It is equivalent to the serial order T1, T2, T3
It is equivalent to the serial order T3, T1, T2
challenges.explanation: The edges form a cycle, so any serial order would break at least one of them; for example T1, T2, T3 violates T3 -> T1. That means the schedule is not conflict serializable. A precedence graph describes conflict order, not waiting, so it says nothing about deadlock.
challenges.hint: Look for a cycle.

challenges.title: Wait-die in action
challenges.prompt: Using wait-die, T1 has timestamp 5 and holds a lock on X. T2, with timestamp 10, requests a conflicting lock on X. What happens?
options: T2 waits for T1 to finish
T2 is aborted and later restarts with timestamp 10
T1 is aborted so T2 can proceed
T2 is restarted with a fresh, larger timestamp
challenges.explanation: T2 is younger, with a larger timestamp. In wait-die only older transactions may wait, so the younger requester dies. It restarts with its original timestamp so it ages and cannot starve. Aborting the holder is what wound-wait does when an older transaction requests, which is not this case.
challenges.hint: In wait-die, who is allowed to wait: the older or the younger?

guides.subject: OOP
guides.title: Classes and objects
guides.summary: A class is a blueprint that describes state and behaviour, and an object is one concrete instance built from it at runtime.

sections.title: Blueprint versus instance
sections.text:
A class is a definition. It says what data each instance will hold (its fields) and what it can do (its methods). An object is a real thing in memory, created from that definition, with its own copy of the fields.

Think of a class Account with fields owner and balance and a method deposit. Writing the class creates no accounts. Each time you write new Account(), the JVM allocates a fresh object on the heap, and two accounts can hold different balances at the same time.

A useful way to say it in an interview: the class defines the type, and objects are values of that type. One class can produce any number of objects, and every object knows which class it came from. State is what an object knows, behaviour is what it can do, and identity is what makes it a separate object even when its state matches another one.

sections.title: Constructors and the new keyword
sections.text:
A constructor is a special block that runs once when an object is created. It has the same name as the class and no return type, not even void. Its job is to put the object into a valid starting state.

class Point { int x, y; Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } }

Here this.x refers to the field and plain x refers to the parameter. If you write no constructor at all, Java supplies a default no-argument constructor for you. The moment you write any constructor yourself, that free default disappears, so new Point() would no longer compile unless you add a no-argument version too. This catches many students out.

Constructors can be overloaded, and one constructor can call another with this(...) as its first statement. Fields you do not set get default values: 0 for numbers, false for booleans and null for references. Local variables get no default and must be assigned before use.

sections.title: Instance members and static members
sections.text:
An instance field belongs to each object separately. A static field belongs to the class itself, so there is exactly one copy shared by every object.

class Counter { static int created = 0; int id; Counter() { created++; id = created; } }

After three new Counter() calls, Counter.created is 3, while the three objects have ids 1, 2 and 3.

Static methods follow the same rule. They run without any object, so there is no this inside them. That is why a static method cannot read an instance field directly: it would not know which object's field you mean. It can still work with instance data if you hand it an object reference. The classic public static void main is static for exactly this reason, because the JVM must call it before any object of your class exists.

sections.title: Variables hold references, not objects
sections.text:
In Java, a variable of a class type does not contain the object. It holds a reference that points to the object.

Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point b = a; Point c = new Point(1, 2);

This creates two objects, not three. a and b point to the same object, so changing b.x also changes what you see through a. c points to a separate object that merely has the same values.

The == operator on references asks whether two variables point to the same object. So a == b is true and a == c is false. To compare contents you call equals, but only if the class overrides it. The version inherited from Object behaves just like ==, so without an override a.equals(c) is also false. A common misconception is that equals compares fields automatically. It does not; you, or a record, must define that.

keyPoints: A class is a definition; an object is a runtime instance with its own copy of the instance fields.
Writing any constructor removes the default no-argument constructor Java would otherwise supply.
Static members belong to the class and are shared; static methods have no this.
Class-type variables hold references, so assignment copies the reference, not the object.
== checks identity; equals checks content only when the class overrides it.

challenges.title: Counting objects
challenges.prompt: Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point b = a; Point c = new Point(1, 2); How many Point objects exist after these lines?
challenges.explanation: Only the two new expressions create objects. Point b = a copies the reference, so a and b point to the same object. Three would be right only if assignment copied objects, which Java never does for class types.
challenges.hint: Count the uses of new, not the variables.

challenges.title: Shared counter
challenges.prompt: class Counter { static int count = 0; Counter() { count++; } } If you create three Counter objects, what is Counter.count?
options: 1, because each object has its own count
0, because static fields cannot be changed in a constructor
challenges.explanation: count is static, so there is one copy shared by all objects. Each constructor call increments that single copy, giving 3. It would be 1 per object only if count were an instance field, and constructors are free to modify static fields.
challenges.hint: Ask how many copies of a static field exist.

challenges.title: The missing constructor
challenges.prompt: class Box { int size; Box(int size) { this.size = size; } } Elsewhere you write: Box b = new Box(); What happens?
options: Compile error: there is no Box() constructor
It compiles and size defaults to 0
It compiles but throws an exception at runtime
challenges.explanation: Java only supplies a default no-argument constructor when the class declares no constructors at all. Box declares Box(int), so Box() does not exist and the call fails at compile time. size would indeed default to 0 in a newly created Box, but here no Box is ever created because the code does not compile.
challenges.hint: When does Java add the default constructor for you?

challenges.title: Identity versus equality
challenges.prompt: Point does not override equals. Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point c = new Point(1, 2); What are a == c and a.equals(c)?
challenges.explanation: a and c are different objects, so == is false. Without an override, equals is inherited from Object, which also checks identity, so it is false as well. false and true would need an equals override that compares x and y.
challenges.hint: What does the equals method inherited from Object actually compare?

challenges.title: Static meets instance
challenges.prompt: class User { String name; static void greet() { System.out.println(name); } } What happens when you compile this?
options: It prints the name of the most recently created User
Compile error: a static method cannot use an instance field without an object
challenges.explanation: A static method runs without any object, so there is no this and no way to know whose name to read. The compiler rejects it. Java never picks a recent object for you, and it never gets far enough to print null.
challenges.hint: Inside a static method, which object would name belong to?

guides.subject: OOP
guides.title: Encapsulation
guides.summary: Encapsulation keeps an object's data private and exposes only the operations that keep that data valid.

sections.title: What encapsulation really means
sections.text:
Encapsulation means bundling data with the methods that work on it, and controlling access so outside code cannot put the object into a broken state.

The key idea is the invariant: a rule that must always hold for the object. For a bank account it might be that the balance never goes below zero. If balance is a public field, any line anywhere in the program can write account.balance = -500, and nothing stops it. If balance is private and the only ways to change it are deposit and withdraw, those two methods can check the rule every time.

So encapsulation is not mainly about hiding things for secrecy. It is about having one place that owns the rules for a piece of data. A side benefit is freedom to change: callers depend on the methods, not the fields, so you can change the internal representation later without breaking them.

sections.title: Access modifiers in Java
sections.text:
Java gives you four access levels, from tightest to loosest.

private: visible only inside the declaring class. No modifier (package-private, often called default): visible to any class in the same package. protected: everything package-private allows, plus subclasses in other packages through inheritance. public: visible everywhere.

Two details are often missed. First, protected is wider than default, not narrower, because it includes the whole package. Second, private is checked per class, not per object. A method in Account can read other.balance of a different Account object, because the code is inside the Account class. That is why equals methods can compare private fields directly.

A sensible default is to make fields private and widen access only when you have a reason.

sections.title: Getters and setters are not automatically encapsulation
sections.text:
A private field with a plain getter and a plain setter is barely better than a public field. If setBalance accepts any number, the invariant is still unprotected.

Better designs expose meaningful operations instead of raw writes. deposit(amount) can reject negative amounts, and withdraw(amount) can refuse to overdraw. Ask what the caller wants to do, not which field they want to touch.

Getters can leak too. If an Order keeps a private List of items and getItems() returns that same list, the caller can call clear() on it and empty your order behind your back. The field is private but the object it points to is not protected. The fix is to return a copy or an unmodifiable view, for example List.copyOf(items) or Collections.unmodifiableList(items). The same applies in constructors: copy mutable arguments you store, so the caller cannot change them later.

sections.title: Encapsulation versus abstraction
sections.text:
Interviewers often ask for the difference, and the two are easy to blur.

Abstraction is about design: deciding what a type should expose and what details callers should not need to think about. Encapsulation is about enforcement: using access control to keep the internals behind that boundary. One way to remember it: abstraction chooses the interface, encapsulation protects the implementation.

A strong form of encapsulation is immutability. If a class has only private final fields, sets them in the constructor, offers no methods that change them and never hands out its mutable internals, then once an object is built it can never become invalid. String is the classic example. Immutable objects are also safe to share between threads without locking, which is a good point to mention when asked why encapsulation matters.

keyPoints: Encapsulation protects invariants by routing every change through methods that check the rules.
Access levels from narrow to wide: private, package-private, protected, public.
private is per class, not per object: an instance can read another instance's private fields.
A setter that accepts anything, or a getter that returns a mutable internal object, breaks encapsulation.
Abstraction decides what to expose; encapsulation enforces that the rest stays hidden.

challenges.title: No modifier
challenges.prompt: A field in class A has no access modifier. Which class can read it directly?
options: Only subclasses of A, wherever they are
Any class in the same package as A, subclass or not
challenges.explanation: No modifier means package-private: every class in the same package can access it, and nothing outside the package can, even a subclass. Subclasses in other packages need protected. Only A itself would be private.
challenges.hint: What is the default access level called?

challenges.title: Leaky getter
challenges.prompt: class Order { private List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); public List<String> getItems() { return items; } } A caller runs order.getItems().clear(). What happens?
options: Nothing; the caller received a copy
The order's own item list is emptied
Compile error, because items is private
challenges.explanation: The getter returns the reference to the same list object the Order holds, so clear() empties the order's own data. Java does not copy objects on return. The code compiles because the caller never names the private field; it only calls a public method.
challenges.hint: Does returning a reference copy the list?

challenges.title: Guarding the balance
challenges.prompt: You want an Account whose balance can never become negative. Which design actually guarantees that?
options: A private balance changed only through deposit and withdraw methods that validate the amount
A private balance with a public setBalance(double) and a getter
A public balance field with a comment saying it must stay positive
challenges.explanation: Only the first design gives the class a single checked path for every change. A setter that accepts any value lets callers write a negative number, and a comment enforces nothing.
challenges.hint: Which option puts a check in front of every possible change?

challenges.title: Private across objects
challenges.prompt: class Account { private String owner; boolean sameOwner(Account other) { return owner.equals(other.owner); } } Does this compile?
options: No, other.owner is private to that other object
Yes, because private access is checked per class, not per object
Only if owner is declared final
challenges.explanation: Java access control works at the class level. Code inside Account may access the private fields of any Account instance, not just this. final has nothing to do with visibility.
challenges.hint: Is private about which object or which class the code is in?

challenges.title: Protected from outside
challenges.prompt: Class A in package p has a protected field. Class B is in package q and does not extend A. Can B read the field?
options: Yes, as long as B imports A
Yes, but only from static methods
No, protected reaches the same package and subclasses only
challenges.explanation: protected allows access from the same package and from subclasses through inheritance. B is in another package and is not a subclass, so it has no access. Importing only makes the name usable; it never grants access, and static has no bearing on this.
challenges.hint: List the two groups protected opens the field to.

guides.subject: OOP
guides.title: Inheritance
guides.summary: Inheritance lets a class extend another to reuse and specialise its behaviour, and it should model a true is-a relationship.

sections.title: Is-a relationships and extends
sections.text:
Inheritance lets a new class, the subclass or child, build on an existing class, the superclass or parent. The child gets the parent's accessible fields and methods and can add new ones or override existing behaviour.

class Animal { void eat() { ... } } class Dog extends Animal { void bark() { ... } }

A Dog can eat and bark. Every Dog is an Animal, so you can store one in an Animal variable.

The test for using inheritance is the is-a question. A Dog is an Animal, so it fits. A Car is not an Engine, so Car extends Engine would be wrong even though a car uses one.

In Java a class can extend only one class. It can, however, implement many interfaces. The usual reason given is the diamond problem: if a class inherited state and method bodies from two parents that both define the same method, which one should win would be ambiguous. Every class without an explicit parent extends Object.

sections.title: Constructors and super
sections.text:
Constructors are not inherited, but they are chained. A parent constructor must finish before the child constructor can use the object it is building. If you do not write super(...) yourself, the compiler inserts a call to super() with no arguments as the first statement.

class A { A() { System.out.print('A'); } } class B extends A { B() { System.out.print('B'); } }

new B() prints AB: the parent part of the object is set up first, then the child part.

This leads to a classic compile error. If the parent has only A(int x) and no no-argument constructor, the implicit super() has nothing to call. The child must then call super(someValue) explicitly. Classically, super(...) has to be the first statement in the constructor, and a constructor can call either this(...) or super(...), not both. Java 25 relaxed the ordering slightly: statements that do not touch the object under construction, such as argument checks, may now come before that call, but the one-call rule still holds.

Outside constructors, super.method() calls the parent's version of a method you have overridden.

sections.title: What is and is not inherited
sections.text:
A child object physically contains the parent's fields, including private ones, but the child's code cannot name the private ones directly. It has to go through public or protected methods of the parent. That is why people say private members are not inherited: they are not accessible, even though they exist.

Private methods cannot be overridden. If a child declares a method with the same name as a private parent method, it is a new, unrelated method. Calls made inside the parent still reach the parent's private version.

Static methods are not overridden either. A child static method with the same signature hides the parent one, and which version runs depends on the reference type, not the object.

A final method cannot be overridden at all, and a final class cannot be extended. String is final for exactly this reason: nobody can subclass it and change its behaviour.

sections.title: Composition over inheritance
sections.text:
Inheritance creates a tight link. A change in the parent can silently break children that relied on its internal behaviour, often called the fragile base class problem. The child also inherits every public method of the parent, whether it makes sense or not.

Composition is the alternative: the class holds a reference to another object and delegates to it. class Car { private final Engine engine; void start() { engine.ignite(); } }

This is a has-a relationship. You can swap in a different Engine, expose only the methods you choose, and test parts separately.

A good rule for interviews: use inheritance when the child truly is a specialised kind of the parent and can be used anywhere the parent is expected. Use composition when you mainly want to reuse some code or when the relationship is has-a. Favouring composition is standard advice, not a ban on inheritance.

keyPoints: Use inheritance only for a genuine is-a relationship; use composition for has-a.
Java classes have single inheritance of classes but may implement many interfaces.
Parent constructors always run first; the compiler inserts super() if you do not call one.
Private methods, static methods and final methods are not overridden.
Favour composition to avoid tight coupling and the fragile base class problem.

challenges.title: Constructor order
challenges.prompt: class A { A() { System.out.print('A'); } } class B extends A { B() { System.out.print('B'); } } What does new B() print?
challenges.explanation: The compiler inserts super() as the first statement of B's constructor, so A's constructor finishes before B's body runs. BA gets the order backwards, and B alone ignores that the parent constructor always runs.
challenges.hint: What is the hidden first line of every constructor that does not call this or super?

challenges.title: No default parent constructor
challenges.prompt: class Parent { Parent(int x) { } } class Child extends Parent { Child() { } } What happens?
options: It compiles and x is passed as 0
It compiles but throws when a Child is created
Compile error: the implicit super() has no Parent() to call
challenges.explanation: Child() implicitly calls super(), but Parent only has Parent(int), so the compiler rejects it. Java never invents an argument, and the problem is found at compile time, not runtime. The fix is to call super(someValue) explicitly.
challenges.hint: Which parent constructor does an empty child constructor try to call?

challenges.title: Why one parent
challenges.prompt: Why does Java reject class C extends A, B?
options: Two parents could supply conflicting state and method bodies, making it ambiguous which to use
The JVM can only store one parent pointer per object
Multiple inheritance would make objects too large in memory
challenges.explanation: The design reason is ambiguity, often called the diamond problem: if A and B both define the same method or field, which one does C get? Memory size and pointer storage are not the reason; Java allows many interfaces, which shows the issue is about inherited implementation.
challenges.hint: Think of two parents that both define the same method.

challenges.title: Car and Engine
challenges.prompt: You are modelling a Car that uses an Engine. Which relationship is the best design?
options: Car extends Engine, since a car uses an engine
Engine extends Car, since an engine is part of a car
Both extend a shared Vehicle class
Car holds an Engine field and delegates to it
challenges.explanation: A car has an engine; it is not a kind of engine, and an engine is not a kind of car. That is a has-a relationship, which is composition. A shared Vehicle parent makes no sense for an engine.
challenges.hint: Apply the is-a test in both directions.

challenges.title: Private method in the parent
challenges.prompt: class Parent { private void log() { System.out.print('P'); } void run() { log(); } } class Child extends Parent { public void log() { System.out.print('C'); } } What does new Child().run() print?
options: P, because private methods are not overridden
Compile error, because Child changes the access level
challenges.explanation: A private method is invisible to subclasses, so Child.log is a brand new method, not an override. run() in Parent calls Parent's private log, printing P. Dynamic dispatch only applies to overridable methods, and there is no access-level conflict because nothing is being overridden.
challenges.hint: Can a subclass override something it cannot see?

guides.subject: OOP
guides.title: Polymorphism
guides.summary: Polymorphism lets one call behave differently depending on types, through overloading at compile time and overriding at runtime.

sections.title: One call, many forms
sections.text:
Polymorphism means the same piece of code can work with values of different types and do the right thing for each. If you have a List<Shape> holding circles and squares, a loop calling shape.area() gets the circle formula for circles and the square formula for squares, without any if statements.

Java has two kinds, and interviewers expect you to name both. Compile-time polymorphism, also called static binding, is method overloading: the compiler picks which method to call. Runtime polymorphism, also called dynamic dispatch, is method overriding: the JVM picks the method based on the actual object while the program runs.

Runtime polymorphism is the one that makes OOP flexible. You can add a new Shape subclass later and the existing loop handles it without being edited.

sections.title: Overloading is resolved at compile time
sections.text:
Overloading means several methods in the same class share a name but differ in their parameter list: the number of parameters, their types, or their order.

int add(int a, int b) and double add(double a, double b) are valid overloads. int add(int a, int b) and long add(int a, int b) are not: the return type alone cannot tell them apart, so it is a compile error.

The compiler chooses the overload using the declared types of the arguments, not the runtime object. Given show(Object o) and show(String s), the code Object x = "hi"; show(x); calls show(Object), because x is declared as Object. This surprises people who expect the more specific version.

Overloading does not need inheritance at all. That is a key difference from overriding, which only exists between a parent and a child type.

sections.title: Overriding and dynamic dispatch
sections.text:
Overriding happens when a subclass provides its own version of a method with the same name and parameter list as an inherited one.

class Animal { String sound() { return "..."; } } class Dog extends Animal { @Override String sound() { return "Woof"; } }

Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound() returns Woof. The variable's type is Animal, but the object is a Dog, and the JVM looks up the method on the object.

Rules worth knowing: the overriding method cannot reduce visibility, so a public method cannot become private. The return type must be the same or a subtype, called a covariant return. It cannot throw broader checked exceptions. Static, private and final methods do not take part.

Fields are never polymorphic. If both classes declare a field called name, a.name uses the reference type. Always add @Override so the compiler catches a typo that would otherwise create an accidental overload.

sections.title: Reference type versus object type
sections.text:
A single rule explains most polymorphism puzzles. The reference type decides what you are allowed to call. The object type decides which version runs.

With Animal a = new Dog(), a.sound() compiles because Animal declares sound, and it runs Dog's version. But a.bark() does not compile, even though the object really is a Dog, because the compiler only knows a as an Animal.

Assigning a Dog to an Animal variable is upcasting and is always safe and implicit. Going back down needs an explicit cast: Dog d = (Dog) a. The compiler accepts any cast that could possibly succeed, so the check happens at runtime. If a actually points to a Cat, the cast throws ClassCastException. Use instanceof first when you are not sure, or better, redesign so the parent type has the method you need.

keyPoints: Overloading: same name, different parameters, chosen at compile time from declared types.
Overriding: same signature in a subclass, chosen at runtime from the actual object.
Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.
Static, private and final methods are not overridden, and fields are never polymorphic.
Reference type controls what you can call; object type controls which version runs.

challenges.title: Which sound
challenges.prompt: Dog extends Animal and overrides sound() to return Woof. Animal a = new Dog(); What does a.sound() return?
options: Animal's version, because a is declared as Animal
challenges.explanation: sound is an overridden instance method, so the JVM dispatches on the actual object, which is a Dog. The declared type only matters for deciding whether the call compiles, and it does because Animal declares sound.
challenges.hint: For overridden methods, does the variable type or the object type decide?

challenges.title: Overload choice
challenges.prompt: A class has show(Object o) printing Object and show(String s) printing String. Object x = "hi"; show(x); What is printed?
options: String, since the object really is a String
Nothing; the call is ambiguous and does not compile
Object, since overloads are chosen from the declared type
challenges.explanation: Overload resolution happens at compile time using declared types. x is declared as Object, so only show(Object) matches. The runtime type is not consulted, and there is no ambiguity because show(String) simply does not apply to an Object argument.
challenges.hint: When is an overload picked, and what does the compiler know about x?

challenges.title: Return type only
challenges.prompt: One class declares int add(int a, int b) and long add(int a, int b). What is this?
options: A compile error: return type alone does not distinguish overloads
challenges.explanation: Overloads must differ in their parameter lists. These two have identical parameters, so the compiler sees a duplicate method. It is not overriding either, since both are in the same class.
challenges.hint: What part of a method signature does overloading look at?

challenges.title: Fields and polymorphism
challenges.prompt: class A { String name = "A"; } class B extends A { String name = "B"; } A obj = new B(); What does obj.name give?
options: B, because the object is a B
Compile error: name is declared twice
A, because fields are resolved by the reference type
challenges.explanation: Fields are not overridden; B's field hides A's. Field access is resolved from the declared type, which is A. Declaring a same-named field in a subclass is legal, and both fields are initialised, so neither null nor a compile error is right.
challenges.hint: Is field access dynamic like method calls?

challenges.title: Bad downcast
challenges.prompt: Cat and Dog both extend Animal. Animal a = new Cat(); Dog d = (Dog) a; What happens?
options: Compile error: a Cat can never be a Dog
It compiles, then throws ClassCastException at runtime
It works and d sees the cat through the Dog type
challenges.explanation: The compiler only knows a is an Animal, which could be a Dog, so it allows the cast. At runtime the JVM sees the object is a Cat and throws ClassCastException. A cast never converts an object into a different class.
challenges.hint: What does the compiler know about a, and what does the JVM know?

guides.subject: OOP
guides.title: Abstraction and interfaces
guides.summary: Abstraction exposes what a type does and hides how, using abstract classes and interfaces as the tools.

sections.title: What abstraction means
sections.text:
Abstraction is showing the essential operations of something and hiding the details of how they are done. When you call list.add(x) you do not think about array resizing or node pointers. You rely on what add promises.

In code, abstraction lets you write against a general type instead of a specific one. A method that takes a PaymentMethod and calls pay(amount) works for cards, wallets and bank transfers, including ones written next year.

Java gives you two tools for this: abstract classes and interfaces. Both let you declare methods without bodies and force concrete classes to fill them in. Neither can be instantiated directly.

Remember that abstraction is a design idea, while abstract classes and interfaces are language features that support it. A plain class with a clean public API is also an abstraction.

sections.title: Abstract classes
sections.text:
A class marked abstract cannot be created with new, but it can be used as a type. Shape s = new Circle(2) is fine, and so is new Shape[3], because that creates an array, not a Shape.

abstract class Shape { String label; Shape(String label) { this.label = label; } abstract double area(); String describe() { return label + " " + area(); } }

An abstract class can have fields, constructors and fully written methods alongside abstract ones. The constructor runs when a subclass object is created, through super(...).

If a class has even one abstract method, the class must be declared abstract. The reverse is not required: an abstract class may have no abstract methods at all, which is a way to stop direct instantiation. A concrete subclass must implement every inherited abstract method, or be declared abstract itself.

Abstract classes suit a family of closely related types that share state and some code.

sections.title: Interfaces
sections.text:
An interface is a contract: a set of methods a class promises to provide. A class can implement any number of interfaces.

interface Payable { double RATE = 0.18; double amount(); }

Interface methods without a body are implicitly public and abstract. Interface fields are implicitly public, static and final, so they are constants; trying to assign RATE in a class is a compile error. Interfaces have no constructors and no instance fields.

Since Java 8 an interface can also hold default methods with a body, which implementing classes inherit, and static methods. Java 9 added private methods for sharing code between defaults.

Because interface methods are public, the implementing method must be public too. Writing it with no modifier is a compile error, since that would reduce visibility.

If a class implements two interfaces that both supply a default method with the same signature, it must override that method and can pick one with A.super.method().

sections.title: Choosing between them
sections.text:
This comparison is one of the most asked OOP questions.

An abstract class can hold instance fields, constructors, and concrete methods at any access level; its abstract methods just cannot be private. A class can extend only one. An interface holds no instance state, its abstract methods are public, and a class can implement many.

Choose an abstract class when related types share real state or setup logic, for example a base Employee with a name and id that every subclass needs. Choose an interface when you are describing a capability that unrelated classes might share, such as Comparable or Runnable, or when you want a class to fit several roles at once.

An older misconception is that interfaces can never contain code. Default and static methods changed that in Java 8, but interfaces still cannot hold per-object state, which remains the clearest dividing line. A common pattern uses both: an interface for the contract and an abstract class that implements part of it.

keyPoints: Abstraction exposes what a type does and hides how it does it.
Abstract classes can have state, constructors and concrete methods but cannot be instantiated.
Interface fields are public static final; abstract interface methods are public, so implementations must be public.
Since Java 8 interfaces may have default and static methods, but never instance state.
A class extends at most one class but may implement many interfaces.

challenges.title: Which line fails
challenges.prompt: Shape is an abstract class and Circle is a concrete subclass. Which line does not compile?
challenges.explanation: You cannot instantiate an abstract class with new. Using Shape as a variable type is fine, and new Shape[3] creates an array of three null references, not any Shape objects, so it compiles too.
challenges.hint: Which line actually tries to build a Shape object?

challenges.title: Interface constant
challenges.prompt: interface Config { int MAX = 10; } class App implements Config { void setUp() { MAX = 20; } } What happens?
options: Compile error: interface fields are implicitly public static final
challenges.explanation: Every field in an interface is implicitly final, so it cannot be reassigned anywhere. It is also static, so there is no per-class copy that App could change on its own.
challenges.hint: Which modifiers does Java add to interface fields automatically?

challenges.title: Abstract class facts
challenges.prompt: Which statement about abstract classes in Java is true?
options: They can have constructors, which run when a subclass object is created
They cannot have constructors, because they cannot be instantiated
They must contain at least one abstract method
All their methods are implicitly public
challenges.explanation: An abstract class can declare constructors to initialise shared fields; subclasses call them through super. It may have zero abstract methods, and its methods follow normal access rules, so they are not implicitly public.
challenges.hint: How would an abstract class set up its own fields?

challenges.title: Implementing with no modifier
challenges.prompt: interface Greeter { void greet(); } class Hi implements Greeter { void greet() { } } What happens?
options: Compile error: greet must be public
It compiles, but greet is hidden outside the package
challenges.explanation: Greeter.greet is implicitly public. Hi.greet has package-private access, which is narrower, and an implementation cannot reduce visibility. Adding public fixes it.
challenges.hint: What access does an interface method have by default?

challenges.title: Clashing defaults
challenges.prompt: Interfaces A and B both declare default void hello(). class C implements A, B and does not declare hello(). What happens?
options: A wins because it is listed first
It throws an exception when hello() is called
Both defaults run, one after the other
Compile error until C overrides hello() itself
challenges.explanation: Java refuses to guess between two equally specific defaults, so C fails to compile. C must override hello(), and it can delegate with A.super.hello() if it wants A's behaviour. Declaration order never decides, and the conflict is caught at compile time.
challenges.hint: Does Java resolve this conflict at compile time or runtime?

guides.subject: OOP
guides.title: SOLID principles
guides.summary: SOLID is five design guidelines that keep object-oriented code easy to change, extend and test.

sections.title: Single responsibility principle
sections.text:
SOLID is an acronym for five principles: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation and dependency inversion. They are guidelines for keeping classes small, focused and safe to change.

The single responsibility principle says a class should have one reason to change. A useful reading is one group of people or one concern driving its changes. It does not mean a class may have only one method.

Picture an Invoice class that calculates totals, saves itself to a database and renders a PDF. A tax rule change, a database migration and a new PDF layout would all edit the same file, and each change risks breaking the others. Splitting it into Invoice for the calculations, InvoiceRepository for storage and InvoicePrinter for output gives each piece a single reason to change.

sections.title: Open/closed principle
sections.text:
Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. In practice, you should be able to add new behaviour by adding new code, not by editing working code.

A classic violation is an AreaCalculator with a long if/else on the shape type: if circle, use this formula; if square, use that one. Every new shape forces you to reopen and edit the calculator, and to retest everything in it.

The fix uses polymorphism. Give Shape an area() method and let each shape implement it. The calculator just sums shape.area() over the list. Adding a Triangle now means writing one new class, and the calculator never changes.

Closed does not mean frozen forever. Bug fixes are still edits. The goal is that common, expected kinds of change arrive as extensions.

sections.title: Liskov substitution principle
sections.text:
Objects of a subtype must be usable anywhere the base type is expected without breaking the program. A subclass may add behaviour, but it must keep the promises the parent makes.

The textbook case is Square extends Rectangle. A rectangle lets you set width and height independently. To stay square, Square.setWidth also changes the height. Now code written for rectangles, which sets width to 5 and height to 4 and expects an area of 20, gets 16. Mathematically a square is a rectangle, but behaviourally this Square is not a substitute for this Rectangle.

Warning signs of a violation include a subclass method that throws UnsupportedOperationException, one that silently does nothing, or callers that check instanceof before using the base type. Passing the is-a test in plain English is not enough; the subtype has to honour the parent's contract.

sections.title: Interface segregation principle
sections.text:
Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one large one.

Suppose a Machine interface declares print, scan and fax. A basic printer must implement all three, so it ends up throwing exceptions from scan and fax. Every class that only wants to print now also depends on scanning and faxing, and a change to fax can force them to recompile or change.

Splitting it into Printer, Scanner and FaxMachine lets the basic printer implement only Printer, while an office all-in-one implements all three. Each caller asks for exactly the capability it needs.

Interface segregation and Liskov often show up together: a fat interface tempts classes to stub out methods, and stubbed methods break substitution.

sections.title: Dependency inversion principle
sections.text:
High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Details should depend on abstractions, not the other way round.

If OrderService creates new MySqlOrderRepository() inside itself, your business logic is welded to one database. You cannot test it without MySQL, and switching storage means editing the service.

Instead, define an OrderRepository interface. OrderService receives one through its constructor and only knows the interface. MySqlOrderRepository implements it, and a test can pass an in-memory version.

Do not confuse the principle with dependency injection. Dependency inversion is the design rule about which way dependencies point. Dependency injection is a technique, passing collaborators in from outside, and it is a common way to apply the principle, often with a framework such as Spring doing the wiring.

keyPoints: Single responsibility: one reason to change, not one method.
Open/closed: add behaviour through new classes, typically using polymorphism, instead of editing working code.
Liskov substitution: a subtype must honour the base type's contract wherever the base type is used.
Interface segregation: small focused interfaces so clients depend only on what they use.
Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions; dependency injection is one way to achieve it.

challenges.title: Busy invoice
challenges.prompt: An Invoice class computes totals, saves itself to the database and generates a PDF. Which principle does it most directly violate?
challenges.explanation: The class has three unrelated reasons to change: pricing rules, storage and presentation. That is the definition of breaking single responsibility. Liskov is about subtypes, and interface segregation is about clients being forced to depend on unused methods, neither of which is the issue here.
challenges.hint: Count how many different kinds of change would edit this class.

challenges.title: Growing if/else
challenges.prompt: An AreaCalculator uses if/else on each shape's type, and every new shape requires editing it. Which principle is violated?
challenges.explanation: Adding a feature forces you to modify existing, working code, which is what open/closed warns against. Giving each shape its own area() method lets new shapes be added as extensions. Dependency inversion and Liskov describe different problems.
challenges.hint: Is new behaviour arriving as new code or as edits to old code?

challenges.title: Square and rectangle
challenges.prompt: Square extends Rectangle and setWidth also sets the height. Code that sets width 5 and height 4 on a Rectangle reference expects area 20 but gets 16 for a Square. Which principle is broken?
challenges.explanation: A Square cannot stand in for a Rectangle without changing the result callers rely on, which is exactly a Liskov violation. The class is not doing unrelated jobs, and no client is forced to depend on unused interface methods.
challenges.hint: Can the subtype be used wherever the parent type is expected?

challenges.title: Fat interface fix
challenges.prompt: A Machine interface has print, scan and fax. BasicPrinter implements it and throws UnsupportedOperationException from scan and fax. What is the best fix?
options: Make scan and fax silently do nothing instead of throwing
Add a canScan() method that callers check first
Split Machine into smaller interfaces such as Printer, Scanner and FaxMachine
challenges.explanation: The root problem is an interface that bundles unrelated capabilities, so interface segregation says to split it. Silent no-ops and capability flags hide the problem and still break substitution, and making BasicPrinter abstract means it can never be used at all.
challenges.hint: Fix the interface, not the symptoms in the class.

challenges.title: Following dependency inversion
challenges.prompt: Which version of OrderService follows the dependency inversion principle?
options: It creates a new MySqlOrderRepository inside its constructor
It receives an OrderRepository interface through its constructor
It extends MySqlOrderRepository to reuse its save method
challenges.explanation: Depending on the OrderRepository abstraction means the high-level service no longer depends on a concrete database class, and any implementation can be passed in. Creating or extending MySqlOrderRepository ties the business logic directly to the low-level detail.
challenges.hint: Which option leaves OrderService unaware of MySQL?

guides.subject: Operating systems
guides.title: Processes and threads
guides.summary: A process is a running program with its own address space, while threads are lighter units of execution that share one process's memory.

sections.title: What a process really is
sections.text:
A program is just a file on disk. It becomes a process when the operating system loads it and starts running it. Each process gets its own private address space, which holds the code, global data, a heap for dynamic allocations and a stack for function calls. It also owns resources such as open files and sockets.

The kernel tracks every process in a process control block, or PCB. The PCB stores the process ID, the current state, the saved CPU registers including the program counter, scheduling details such as priority, memory mapping information and the list of open files. When you hear that the OS paused a process and resumed it later, the PCB is where everything needed to resume was kept.

Because each process has a separate address space, one process cannot read or corrupt another's memory by accident. That isolation is the main reason a crash in your browser tab does not take down your text editor.

sections.title: Process states and context switches
sections.text:
