A process moves through a small set of states. It starts as new, becomes ready once it can run, and becomes running when the scheduler gives it a CPU. If it asks for something slow, such as reading from disk, it moves to waiting (also called blocked). When the I/O finishes it goes back to ready, not straight to running. If the timer interrupt fires while it is running, it is preempted and also returns to ready. When it finishes it becomes terminated.

Switching the CPU from one process to another is a context switch. The kernel saves the outgoing process's registers into its PCB, loads the incoming process's registers, and switches the memory mapping. This is pure overhead: no user work happens during it, and caches and the TLB lose much of their useful contents, so the new process starts slower. That is why switching too often hurts throughput.

sections.title: Creating processes with fork
sections.text:
On Unix-like systems a new process is created with fork. The child is a near copy of the parent, and both continue from the line after the fork call. In code, the usual way to tell them apart is the return value: fork returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. A typical pattern is fork followed by exec in the child, which replaces the child's program with a new one.

Counting is a common interview question. Each fork doubles the number of processes executing the code after it. If a program calls fork three times in a row, you end up with 2 times 2 times 2, which is 8 processes, the original included.

Two edge cases matter. A zombie is a child that has exited but whose parent has not yet called wait to collect its exit status, so its PCB entry lingers. An orphan is a child whose parent exited first; it is adopted by init (PID 1) or by a designated subreaper process, which reaps it later.

sections.title: Threads and what they share
sections.text:
A thread is a single sequence of execution inside a process. A process can have many threads, and they all share the same code, global data, heap and open files. Each thread has its own stack, its own register set and its own program counter, because each one is at a different point in the code.

Sharing memory makes threads cheap to create and fast to switch between, since there is no address space change. It also makes communication easy: one thread writes to a shared object and another reads it. The cost is safety. Two threads touching the same data without coordination can produce wrong results, and a bug in one thread can crash the whole process.

Threads can be managed in user space by a library or directly by the kernel. Kernel threads can run truly in parallel on multiple cores and one blocking does not stall the others. Pure user-level threads switch faster but if one makes a blocking system call, the whole process can block.

sections.title: Choosing between processes and threads
sections.text:
Use separate processes when you want isolation. A web browser that runs each site in its own process limits the damage a crashing or malicious page can do. Processes talk to each other through inter-process communication such as pipes, message queues, sockets or explicitly shared memory, all of which cost more than a plain memory write.

Use threads when tasks need to share a lot of data and you can manage the synchronization. A server handling many requests against the same in-memory cache is a natural fit.

A clean way to say it in an interview: a process is the unit of resource ownership, and a thread is the unit of scheduling. The OS gives memory and files to processes, and it gives CPU time to threads.

keyPoints: A process has its own address space; threads in a process share code, data, heap and files.
Each thread keeps its own stack, registers and program counter.
The PCB stores everything the kernel needs to pause and resume a process.
After I/O completes, a waiting process goes to ready, not directly to running.
fork returns 0 in the child and the child PID in the parent; n forks in a row give 2^n processes.
Context switches are overhead, and process switches cost more than thread switches.

challenges.title: Counting forks
challenges.prompt: A program runs fork(); fork(); printf("hi"); with no error checks. How many times is "hi" printed?
challenges.explanation: The first fork turns one process into two. Both run the second fork, so there are four processes, and each prints once, giving 4. Answer 2 forgets that the child also runs the second fork, 3 counts forks plus one instead of doubling, and 6 does not follow from any doubling pattern.
challenges.hint: Every process alive at a fork call splits into two.

challenges.title: Not shared between threads
challenges.prompt: Two threads belong to the same process. Which of these does each thread have its own copy of?
challenges.explanation: Each thread runs its own sequence of function calls, so it needs a private stack along with its own registers and program counter. The heap, globals and open files belong to the process and are shared by all its threads, which is exactly why threads need synchronization when they touch them.
challenges.hint: Think about what records where each thread is in its own chain of function calls.

challenges.title: After the disk read
challenges.prompt: A process is waiting for a disk read. The read completes. What state does the process move to next?
challenges.explanation: Finishing I/O only makes the process eligible to run again, so it joins the ready queue and waits for the scheduler to pick it. It does not jump straight to running, because another process may already be on the CPU. It is not terminated, since it has more work to do, and new applies only to a process being created.
challenges.hint: Being able to run is not the same as being given the CPU.

challenges.title: Zombie process
challenges.prompt: Which situation creates a zombie process?
options: A child has exited but its parent has not yet called wait for it
A parent exits while its child is still running
A process is stuck waiting forever on I/O
A process uses too much memory and gets swapped out
challenges.explanation: A zombie is a finished child whose exit status has not been collected, so its process table entry stays around until the parent calls wait. A parent exiting first creates an orphan, not a zombie. A process stuck on I/O is simply blocked, and being swapped out is a memory management event that has nothing to do with exit status.
challenges.hint: The process is dead, but someone has not picked up its exit status yet.

challenges.title: Why thread switches are cheaper
challenges.prompt: Why is switching between two threads of the same process usually cheaper than switching between two processes?
options: Threads do not need their registers saved
Threads never get preempted by the timer
Threads always run on separate cores
The address space stays the same, so no memory map switch or TLB flush is needed
challenges.explanation: Threads of one process share the same address space, so the kernel only swaps registers and the stack pointer and keeps the memory mapping and the TLB contents. Registers still have to be saved for threads, threads can be preempted like anything else, and nothing guarantees they run on separate cores.
challenges.hint: Ask what stays the same when both threads live inside the same process.

guides.subject: Operating systems
guides.title: CPU scheduling
guides.summary: CPU scheduling decides which ready process runs next, and each algorithm trades off waiting time, fairness and responsiveness differently.

sections.title: What the scheduler is optimising
sections.text:
When several processes are ready, the short-term scheduler picks which one gets the CPU. You will be asked to compare algorithms using a few measures. Turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time. Waiting time is turnaround time minus the CPU burst, so it is the total time spent sitting in the ready queue. Response time is the gap between arrival and the first time the process gets the CPU. Throughput is how many processes finish per unit of time.

Algorithms are either non-preemptive, where a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks, or preemptive, where the OS can take the CPU away, for example when a timer fires or a more urgent process arrives. Interactive systems need preemption, otherwise one long job can freeze everything behind it.

sections.title: FCFS and SJF with a worked example
sections.text:
First come first served runs processes in arrival order. It is simple and fair in a queueing sense, but it suffers from the convoy effect: short jobs stuck behind a long one wait a long time.

Take three processes that all arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3, with CPU bursts of 10, 4 and 2. Under FCFS, P1 runs from 0 to 10, P2 from 10 to 14 and P3 from 14 to 16. The waiting times are 0, 10 and 14, so the average waiting time is 24 divided by 3, which is 8.

Shortest job first picks the smallest burst. The order becomes P3, P2, P1. P3 waits 0, P2 waits 2 and P1 waits 6, so the average is 8 divided by 3, about 2.67. Non-preemptive SJF gives the minimum average waiting time for a set of jobs that are all available. The catch is that the OS cannot know future burst lengths, so real systems estimate them, often with an exponential average of past bursts.

sections.title: SRTF, the preemptive version of SJF
sections.text:
Shortest remaining time first is SJF with preemption. Whenever a new process arrives, the scheduler compares its burst with the remaining time of the running process and switches if the newcomer is shorter.

Suppose P1 arrives at 0 with burst 7, P2 arrives at 2 with burst 3 and P3 arrives at 3 with burst 1. P1 runs from 0 to 2. At time 2 P1 has 5 left and P2 needs 3, so P2 takes over. At time 3 P2 has 2 left and P3 needs 1, so P3 runs from 3 to 4. Then P2 finishes from 4 to 6 and P1 finishes from 6 to 11.

Waiting time is completion minus arrival minus burst. P1 waits 11 minus 0 minus 7, which is 4. P2 waits 6 minus 2 minus 3, which is 1. P3 waits 4 minus 3 minus 1, which is 0. The average is 5 divided by 3, about 1.67. Both SJF and SRTF can starve a long job if short jobs keep arriving.

sections.title: Round robin and the time quantum
sections.text:
Round robin gives each ready process a fixed time quantum in turn. If a process is not done when its quantum expires, it goes to the back of the ready queue.

Use the same bursts as before, 10, 4 and 2, all arriving at 0, with a quantum of 4. P1 runs 0 to 4 and has 6 left. P2 runs 4 to 8 and finishes. P3 runs 8 to 10 and finishes. P1 then runs 10 to 16. Completion times are 16, 8 and 10, so waiting times are 6, 4 and 8, an average of 18 divided by 3, which is 6.

That average is worse than SJF, but round robin's strength is response time: no process waits more than (n minus 1) quanta before its first turn. The quantum size matters. If it is very large, round robin behaves like FCFS. If it is very small, the CPU spends a large share of its time on context switches.

sections.title: Priority scheduling and starvation
sections.text:
Priority scheduling runs the highest priority ready process. It can be preemptive or not. SJF is really a special case where priority is the inverse of the predicted burst.

The classic problem is starvation, also called indefinite blocking. A low priority process can sit in the ready queue forever if higher priority work keeps arriving. The standard fix is aging: the longer a process waits, the more its priority is raised, so eventually it must run.

Real systems often combine ideas. A multilevel queue keeps separate queues, for example one for interactive jobs and one for batch jobs, each with its own algorithm. A multilevel feedback queue lets processes move between levels, so a process that keeps using its full quantum drifts down and a process that often blocks for I/O stays near the top.

keyPoints: Waiting time = turnaround time - burst time; turnaround time = completion time - arrival time.
FCFS is simple but causes the convoy effect when a long job runs first.
Non-preemptive SJF minimises average waiting time when all jobs are available; SRTF is its preemptive form.
Round robin gives good response time; a huge quantum makes it FCFS, a tiny one wastes time switching.
SJF, SRTF and priority scheduling can starve processes; aging fixes priority starvation.

challenges.title: SJF average waiting time
challenges.prompt: Three processes arrive at time 0 with bursts 6, 2 and 4. Using non-preemptive SJF, what is the average waiting time?
challenges.explanation: SJF runs the bursts in the order 2, 4, 6. The waits are 0, then 2, then 2 plus 4 which is 6, for a total of 8 and an average of 8 divided by 3, about 2.67. The value 4.67 is what FCFS gives in the order 6, 2, 4 (waits 0, 6, 8). The others come from summing the wrong waits.
challenges.hint: Sort the bursts, then each process waits for the sum of the bursts before it.

challenges.title: Round robin finish time
challenges.prompt: P1 (burst 5) and P2 (burst 3) both arrive at time 0, P1 first. Round robin uses a quantum of 2. At what time does P2 finish?
challenges.explanation: P1 runs 0 to 2 (3 left), P2 runs 2 to 4 (1 left), P1 runs 4 to 6 (1 left), then P2 runs 6 to 7 and finishes. P1 finishes at 8, which is the distractor for anyone who mixes up the two. 5 is P2's burst plus one slice of P1, and 6 is when P1's second slice ends, but P2 still needs one more unit after that.
challenges.hint: Write the timeline in slices of 2 and alternate between the two processes.

challenges.title: Huge time quantum
challenges.prompt: In round robin, what happens if the time quantum is larger than every process burst?
challenges.explanation: If no process ever uses up its quantum, each one runs to completion in queue order, which is exactly first come first served. It does not reorder by burst length, so it is not SJF, it ignores priorities, and since every process gets its turn in order nothing starves.
challenges.hint: Ask whether a quantum ever actually expires.

challenges.title: Fixing starvation
challenges.prompt: Under priority scheduling, a low priority job has been waiting for hours. Which technique directly addresses this?
options: Aging, which raises the priority of jobs the longer they wait
challenges.explanation: Aging steadily raises a waiting job's priority, so it eventually outranks newer work and runs. A smaller quantum only matters for round robin within a priority level, non-preemptive scheduling still always picks the highest priority job, and memory has nothing to do with which job the CPU picks.
challenges.hint: The fix should change something about the waiting job over time.

challenges.title: SRTF completion
challenges.prompt: Under SRTF, P1 arrives at 0 with burst 6, P2 at 1 with burst 3, P3 at 2 with burst 1. When does P2 complete?
challenges.explanation: P1 runs 0 to 1 and is preempted by P2 (3 versus 5 remaining). At 2 P3 arrives needing 1 while P2 has 2 left, so P3 runs 2 to 3. P2 then runs its last 2 units from 3 to 5, and P1 finishes from 5 to 10. 4 forgets that P3 preempts P2, 9 is FCFS (P1 0 to 6, then P2 6 to 9), and 10 is non-preemptive SJF (P1 0 to 6, P3 6 to 7, P2 7 to 10), which is also when P1 finishes under SRTF.
challenges.hint: Recompare remaining times at every arrival, not just when a process finishes.

guides.subject: Operating systems
guides.title: Synchronization
guides.summary: Synchronization makes sure threads that share data take turns in critical sections, using tools such as mutexes, semaphores and condition variables.

sections.title: Race conditions and critical sections
sections.text:
A race condition happens when the result depends on the exact timing of threads that share data. The textbook case is count++ run by two threads. That one line is really three steps: load count into a register, add 1, store it back. If count is 0 and both threads load 0 before either stores, both store 1, and one increment is lost. The final value can be 1 even though you expected 2.

The piece of code that touches shared data is called a critical section. A correct solution must guarantee three things. Mutual exclusion: at most one thread is inside at a time. Progress: if nobody is inside and some threads want in, the choice cannot be postponed forever. Bounded waiting: once a thread asks to enter, there is a limit on how many times others can go ahead of it.

sections.title: Locks and mutexes
sections.text:
A mutex, short for mutual exclusion lock, is the simplest tool. A thread calls lock before the critical section and unlock after it. If the mutex is already held, the caller waits. A key property is ownership: only the thread that locked a mutex should unlock it.

Locks are built on atomic hardware instructions such as test-and-set or compare-and-swap, which read and update a memory word in one indivisible step. A spinlock keeps retrying in a loop while it waits. That burns CPU, but it avoids the cost of sleeping and waking, so it suits very short critical sections on a multi-core machine. A blocking mutex instead puts the waiting thread to sleep, which is better when the wait may be long.

Keep critical sections short. Holding a lock while doing slow work such as I/O forces every other thread to wait for no reason.

sections.title: Semaphores
sections.text:
A semaphore is an integer counter with two atomic operations. Wait, also called P or down, decrements the counter and blocks the caller if no units are available. Signal, also called V or up, increments the counter and wakes a waiting thread if there is one.

A counting semaphore starts at the number of identical resources. If you have 3 database connections, initialise it to 3. The first three threads that call wait get through, and a fourth or fifth caller blocks until someone signals. A binary semaphore only takes the values 0 and 1, so it can act like a lock.

The interview distinction between a mutex and a binary semaphore is ownership and purpose. A mutex is a lock owned by the thread that took it. A semaphore has no owner, so one thread can wait and a different thread can signal. That makes semaphores good for signalling between threads, for example a producer telling a consumer that data is ready.

sections.title: Producer and consumer with a bounded buffer
sections.text:
In the bounded buffer problem, producers add items to a buffer of size N and consumers remove them. You need three semaphores. Empty starts at N and counts free slots. Full starts at 0 and counts filled slots. Mutex starts at 1 and protects the buffer itself.

A producer does wait on empty, wait on mutex, adds the item, signal on mutex, signal on full. A consumer does wait on full, wait on mutex, removes an item, signal on mutex, signal on empty.

The order of the two waits matters. Suppose a producer takes the mutex first and then waits on empty while the buffer is full. It sleeps while holding the mutex, so no consumer can enter to free a slot, and everyone is stuck. Always wait for the resource count first and take the mutex last. This is a neat example of how a small ordering mistake becomes a deadlock.

sections.title: Monitors and condition variables
sections.text:
Semaphores are powerful but easy to misuse, since a single missing signal can hang a program. Monitors package shared data with the procedures that use it, and the language guarantees that only one thread is active inside the monitor at a time. Java's synchronized methods follow this idea.

Inside a monitor, a condition variable lets a thread wait until some state becomes true. Calling wait releases the monitor lock and sleeps atomically, so no wake-up is missed. Another thread changes the state and calls signal or notify.

Always recheck the condition in a while loop after waking, not with an if. Another thread may have changed the state between the signal and your thread getting the lock back, and many systems allow spurious wake-ups. Unlike a semaphore, a condition variable has no memory: a signal sent when nobody is waiting is simply lost.

keyPoints: count++ is load, add, store, so two unsynchronised threads can lose an update.
A critical section solution needs mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
A mutex has an owner; a semaphore is a counter that any thread can signal.
Spinlocks suit very short waits on multi-core systems; blocking locks suit longer waits.
In producer-consumer, wait on empty or full before taking the mutex, or you can deadlock.
Recheck a condition variable predicate in a while loop after waking.

challenges.title: Lost update
challenges.prompt: Shared x starts at 0. Two threads each run x++ once with no lock. Which final values of x are possible?
challenges.explanation: If the increments do not overlap, x ends at 2. If both threads load 0 before either stores, both store 1 and one update is lost, giving 1. It cannot end at 0 because at least one store of a value of 1 or more happens last. Saying only 2 ignores the race, and only 1 ignores the safe interleaving.
challenges.hint: Split x++ into load, add and store, then try interleaving them.

challenges.title: Counting semaphore
challenges.prompt: A semaphore is initialised to 3. Five threads call wait on it and nobody has called signal yet. How many threads are blocked?
challenges.explanation: The counter allows three threads through, one per unit. The fourth and fifth find no units left and block, so 2 are blocked. 3 confuses the threads that got in with those that are blocked, 0 ignores the limit, and 5 would only happen if the semaphore started at 0.
challenges.hint: The initial value is how many can pass before anyone has to wait.

challenges.title: Mutex versus semaphore
challenges.prompt: Thread A must tell thread B that a file has finished downloading. Which primitive fits best, and why?
options: A semaphore starting at 0, because a different thread from the waiter can signal it
A mutex, because only the locking thread can unlock it
A spinlock, because downloads are short
No primitive is needed, since threads share memory
challenges.explanation: B waits on a semaphore initialised to 0, and A signals it when the download is done. Semaphores have no owner, so cross-thread signalling is exactly their use. The ownership rule of a mutex is what makes it wrong here, a spinlock would waste CPU for a long wait, and sharing memory alone gives B no safe way to sleep until the event.
challenges.hint: One thread waits and a different thread announces the event.

challenges.title: Wrong order of waits
challenges.prompt: A producer calls wait(mutex) and then wait(empty) while the buffer is full. What happens?
options: The producer overwrites the oldest item
The consumer removes an item and the producer continues normally
Deadlock: the producer sleeps holding the mutex, so no consumer can free a slot
The semaphore value goes negative and the program crashes
challenges.explanation: The producer blocks on empty while still holding mutex. Every consumer needs the mutex before it can remove an item and signal empty, so nobody can proceed. The consumer cannot run normally for that reason, nothing overwrites items because the producer never reaches the buffer, and blocking is not a crash.
challenges.hint: Ask what the consumer needs before it can free a slot.

challenges.title: When a spinlock makes sense
challenges.prompt: When is a spinlock a better choice than a blocking mutex?
options: When the lock is held during disk I/O
On a single-core machine with long critical sections
When the thread holding the lock is likely to sleep
On a multi-core machine where the lock is held for only a few instructions
challenges.explanation: Spinning wastes CPU, but if the holder is running on another core and releases the lock almost immediately, spinning is cheaper than sleeping and waking. During disk I/O or when the holder sleeps, the spinner burns CPU for a long time. On a single core the spinner even prevents the holder from running to release it.
challenges.hint: Spinning only pays off if the lock is about to be released by someone running in parallel.

guides.subject: Operating systems
guides.title: Deadlocks
guides.summary: A deadlock is a set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another in the set, and it needs all four Coffman conditions to occur.

sections.title: What a deadlock is
sections.text:
A deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are all blocked, and each one is waiting for a resource that another process in the same set holds. None of them can move, so none of them will ever release what the others need.

The simplest example uses two locks. Thread T1 takes lock A and then asks for lock B. At the same moment thread T2 takes lock B and then asks for lock A. T1 waits for T2 and T2 waits for T1, forever.

Do not confuse deadlock with starvation. In starvation a process could run in principle, but the scheduler or other processes keep pushing it aside. In deadlock nobody in the set can run at all. A livelock is a third case where processes keep changing state in response to each other, like two people stepping aside in a corridor, but no real progress happens.

sections.title: The four Coffman conditions
sections.text:
A deadlock can only happen if all four of these conditions hold at the same time.

Mutual exclusion: at least one resource can be held by only one process at a time. Hold and wait: a process holds at least one resource while waiting to get more. No preemption: a resource cannot be taken away from a process; it must be released voluntarily. Circular wait: there is a cycle of processes where each waits for a resource held by the next one in the cycle.

These are necessary conditions, so breaking any one of them is enough to make deadlock impossible. In a resource allocation graph, processes and resources are nodes, and edges show requests and assignments. If every resource has a single instance, a cycle in the graph means deadlock. If resources have several instances, a cycle means deadlock is possible but not certain.

sections.title: Prevention and the four strategies
sections.text:
There are four broad ways to handle deadlock. Prevention designs the system so one Coffman condition can never hold. Avoidance checks each request at run time and refuses any that could lead to trouble. Detection and recovery lets deadlocks happen, finds them, and breaks them. Ignoring the problem, sometimes called the ostrich approach, is what most general purpose systems do for application-level locks, because deadlocks are rare and prevention is costly.

Prevention in practice usually attacks circular wait. Number every lock and require each thread to acquire locks in increasing order. In the two-lock example, both threads would take A before B, so no cycle can form. Hold and wait can be removed by requesting everything at once, which wastes resources. No preemption can be removed for things like CPU registers or memory pages whose state can be saved, but not for a printer halfway through a job. Mutual exclusion usually cannot be removed for truly unsharable resources.

sections.title: Avoidance with the Banker's algorithm
sections.text:
The Banker's algorithm needs each process to declare its maximum demand in advance. A state is safe if there is some order in which every process can get its remaining need, finish, and return its resources. Before granting a request, the OS pretends to grant it and checks whether the resulting state is still safe. If not, the process waits.

Take one resource type with 10 units. P1 holds 3 with a maximum of 7, P2 holds 2 with a maximum of 4, and P3 holds 2 with a maximum of 5. That is 7 allocated, so 3 are available. The remaining needs are 4, 2 and 3. P2 can finish with 2 more, leaving 5 available. Then P3 needs 3, finishes, and leaves 7. Then P1 needs 4 and finishes. The order P2, P3, P1 shows the state is safe.

Now suppose P1 asks for 2 more. Available would drop to 1 while the needs become 2, 2 and 3. Nobody could finish, so the state is unsafe and the request is postponed. Note that unsafe does not mean deadlocked yet; it means the OS can no longer guarantee avoiding one.

sections.title: Detection and recovery
sections.text:
If you allow deadlocks to happen, you need a way to find them. With single-instance resources, the system builds a wait-for graph, where an edge from P1 to P2 means P1 waits for something P2 holds, and looks for a cycle. With multiple instances, it runs a detection algorithm similar to the Banker's safety check, but using current requests instead of declared maximums.

Recovery has two main options. You can terminate processes, either all of those in the deadlock or one at a time until the cycle breaks. Or you can preempt resources, taking a resource from a victim and rolling that process back to a safe checkpoint. Victims are usually chosen by cost: how long they have run, how much they hold, and how much work rollback would lose. Databases do this all the time. When two transactions deadlock on row locks, the database aborts one of them and the application retries.

keyPoints: Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait together.
Breaking any one Coffman condition prevents deadlock; global lock ordering breaks circular wait.
With single-instance resources, a cycle in the allocation graph means deadlock.
The Banker's algorithm grants a request only if a safe sequence still exists afterwards.
An unsafe state is not necessarily a deadlock, but the OS can no longer guarantee avoiding one.

challenges.title: Lock ordering
challenges.prompt: Every thread in a program must acquire locks in a fixed global order. Which Coffman condition does this break?
challenges.explanation: If everyone climbs the same ordering, no thread can hold a higher lock while waiting for a lower one, so a cycle of waits cannot form. Threads still hold locks exclusively, still hold one lock while waiting for the next, and locks still cannot be taken away, so the other three conditions remain.
challenges.hint: Picture the wait-for graph and ask what shape the ordering rules out.

challenges.title: Banker's request
challenges.prompt: 10 units of one resource. P1 holds 3 (max 7), P2 holds 2 (max 4), P3 holds 2 (max 5). P1 requests 2 more. What does the Banker's algorithm do?
options: Grants it, because 3 units are available
Refuses for now, because afterwards no process could be sure to finish
Grants it, because P1 is still under its maximum
challenges.explanation: After granting, available would be 1 and the remaining needs would be 2, 2 and 3, so no process could finish and the state would be unsafe. Having enough units available and staying under the maximum are both required but not sufficient. The Banker's algorithm makes the request wait; it never kills processes.
challenges.hint: Pretend to grant it, then look for any process whose remaining need fits in what is left.

challenges.title: Minimum resources
challenges.prompt: Three processes each need at most 3 units of one resource type. What is the smallest number of units that guarantees no deadlock?
challenges.explanation: In the worst case each process holds 2 units and waits for its third, using 6. One more unit, 7 in total, lets one process finish and release 3, which unblocks the rest. With 6 everyone can be stuck at 2. 8 and 9 also work but are not the minimum.
challenges.hint: Give every process one less than its maximum, then add just enough to break the tie.

challenges.title: Cycle with many instances
challenges.prompt: A resource allocation graph has a cycle, but one resource type in the cycle has two instances. What can you conclude?
options: A deadlock is possible but not certain
The system is definitely not deadlocked
challenges.explanation: With multiple instances, a process outside the cycle may hold the other instance and release it, breaking the wait. So a cycle is necessary but not sufficient. Only with single-instance resources does a cycle prove deadlock, and the graph is perfectly valid.
challenges.hint: Could someone outside the cycle free the extra instance?

challenges.title: Deadlock or starvation
challenges.prompt: A low priority process is ready to run but never gets the CPU because higher priority work keeps arriving. What is this?
challenges.explanation: The process could run if chosen, but it keeps being passed over, which is starvation. Deadlock and circular wait need processes blocked on resources held by each other, and livelock needs processes actively reacting to each other without progress.
challenges.hint: Is the process blocked on a resource, or just never picked?

guides.subject: Operating systems
guides.title: Memory management and paging
guides.summary: Paging splits memory into fixed-size pages and frames, with the TLB speeding up translation and page replacement handling memory that is overcommitted.

sections.title: Logical addresses and fragmentation
sections.text:
Every address your program uses is a logical, or virtual, address. The memory management unit translates it to a physical address in RAM. This lets each process believe it has a clean address space starting at zero, while the OS places its pieces wherever there is room.

Early systems gave each process one contiguous block. That leads to external fragmentation: there may be 100 MB free in total, but split into small gaps so no 50 MB process fits. Compaction can fix it but is expensive.

Internal fragmentation is waste inside an allocated unit. If memory is handed out in 4 KB pages and a process needs 10,300 bytes, it gets three pages, 12,288 bytes, and wastes 1,988 bytes in the last page. Paging removes external fragmentation entirely but keeps a little internal fragmentation, at most one page minus one byte per region.

sections.title: How paging translates an address
sections.text:
Paging cuts logical memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size. Any page can go in any free frame. A per-process page table maps page numbers to frame numbers.

A logical address splits into a page number and an offset. With a page size of 2 to the power d, the low d bits are the offset. For 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages, 12 bits are the offset and 20 bits are the page number, so the page table can have 2 to the power 20 entries, about a million.

Here is a small worked example with 4,096-byte pages. Logical address 8,200 is in page 8,200 divided by 4,096, which is page 2, at offset 8,200 minus 8,192, which is 8. If the page table says page 2 lives in frame 5, the physical address is 5 times 4,096 plus 8, which is 20,488. Large page tables are handled with multi-level page tables or inverted page tables.

sections.title: The TLB and effective access time
sections.text:
With a page table in memory, every load or store would need two memory accesses: one to read the page table entry and one for the data. The translation lookaside buffer, or TLB, is a small fast cache of recent page-to-frame mappings inside the CPU. On a TLB hit, translation costs almost nothing. On a miss, the hardware or OS walks the page table and fills the TLB.

You may be asked for the effective access time. Suppose a memory access takes 50 ns, a TLB lookup takes 5 ns, and the hit ratio is 90 percent. A hit costs 5 plus 50, which is 55 ns. A miss costs 5 plus 50 for the page table plus 50 for the data, which is 105 ns. The effective time is 0.9 times 55 plus 0.1 times 105, which is 49.5 plus 10.5, or 60 ns.

TLBs work well because programs have locality: they keep touching the same few pages for a while.

sections.title: Page faults and replacement
sections.text:
With demand paging, a page is loaded only when it is first touched. Each page table entry has a valid bit. Accessing an invalid page triggers a page fault: the OS finds the page on disk, picks a free frame, reads the page in, updates the table, and restarts the instruction. Faults are very expensive because disk is far slower than RAM.

When no frame is free, a replacement policy chooses a victim. FIFO evicts the oldest loaded page. LRU evicts the page not used for the longest time. Optimal evicts the page that will not be needed for the longest time in the future; it cannot be built but is the yardstick for others.

With 3 frames and the reference string 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, FIFO faults on 1, 2 and 3, hits on 1, faults on 4 and evicts 1, hits on 2, then faults on 5 and evicts 2, for 5 faults in total. FIFO can also show Belady's anomaly, where giving it more frames causes more faults. LRU and optimal never do.

sections.title: Thrashing and the working set
sections.text:
Thrashing is when the system spends most of its time moving pages in and out instead of doing useful work. It happens when the processes in memory together need more frames than exist, so each one keeps faulting and stealing frames from the others.

The classic trap is a naive scheduler. It sees low CPU utilisation, because everyone is waiting on page faults, and admits more processes to keep the CPU busy. That makes the shortage worse and utilisation falls further.

The working set of a process is the set of pages it used in a recent window of time. If the OS keeps each process's working set in memory, faults stay low. When the total working sets exceed physical memory, the right move is to suspend or swap out a whole process, not add more. A related approach watches each process's page fault frequency and gives it more frames when the rate is high or takes some away when it is low.

keyPoints: Paging removes external fragmentation but leaves some internal fragmentation in the last page.
A logical address is page number plus offset; physical address = frame number x page size + offset.
The TLB caches translations; a miss costs an extra memory access for the page table.
A page fault means the page is not in memory, so the OS must load it from disk.
FIFO can suffer Belady's anomaly; LRU and optimal cannot.
Thrashing happens when working sets exceed physical memory; reduce the number of processes to fix it.

challenges.title: Address translation
challenges.prompt: Page size is 1,024 bytes. Logical address 3,000 is accessed and its page maps to frame 7. What is the physical address?
challenges.explanation: 3,000 divided by 1,024 is page 2 with offset 3,000 minus 2,048, which is 952. Frame 7 starts at 7 times 1,024, which is 7,168, so the physical address is 7,168 plus 952, which is 8,120. 7,952 multiplies the frame number by 1,000 instead of 1,024, 10,168 adds the whole logical address to the frame base, and 3,952 adds the offset to the logical address instead of to the frame's base address.
challenges.hint: First split the address into page number and offset, then rebuild it with the frame number.

challenges.title: Effective access time
challenges.prompt: Memory access is 100 ns, TLB lookup is 10 ns and the TLB hit ratio is 90 percent. What is the effective memory access time?
challenges.explanation: A hit costs 10 + 100 = 110 ns. A miss costs 10 + 100 for the page table + 100 for the data = 210 ns. The average is 0.9 x 110 + 0.1 x 210 = 99 + 21 = 120 ns. 110 and 210 are just the hit and miss costs, and 130 counts the extra page table access twice on a miss.
challenges.hint: Work out the cost of a hit and of a miss, then weight them by how often each happens.

challenges.title: FIFO page faults
challenges.prompt: With 3 frames, initially empty, and the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, how many page faults does FIFO cause?
challenges.explanation: 1, 2 and 3 fault and fill the frames. 4 faults and evicts 1. Then 1 faults and evicts 2, and 2 faults and evicts 3. Every reference faults, so the total is 6. Answers of 4 or 5 assume 1 or 2 are still resident, but FIFO evicted each one just before it was needed again.
challenges.hint: Track the frames after each reference and remember FIFO evicts the earliest loaded page.

challenges.title: Internal fragmentation
challenges.prompt: Pages are 2,048 bytes. A process needs 9,000 bytes of memory. How many bytes are lost to internal fragmentation?
challenges.explanation: 9,000 bytes need 5 pages, since 4 pages hold only 8,192. Five pages hold 10,240 bytes, and 10,240 minus 9,000 is 1,240. 808 is 9,000 minus 8,192, the amount that spills into the fifth page rather than the waste. 2,048 is a whole page, but most of the last page is used, and 0 would only be true if the size were an exact multiple of the page size.
challenges.hint: Round the size up to whole pages, then subtract what is actually needed.

challenges.title: Responding to thrashing
challenges.prompt: CPU utilisation is low and the disk is busy with paging. What is the right response?
options: Admit more processes to keep the CPU busy
Switch from LRU to FIFO replacement
Suspend some processes so the rest can keep their working sets in memory
challenges.explanation: This is thrashing: the working sets of the running processes do not fit in memory. Reducing the number of processes frees frames so the others stop faulting. Admitting more processes makes it worse, FIFO is not better than LRU at this, and a shorter quantum changes CPU sharing, not memory pressure.
challenges.hint: The CPU is idle because processes are waiting on the disk, not because there is too little work.

guides.subject: Operating systems
guides.title: File systems
guides.summary: A file system maps names to data blocks on disk, using directories, inodes, allocation schemes and journaling to keep files organised and safe.

sections.title: Files, directories and metadata
sections.text:
To a user, a file is a named sequence of bytes. To the file system, it is metadata plus a set of disk blocks holding the data. Metadata includes the size, owner, permissions, timestamps and the locations of the data blocks.

A directory is itself a special file whose contents are a list of entries, each mapping a name to the file it refers to. Directories nest to form a tree, and a path such as /home/asha/notes.txt is resolved one component at a time, starting from the root directory.

When a program opens a file, the OS resolves the path once, loads the metadata, and returns a file descriptor, a small integer that indexes a per-process table of open files. Later reads and writes use the descriptor, so the path is not looked up again on every call. The open file entry also tracks the current offset, which is why two successive reads continue where the last one stopped.

sections.title: Inodes in Unix file systems
sections.text:
Unix-style file systems store each file's metadata in an inode, short for index node. An inode holds the file type, size, owner, permissions, timestamps, a link count and pointers to the data blocks. Notably, it does not hold the file name. Names live only in directory entries, which map a name to an inode number.

An inode usually has a handful of direct pointers plus single, double and triple indirect pointers. A single indirect pointer points to a block that contains more block pointers. Say blocks are 4 KB, pointers are 4 bytes, and there are 12 direct pointers. Direct pointers cover 12 times 4 KB, which is 48 KB. One indirect block holds 4,096 divided by 4, which is 1,024 pointers, covering 1,024 times 4 KB, which is 4 MB. This design makes small files fast to reach while still allowing very large files through the deeper levels.

sections.title: Hard links and soft links
sections.text:
Because names are separate from inodes, a single file can have several names. A hard link is just another directory entry pointing to the same inode. The inode's link count tracks how many names exist. Deleting a name removes one entry and decrements the count; the data is freed only when the count reaches zero and no process has the file open.

So if a.txt has a hard link b.txt and you delete a.txt, b.txt still opens the same data. Hard links normally cannot point to directories and cannot cross file systems, since inode numbers are only unique within one file system.

A soft link, or symbolic link, is a small separate file whose content is a path. Opening it makes the OS follow that path. Soft links can cross file systems and point to directories, but if the target is deleted or moved, the link dangles and opening it fails.

sections.title: How blocks are allocated
sections.text:
The file system must decide which disk blocks belong to each file. Contiguous allocation gives a file one run of consecutive blocks. Sequential and random access are both fast, since block i is just the start plus i, but it causes external fragmentation and makes files hard to grow.

Linked allocation stores a pointer to the next block inside each block. There is no external fragmentation and files grow easily, but reaching block 500 means following 499 pointers, and one corrupted pointer loses the rest of the file. The FAT design moves those next pointers into a file allocation table at the start of the volume, which is small enough to cache in memory, so following the chain no longer needs a disk read per block.

Indexed allocation, which inodes use, keeps all of a file's block pointers in one place. Random access is fast and there is no external fragmentation, at the cost of space for the index. Free blocks are often tracked with a bitmap, one bit per block, which makes finding runs of free space quick.

sections.title: Crash consistency and journaling
sections.text:
Creating or growing a file updates several structures: the data block, the inode, the free-space bitmap and maybe a directory. If power fails halfway through, the disk can be left inconsistent, for example a block marked used that no file points to, or an inode pointing to a block still marked free.

Older systems fixed this with a full check at boot, such as fsck, which scans every structure and can take a very long time on large disks. Journaling file systems such as ext4 and NTFS first write a description of the planned changes to a log, called the journal, and mark it committed. Only then do they apply the changes in place. After a crash, the system replays committed journal entries and discards incomplete ones, so recovery takes seconds.

ext4 by default (data=ordered mode) and NTFS journal only metadata, not file contents. That keeps the structure consistent after a crash, but data written just before the crash can still be lost or only partly written. ext4's data=journal mode also logs file data, at the cost of writing it twice.

keyPoints: A directory maps names to inode numbers; the inode stores metadata and block pointers, not the name.
A hard link is another name for the same inode; data is freed when the link count hits zero.
A soft link stores a path and dangles if the target is removed.
Contiguous allocation is fast but fragments; linked is slow for random access; indexed balances both.
Journaling logs changes before applying them, so crash recovery is fast.

challenges.title: Where the name lives
challenges.prompt: In a Unix file system, where is a file's name stored?
options: In the directory entry that points to the inode
In the first data block of the file
challenges.explanation: Directory entries map names to inode numbers, and the inode holds everything else. That separation is what lets one inode have several hard-linked names. The data blocks hold only file content, and the superblock describes the whole file system, not individual files.
challenges.hint: If one file can have two names, the name cannot be part of the file itself.

challenges.title: Deleting a hard-linked file
challenges.prompt: a.txt has a hard link named b.txt. You delete a.txt. What happens when you open b.txt?
options: It fails because the data was freed
It opens normally with the same contents
It opens a copy taken when the link was made
challenges.explanation: Both names point to the same inode. Deleting a.txt drops the link count from 2 to 1, so the inode and its data stay. The data is not freed until the count reaches zero, nothing is emptied, and a hard link never makes a copy. A soft link, by contrast, would dangle here.
challenges.hint: Think about the inode link count before and after the delete.

challenges.title: Inode reach
challenges.prompt: Blocks are 4 KB, block pointers are 4 bytes, and an inode has 12 direct pointers and one single indirect pointer. What is the largest file it can address?
challenges.explanation: Direct pointers reach 12 x 4 KB = 48 KB. The indirect block holds 4,096 / 4 = 1,024 pointers, reaching 1,024 x 4 KB = 4,096 KB. Together that is 48 + 4,096 = 4,144 KB. 48 KB ignores the indirect pointer, 4 MB ignores the direct ones, and 52 KB counts the indirect block as a single data block.
challenges.hint: Add what the direct pointers cover to what one full block of pointers covers.

challenges.title: Random access
challenges.prompt: Which allocation method is slowest for reading block 1,000 of a large file directly?
options: Linked allocation with pointers stored in each block
challenges.explanation: Linked allocation must read through the chain from the start, following 999 pointers stored on disk. Contiguous allocation computes the block address directly, and indexed allocation looks it up in the index, so both are fast. They clearly are not equal.
challenges.hint: Which method has to visit earlier blocks just to find the next one?

challenges.title: Why journaling helps
challenges.prompt: What is the main benefit of a journaling file system?
options: It makes files smaller on disk
It removes the need for inodes
It lets each file have multiple names
After a crash it can recover a consistent state quickly by replaying the log instead of scanning the whole disk
challenges.explanation: Journaling records intended changes before applying them, so after a crash the system replays committed entries and drops incomplete ones without a full scan. It does not compress files, ext4 and others still use inodes, and multiple names come from hard links, not from journaling.
challenges.hint: Think about what happens when power fails in the middle of an update.

guides.subject: SQL
guides.title: SELECT and filtering
guides.summary: How a SELECT query is evaluated, how WHERE decides which rows survive, and why NULL breaks the usual rules of comparison.

sections.title: The order a query is evaluated in
sections.text:
A SELECT statement is written in one order but evaluated in another. Logically, the database starts with FROM to decide which tables supply rows, applies WHERE to keep only the rows that pass, forms groups with GROUP BY, filters those groups with HAVING, computes the SELECT list, and finally sorts with ORDER BY. A row limit such as LIMIT or FETCH FIRST comes last of all. Real engines reorder the physical work for speed, but the result must always match this logical order.

This order explains rules that otherwise look arbitrary. Take a table students(id, name, city, year, score). In standard SQL you cannot write SELECT name, score * 2 AS doubled FROM students WHERE doubled > 100, because WHERE runs before the SELECT list has created the alias doubled. You can write ORDER BY doubled, since ORDER BY runs after SELECT. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server reject the alias in WHERE; SQLite accepts it as an extension, but interviewers expect the standard answer. When a query surprises you, walk it through the logical order and ask what exists at each step.

sections.title: Filtering rows with WHERE
sections.text:
WHERE takes a condition and keeps each row for which that condition is true. You build conditions from comparisons (=, <>, <, >, <=, >=) joined with AND, OR and NOT. AND binds more tightly than OR, so city = 'Pune' OR city = 'Delhi' AND year = 2 means city = 'Pune' OR (city = 'Delhi' AND year = 2). Add parentheses whenever you mix the two; they cost nothing and remove all doubt for the next reader.

A few shorthands are worth knowing well. BETWEEN 50 AND 70 is inclusive at both ends, exactly the same as score >= 50 AND score <= 70. IN ('Pune', 'Delhi') is shorthand for a chain of equalities joined by OR. LIKE matches text patterns: % stands for any run of characters, including none, and _ stands for exactly one character. So name LIKE 'Ra_%' matches Ravi and Raj but not a name that is just Ra. Whether LIKE is case sensitive depends on the database and its collation: PostgreSQL's LIKE is case sensitive (ILIKE is not), SQLite's ignores case for ASCII letters by default, so 'Ra_%' also matches ravi there, and MySQL follows the column's collation, which is usually case insensitive.

sections.title: NULL and three-valued logic
sections.text:
NULL means a value is missing or unknown. It is not zero and not an empty string, and it is not equal to anything, not even another NULL. Any ordinary comparison involving NULL, such as city = NULL or NULL = NULL, evaluates to unknown rather than true or false. SQL therefore works with three truth values: true, false and unknown.

WHERE keeps a row only when its condition is true. Rows where the condition is false or unknown are both dropped. This is why WHERE city <> 'Pune' silently skips students whose city is NULL: for them the comparison is unknown, not true. To test for a missing value, use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL, which always give a plain true or false. If you want the NULL rows kept in the earlier filter, say so: WHERE city <> 'Pune' OR city IS NULL.

NOT does not rescue you either. NOT unknown is still unknown, so wrapping a comparison in NOT never brings back rows that were lost to NULL.

sections.title: Removing duplicates, sorting and limiting
sections.text:
SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result, comparing whole rows across every selected column. For this purpose NULLs count as equal to each other, so a city column holding Pune, NULL, Pune and NULL gives two distinct rows: Pune and NULL. GROUP BY treats NULLs the same way.

ORDER BY sorts the final result. You can sort by several columns, as in ORDER BY year DESC, name, where the second column only breaks ties in the first. Where NULLs land by default depends on the database: PostgreSQL and Oracle sort NULL as if it were larger than every value, so NULLs come last ascending and first descending, while MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server sort it as smaller, so NULLs come first ascending and last descending. Standard SQL lets you write NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST; PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite (from version 3.30) accept it, but MySQL and SQL Server do not, so there you put a key such as CASE WHEN city IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ahead of the column.

Without ORDER BY, the database may return rows in any order, and that order can change between runs, so never rely on it. To keep only part of a result, standard SQL uses FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY, and MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite also accept LIMIT 5. A limit without ORDER BY gives you some five rows, not the top five.

keyPoints: Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, then any row limit.
A SELECT alias is not visible in WHERE in standard SQL, but it is visible in ORDER BY.
AND binds tighter than OR; use parentheses whenever you mix them.
Any comparison with NULL is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows that are true; test with IS NULL.
BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends, and DISTINCT treats NULLs as one value.
Row order is only guaranteed by ORDER BY, so a limit without it is not a top-N.

challenges.title: Not equal and NULL
challenges.prompt: The students table has five rows whose city values are Pune, Delhi, NULL, Pune and Mumbai. What does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students WHERE city <> 'Pune' return?
challenges.explanation: Delhi and Mumbai pass the test. For the NULL row, NULL <> 'Pune' is unknown, and WHERE drops anything that is not true, so the count is 2. Answering 3 assumes NULL counts as different from Pune, which SQL does not do. 1 and 5 do not match any reading of the rows.
challenges.hint: Work out the truth value of the condition for the row whose city is NULL.

challenges.title: AND and OR together
challenges.prompt: Rows: (Asha, Pune, year 1), (Ben, Delhi, year 1), (Chen, Delhi, year 2), (Dev, Pune, year 3). Which names does SELECT name FROM students WHERE city = 'Pune' OR city = 'Delhi' AND year = 2 return?
challenges.explanation: AND binds tighter than OR, so the condition is city = 'Pune' OR (city = 'Delhi' AND year = 2). Asha and Dev pass the first part, Chen passes the second, and Ben fails both. Chen only would be the result of (Pune OR Delhi) AND year = 2. All four would need year = 2 to be ignored entirely.
challenges.hint: Put in the parentheses SQL adds for you before evaluating each row.

challenges.title: Alias in WHERE
challenges.prompt: What happens in standard SQL when you run SELECT name, score * 2 AS doubled FROM students WHERE doubled > 100?
options: It fails, because WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list defines doubled
It works and returns students whose score is above 50
It works but ignores the WHERE clause, so every student is returned
challenges.explanation: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias doubled does not exist yet and the column reference cannot be resolved. You would repeat the expression (WHERE score * 2 > 100) or wrap the query in a subquery. SQLite accepts the alias as an extension and would return students scoring above 50, but that is not standard. No database silently ignores a WHERE clause.
challenges.hint: Walk the query through the logical evaluation order and ask what exists at each step.

challenges.title: BETWEEN boundaries
challenges.prompt: A results table has scores 49, 50, 65, 70 and 71. How many rows does WHERE score BETWEEN 50 AND 70 keep?
challenges.explanation: BETWEEN includes both ends, so 50, 65 and 70 pass, giving 3. Answering 1 treats both ends as exclusive, 2 treats one end as exclusive, and 4 wrongly lets one of the outside values through.
challenges.hint: Rewrite BETWEEN as two comparisons and check each boundary value.

challenges.title: DISTINCT with NULLs
challenges.prompt: A city column holds Pune, NULL, Pune, NULL and Delhi. How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students return?
challenges.explanation: DISTINCT treats NULLs as duplicates of each other, so the result is Pune, Delhi and a single NULL: 3 rows. Answering 2 drops NULL entirely, and 4 keeps both NULLs as separate values, which DISTINCT does not do even though NULL = NULL is unknown in a WHERE clause.
challenges.hint: Recall how GROUP BY city would split these same five values.

guides.subject: SQL
guides.title: Joins
guides.summary: How inner, outer, cross and self joins combine rows, and how to predict the exact number of rows a join returns.

sections.title: What a join does
sections.text:
A join combines rows from two tables into wider rows. Use a small schema: students(id, name), courses(id, title) and enrollments(student_id, course_id), where each enrollment links one student to one course.

Conceptually, an inner join considers every pairing of a row from the left table with a row from the right table and keeps the pairs for which the ON condition is true. SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s INNER JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id produces one row for each enrollment that has a matching student. Writing plain JOIN means the same thing as INNER JOIN.

Two consequences matter for predicting results. First, rows multiply: a student with three enrollments appears three times, once per match. Second, rows without a match disappear: a student with no enrollments is not in the result at all. Most surprises with joins come from forgetting one of these two facts, so count matches per key before you trust a total.

sections.title: Outer joins keep unmatched rows
sections.text:
A LEFT JOIN returns everything an inner join would, plus every left row that found no match, padded with NULLs in the right table's columns. SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id lists every student; those with no enrollments appear once with course_id NULL. RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image, keeping every right row, and you can always rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN by swapping the tables. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.

The classic trap is where you put an extra condition. In a LEFT JOIN, a condition in ON decides which right rows match, and unmatched left rows survive regardless. The same condition in WHERE is applied after the join, to the padded rows too. Writing WHERE e.course_id = 10 throws away every padded row, because NULL = 10 is unknown, so the query quietly behaves like an inner join. If you want all students with their course 10 enrollment where one exists, the filter belongs in ON.

sections.title: Cross joins and self joins
sections.text:
A CROSS JOIN has no condition at all: it pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, so tables with m and n rows give m times n rows. That is useful for generating combinations, such as every student paired with every available exam slot. It also means that if either table is empty, the result is empty, because there is nothing to pair with. Forgetting the ON condition in older comma-style joins (FROM a, b) produces this same explosion by accident.

A self join joins a table to itself, using two aliases so you can tell the copies apart. With employees(id, name, manager_id), the query SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id pairs each employee with their manager's row. Because it is an inner join, the person at the top, whose manager_id is NULL, is left out. Change it to LEFT JOIN employees m and that person appears with a NULL manager name.

sections.title: Finding rows with no match
sections.text:
A frequent interview task is to find rows in one table that have no partner in another, such as students who have never enrolled. One standard pattern is the anti-join: SELECT s.name FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id WHERE e.student_id IS NULL. The LEFT JOIN keeps every student, and the WHERE then keeps only the padded rows, which are exactly the students with no match. Test a column that cannot be NULL in a real match, such as the join key itself. NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery does the same job and is often clearer.

Remember that NULL keys never match in an ordinary join. If both tables contain a NULL in the join column, a = b is unknown for that pair, so they are not joined. An enrollment row with a NULL student_id simply drops out of an inner join, and in a LEFT JOIN from enrollments it would appear with NULL student columns.

keyPoints: An inner join keeps only pairs where ON is true; unmatched rows vanish and multiple matches multiply rows.
LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills the right side with NULLs when nothing matches.
In an outer join, a filter on the right table in WHERE turns it back into an inner join; put it in ON instead.
CROSS JOIN returns m times n rows, so an empty table on either side gives an empty result.
A self join uses two aliases of one table, such as employees and their managers.
NULL join keys never match, and LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL finds rows with no partner.

challenges.title: Counting LEFT JOIN rows
challenges.prompt: students has ids 1, 2, 3 and 4. enrollments has (student_id, course_id) rows (1, 10), (1, 20) and (2, 20). How many rows does SELECT * FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id return?
challenges.explanation: Student 1 matches twice, student 2 once, and students 3 and 4 have no match, so each appears once with NULLs: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5. 4 assumes a left join never adds rows beyond the left table, 3 is the inner join count, and 7 adds the two table sizes.
challenges.hint: Count the matches for each student, using one for a student with no matches.

challenges.title: Filter in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN
challenges.prompt: Using the same data, how many rows does SELECT s.id, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id WHERE e.course_id = 10 return?
challenges.explanation: The join produces 5 rows, then WHERE keeps only rows where course_id = 10 is true. Only (1, 10) qualifies; the padded rows have course_id NULL, and NULL = 10 is unknown, so they are dropped. 4 is what you get with the condition moved into ON. 2 would count student 1's two enrollments.
challenges.hint: Decide whether this filter runs before or after the NULL padding is added.

challenges.title: Cross join with an empty table
challenges.prompt: Table a has 3 rows and table b has no rows. What does SELECT * FROM a CROSS JOIN b return?
options: 3 rows, one per row of a, with NULLs for b
challenges.explanation: A cross join returns every pairing, and 3 times 0 is 0. There is no padding in a cross join; that behaviour belongs to outer joins. A single row of NULLs is not produced by any join type here.
challenges.hint: Think about what each row of a has to be paired with.

challenges.title: NULL join keys
challenges.prompt: Table a has x values 1, NULL and 2. Table b has x values NULL, 2 and 2. How many rows does SELECT * FROM a JOIN b ON a.x = b.x return?
challenges.explanation: The value 2 in a matches both 2s in b, giving 2 rows. The NULLs never match because NULL = NULL is unknown, and 1 has no partner. Answering 3 counts the NULL pair as a match, and 1 forgets that one row can match several.
challenges.hint: Treat NULL = NULL exactly as the ON clause would.

challenges.title: Keeping the top of a hierarchy
challenges.prompt: employees has (id, name, manager_id): (1, Ria, NULL), (2, Sam, 1), (3, Tom, 1), (4, Uma, 2). SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id returns Sam, Tom and Uma with their managers. Which change also returns Ria with a NULL manager name?
options: Change the ON clause to m.manager_id = e.id
challenges.explanation: Ria is lost because her manager_id is NULL, so the inner join finds no match. A LEFT JOIN keeps her and fills m.name with NULL, giving 4 rows. Adding WHERE e.manager_id IS NULL to the inner join returns nothing, since Ria was already gone. Swapping the ON columns pairs each manager with their reports instead, which answers a different question.
challenges.hint: Work out why Ria's row disappears from the original query.

guides.subject: SQL
guides.title: Aggregation and GROUP BY
guides.summary: How aggregate functions treat NULLs, how GROUP BY forms groups, and when to filter with WHERE versus HAVING.

sections.title: Aggregate functions and NULL
sections.text:
An aggregate function reduces many rows to one value. The common ones are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. Without GROUP BY, the whole filtered table is one group, so SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments returns a single row.

NULL handling is where most interview questions live. COUNT(*) counts rows, whatever they contain. COUNT(score) counts only rows where score is not NULL. SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX also skip NULLs. So for scores 40, NULL, 50, NULL and 60, COUNT(*) is 5, COUNT(score) is 3 and AVG(score) is 50, because the total of 150 is divided by 3, not by 5. If you want missing scores treated as zero, say so with COALESCE(score, 0).

An aggregate over no rows at all still returns one row when there is no GROUP BY. COUNT gives 0, but SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX give NULL, because there is nothing to add up or compare. Wrap them in COALESCE when you need a 0 instead. With a GROUP BY, the same empty input forms no groups, so the query returns no rows at all.

sections.title: Grouping rows with GROUP BY
sections.text:
GROUP BY splits the rows into groups that share the same values in the listed columns, then produces one output row per group. SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id gives each course with its number of enrollments. Grouping by two columns, such as GROUP BY course_id, year, makes one group per distinct pair.

Since each group becomes one row, every expression in the SELECT list must have one value per group. The safe rule is that each selected column is either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate. (Newer standards, PostgreSQL and MySQL also accept a column that is fixed by the grouped columns, such as any column of a table grouped by its primary key.) Selecting student_id while grouping only by course_id is an error in PostgreSQL and SQL Server, because a course has many students. MySQL rejects it too while its default ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode is on, but accepts it with that mode switched off, and SQLite always accepts it. Both then return student_id from some row of the group, which hides the bug.

NULLs in the grouping column form a single group of their own. If three rows have city NULL, they become one group, where COUNT(*) is 3 but COUNT(city) is 0.

sections.title: WHERE versus HAVING
sections.text:
WHERE and HAVING both filter, but at different moments. WHERE runs before grouping and removes individual rows. HAVING runs after grouping and removes whole groups. Because aggregates are only computed once groups exist, you cannot use COUNT or SUM in WHERE; that is exactly what HAVING is for.

Consider this query: SELECT student_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE score >= 50 GROUP BY student_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2. Read it in logical order. WHERE first throws away every enrollment below 50. GROUP BY then collects what is left per student. HAVING keeps the students who still have at least two rows. The answer is students with at least two passing scores, which is different from students with at least two scores of any kind.

A good habit: if a condition is about a single row, put it in WHERE so fewer rows reach the grouping step. Only conditions about the group as a whole belong in HAVING.

sections.title: Common aggregation mistakes
sections.text:
The first mistake is aggregating after a join that multiplied rows. If you join students to enrollments and then to payments, a student with three enrollments and two payments produces six joined rows, and SUM(payments.amount) counts each payment three times. Aggregate each child table separately in a subquery, then join the totals.

The second is mixing up COUNT(*), COUNT(col) and COUNT(DISTINCT col). COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) counts different courses, ignoring NULLs, while COUNT(*) counts rows. Asking how many courses a student took and how many enrollments they have are different questions.

The third is expecting an empty group to appear. GROUP BY only creates groups for values present in the filtered rows. A course with no enrollments will not show up with a count of 0 unless you start from courses and LEFT JOIN enrollments, then count a column from the enrollments side, such as COUNT(e.student_id), so the padded row counts as 0.

keyPoints: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) and the other aggregates skip NULLs.
Over zero rows, COUNT returns 0 while SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX return NULL.
Every selected column should be grouped or aggregated; SQLite, and MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off, let it slide.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after, and only HAVING can use aggregates.
NULLs in a grouping column form one group of their own.
Joins that multiply rows inflate SUM and COUNT, so aggregate before joining when needed.

challenges.title: Three aggregates, one NULL
challenges.prompt: A column score holds 10, NULL, 20 and 30. What does SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(score), AVG(score) return?
challenges.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all 4 rows. COUNT(score) skips the NULL, giving 3. AVG also skips NULL, so it is 60 / 3 = 20. Answering 15 divides 60 by 4 as if the NULL were zero, and 3 for COUNT(*) wrongly skips the NULL row.
challenges.hint: Check which of these three functions looks at the value and which only counts rows.

challenges.title: Filtering on a count
challenges.prompt: You want departments that offer more than two courses, from courses(id, title, dept). Which query is correct?
options: SELECT dept FROM courses WHERE COUNT(*) > 2 GROUP BY dept
SELECT dept FROM courses GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) > 2 FROM courses GROUP BY dept
challenges.explanation: The condition is about each group's size, so it must go in HAVING, which runs after grouping. The WHERE version is an error because aggregates do not exist yet when WHERE runs. The third query returns every department with a true or false flag (1 or 0 in SQLite and MySQL) instead of filtering them.
challenges.hint: Ask whether the condition is about one row or about a whole group.

challenges.title: The NULL group
challenges.prompt: A city column holds Pune, Pune, NULL, Delhi and NULL. SELECT city, COUNT(*), COUNT(city) FROM students GROUP BY city. What is COUNT(city) on the row for the NULL group?
challenges.explanation: The two NULL rows form one group, so COUNT(*) there is 2. COUNT(city) counts non-NULL values of city, and the group has none, so it is 0. COUNT never returns NULL, so that option is out, and 2 is the COUNT(*) value.
challenges.hint: Compare what COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) each count.

challenges.title: WHERE then HAVING
challenges.prompt: enrollments has (student_id, score) rows (1, 60), (1, 80), (2, 90), (2, 30), (3, 70), (3, 75), (3, 20). How many rows does SELECT student_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE score >= 50 GROUP BY student_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 return?
challenges.explanation: WHERE first removes 30 and 20. What remains is student 1 with 2 rows, student 2 with 1 and student 3 with 2. HAVING keeps students 1 and 3, so 2 rows. Answering 3 applies HAVING to the unfiltered counts, as if WHERE ran after grouping.
challenges.hint: Apply WHERE to each row first, then count what is left per student.

challenges.title: Summing nothing
challenges.prompt: No enrollment has a score above 100. What does SELECT SUM(score) FROM enrollments WHERE score > 100 return?
challenges.explanation: Without GROUP BY, an aggregate query always returns exactly one row, even if no input rows qualify. SUM of nothing is NULL, not 0; only COUNT returns 0 for an empty input. You would write COALESCE(SUM(score), 0) to get 0.
challenges.hint: Think about how many groups exist when there is no GROUP BY.

guides.subject: SQL
guides.title: Subqueries
guides.summary: Scalar, list and table subqueries, correlated versus non-correlated ones, and why NOT IN fails when a NULL is present.

sections.title: Three shapes of subquery
sections.text:
A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another statement, and what you may do with it depends on the shape of its result.

A scalar subquery returns one row and one column, so it can stand anywhere a single value can. SELECT name FROM students WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM students) compares each student with the overall average. If a scalar subquery returns more than one row, standard SQL raises an error at run time; PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle all do. SQLite is an exception: it raises no error and quietly uses whichever row the subquery happens to produce first, so the answer can change with the data's physical order.

A single-column subquery returning many rows feeds IN, ANY or ALL, as in WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments).

A subquery that returns a whole table can sit in FROM, where it is called a derived table. Standard SQL, MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL before version 16 require it to have an alias (SQLite does not), so always give one: SELECT * FROM (SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) t WHERE t.n > 30. This is a common way to filter on an aggregate or a window result computed one level down.

sections.title: Correlated and non-correlated subqueries
sections.text:
A non-correlated subquery stands on its own. You could cut it out and run it by itself, and the database can evaluate it once and reuse the result. The average in the previous section is an example.

A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer query, so its value depends on the current outer row. Using results(student, course, score), the query SELECT student FROM results r WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM results r2 WHERE r2.course = r.course) compares each score with the average of that row's own course. The reference to r.course is what makes it correlated.

Logically, a correlated subquery is evaluated once for every outer row. Optimizers frequently rewrite it into a join or a grouped computation, so it is not automatically slow, but that per-row model is the right way to reason about its result. A quick test in an interview: look inside the subquery for an alias that is only defined outside it.

sections.title: IN, EXISTS and the NOT IN trap
sections.text:
EXISTS (subquery) is true if the subquery returns at least one row; the values it returns do not matter, which is why people write SELECT 1 inside it. It is usually correlated: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id). IN compares a value with a list. For positive tests, IN and EXISTS normally give the same rows.

The negative forms differ when NULLs appear. x NOT IN (1, NULL) means x <> 1 AND x <> NULL. The second comparison is unknown, so the whole condition can never be true. If the subquery behind NOT IN returns even one NULL, the outer query returns no rows at all. Suppose students has ids 4, 5, 6 and 7, and enrollments.student_id holds 5, 6 and NULL. WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments) returns nothing, while WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id) returns students 4 and 7.

Prefer NOT EXISTS for anti-joins, or add WHERE student_id IS NOT NULL inside the NOT IN subquery.

sections.title: Subquery, join or CTE?
sections.text:
Many subqueries can be written as joins, but the two are not always equivalent. IN and EXISTS test membership, so each outer row appears at most once. A join returns one row per match. If student 1 has two enrollments, WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments) returns student 1 once, while joining students to enrollments returns them twice. Pick the form whose row count matches the question.

A common table expression, written with WITH, names a subquery up front: WITH course_avg AS (SELECT course, AVG(score) AS avg_score FROM results GROUP BY course) SELECT r.student FROM results r JOIN course_avg c ON c.course = r.course WHERE r.score > c.avg_score. This gives the same answer as the correlated version but reads top to bottom, and you can reference the CTE more than once.

For performance, do not assume one form always wins. Modern optimizers often produce the same plan for IN, EXISTS and the equivalent join. Write the clearest correct query first, then check the plan.

keyPoints: A scalar subquery must return at most one row; more than one is a run-time error in standard SQL.
A correlated subquery references the outer row and is logically evaluated once per outer row.
EXISTS cares only whether any row comes back, not what the row contains.
NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields a NULL; NOT EXISTS does not have this problem.
IN never duplicates outer rows, but a join returns one row per match.
A CTE (WITH) names a subquery so the main query reads top to bottom.

challenges.title: NOT IN meets NULL
challenges.prompt: students has (1, Al), (2, Bo), (3, Cy). enrollments.student_id holds 1 and NULL. What does SELECT name FROM students WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments) return?
challenges.explanation: For Bo the test is 2 <> 1 AND 2 <> NULL, which is true AND unknown, so unknown, and WHERE drops the row. The same happens for Cy, and Al fails outright. Bo and Cy is what NOT EXISTS returns. Only Cy has no basis in the data.
challenges.hint: Expand NOT IN into a chain of <> comparisons joined by AND.

challenges.title: IN does not duplicate
