challenges.prompt: students has (1, Al) and (2, Bo). enrollments has two rows, both with student_id 1. How many rows does SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments) return?
challenges.explanation: IN asks whether each student's id is in the list, so Al qualifies once and Bo does not: 1 row. 2 rows is what an inner join of students to enrollments would return, one per matching enrollment. 3 rows has no basis.
challenges.hint: Ask what IN checks for each student, and what a join would produce instead.

challenges.title: Spot the correlated subquery
challenges.prompt: Which of these queries contains a correlated subquery?
options: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE s.id IN (SELECT e.student_id FROM enrollments e WHERE e.course_id = 10)
SELECT name FROM students WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM students)
SELECT * FROM (SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) t WHERE n > 5
SELECT name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id)
challenges.explanation: Only the last subquery refers to s.id, a column of the outer query, so its result changes from one student to the next. The other three subqueries can each be run on their own and give the same result regardless of the outer row.
challenges.hint: Ask which subquery could not be cut out and run on its own.

challenges.title: Above the course average
challenges.prompt: results has (student, course, score): (A, DB, 70), (B, DB, 90), (C, OS, 60), (D, OS, 65), (E, OS, 70). Which students does SELECT student FROM results r WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM results r2 WHERE r2.course = r.course) return?
challenges.explanation: The subquery is correlated, so each row is compared with its own course average. DB averages 80, so B (90) passes and A fails. OS averages 65, so E (70) passes, while D (65) is equal, not greater, and C is below. B only is the answer against the overall average of 71. Including D ignores the strict greater-than.
challenges.hint: Compute one average per course, then compare each row with its own course's value.

challenges.title: Scalar subquery with many rows
challenges.prompt: In standard SQL, what happens with SELECT name FROM results WHERE score = (SELECT score FROM results WHERE course = 'OS') when three OS rows exist?
options: The query fails at run time because a scalar subquery returned more than one row
It behaves like IN and keeps rows whose score matches any OS score
It compares only against the first OS score
challenges.explanation: Using = with a subquery treats it as a single value, and three rows cannot be one value, so PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle raise an error. To match any of them, write IN or = ANY. SQLite is the exception: run there, the query succeeds and compares only against the first OS score the subquery yields, which is nonstandard and depends on an undefined row order, so it is not a result you should rely on.
challenges.hint: Consider what = expects on its right-hand side.

guides.subject: SQL
guides.title: Window functions
guides.summary: How window functions compute across related rows without collapsing them, and how ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK differ.

sections.title: Calculations that keep every row
sections.text:
GROUP BY collapses each group into a single row, so you lose the detail. A window function computes a value across a set of related rows but leaves every row in place. You recognise one by the OVER clause after the function.

With results(student, course, score), SELECT student, course, score, AVG(score) OVER (PARTITION BY course) AS course_avg FROM results returns every result row, each carrying the average of its own course. Doing the same with GROUP BY would need a grouped subquery joined back to the table.

Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, alongside the SELECT list, and before ORDER BY. That placement explains two things. A window sees only the rows that survived WHERE, and you can use a window function in SELECT and ORDER BY but not in WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING. Ordinary aggregates such as SUM and COUNT become window functions when you add OVER, and there are dedicated ones such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG and LEAD.

sections.title: PARTITION BY and ORDER BY inside OVER
sections.text:
PARTITION BY splits rows into independent windows, much as GROUP BY splits them into groups, except that no rows are merged. Each calculation restarts in every partition. Leave PARTITION BY out and the whole result is one window. COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY course) puts the size of each course on every row of that course.

ORDER BY inside OVER gives the rows within each partition an order. Ranking functions need it, and for aggregates it turns the result into a running calculation. SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) gives a running total.

Watch out for ties. When ORDER BY is present and no frame is written, the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and RANGE includes all peers, meaning rows with the same ORDER BY value. With amounts 40 on day 1, 25 and 15 on day 2, and 30 on day 3, both day 2 rows show 80, not 65 and then 80. If you want a strict row-by-row running total, write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW and add a tiebreaker column to the ORDER BY.

sections.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK
sections.text:
All three number rows according to the ORDER BY in OVER. They differ only in how they treat ties. Take scores 92, 85, 85, 85 and 70 ordered by score descending.

ROW_NUMBER gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Every row gets a unique number, so the three 85s get 2, 3 and 4, and which of them gets which is not defined unless you add a tiebreaker such as ORDER BY score DESC, student.

RANK gives 1, 2, 2, 2, 5. Tied rows share a rank, and the next row's rank is one more than the number of rows ahead of it, the way a race result works: three runners tied for second means nobody is third or fourth.

DENSE_RANK gives 1, 2, 2, 2, 3. Tied rows share a rank, but there are no gaps afterwards.

Choose by the question. Exactly N rows per group, ties broken arbitrarily: ROW_NUMBER. Everyone in the top N positions, ties included: RANK. The Nth highest distinct value, such as the second highest salary: DENSE_RANK.

sections.title: Filtering on a window result
sections.text:
A common task is the top N rows per group, such as the best two scores in each course. You cannot write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 2, because WHERE runs before window functions are computed. Instead, compute the number one level down and filter outside: SELECT * FROM (SELECT student, course, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY course ORDER BY score DESC) AS rn FROM results) t WHERE rn <= 2. A CTE written with WITH works the same way. Some databases add a QUALIFY clause for this, but it is not part of every engine.

Two more functions are worth knowing. LAG(score) OVER (PARTITION BY student ORDER BY exam_date) returns the value from the previous row in the window, and LEAD returns the next one. On the first row there is no previous row, so LAG returns NULL unless you pass a default as its third argument. They make questions such as change since the last exam a single pass with no self join.

keyPoints: A window function, marked by OVER, computes across related rows without collapsing them.
PARTITION BY restarts the calculation per group; ORDER BY inside OVER gives order and running results.
With ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default RANGE frame includes tied rows, so ties share a running total.
For ties: ROW_NUMBER is always unique, RANK leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK does not.
Window functions run after WHERE, so filter on them in an outer query or CTE.
LAG and LEAD read the previous and next row in the window.

challenges.title: DENSE_RANK after a tie
challenges.prompt: Scores are 95, 88, 88, 80 and 75. With DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC), what value does the 80 receive?
challenges.explanation: DENSE_RANK gives 95 rank 1, both 88s rank 2, and the next value continues without a gap, so 80 is 3. 4 is what RANK would give, since it skips a number after the two-way tie. 2 would mean 80 tied with the 88s.
challenges.hint: Write out the value DENSE_RANK gives each of the five scores in turn.

challenges.title: Exactly two per course
challenges.prompt: You need exactly two rows per course, the two highest scores, even when scores tie. Which function should number the rows inside each course partition?
challenges.explanation: ROW_NUMBER never repeats a number, so rn <= 2 gives exactly two rows per course. RANK and DENSE_RANK give tied rows the same number, so filtering on 2 or less can return three or more rows when there is a tie.
challenges.hint: Imagine the second and third highest scores in a course are equal, and apply rn <= 2 under each function.

challenges.title: Running total with a tie
challenges.prompt: payments has (day, amount): (1, 10), (2, 20), (2, 5), (3, 15). Using SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) with no frame clause, what running total is shown on each day 2 row?
challenges.explanation: With ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes every row with the same day. Both day 2 rows therefore see 10 + 20 + 5 = 35. 30 or 15 would only appear with a ROWS frame, and then which one came first would depend on the undefined order of the tied rows.
challenges.hint: Recall which frame applies when OVER has ORDER BY but no ROWS or RANGE clause.

challenges.title: Window function in WHERE
challenges.prompt: Why does SELECT student FROM results WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) = 1 fail?
options: ROW_NUMBER requires a PARTITION BY clause
It does not fail; it returns every row because each row is numbered 1
Window functions are only allowed inside a GROUP BY query
Window functions are computed after WHERE, so WHERE cannot use them
challenges.explanation: Window functions are evaluated with the SELECT list, after WHERE, so WHERE cannot reference them. Compute the number in a subquery or CTE and filter in the outer query. PARTITION BY is optional, and window functions do not need GROUP BY. The query is an error, not a silent wrong result.
challenges.hint: Place WHERE and window functions in the logical order of evaluation.

challenges.title: Count per partition
challenges.prompt: results has 2 rows for course DB and 3 rows for course OS. What does SELECT course, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY course) FROM results return?
options: 5 rows, with 3 on each OS row
challenges.explanation: A window function keeps every input row, so there are 5 rows. Each partition is counted on its own, so DB rows show 2 and OS rows show 3. Two rows is what GROUP BY course would return. 5 on every row would be COUNT(*) OVER () with no partition.
challenges.hint: Work out the number of output rows first, then the value on each row.

guides.subject: SQL
guides.title: Indexes and query plans
guides.summary: What an index is, when the database can use one and when it cannot, and how to read a query plan to tell which happened.

sections.title: What an index is
sections.text:
Without an index, the only way to find the enrollments for student 7 is to read every row in the table and check each one. That is a full table scan, and its cost grows with the size of the table.

An index is a separate structure, kept sorted by one or more columns, that points back to the rows. Most databases use a B-tree by default: a shallow, balanced tree where each step narrows the search, so finding a key takes logarithmic time. Even with millions of rows, the database reaches the right entries in a handful of page reads and then follows pointers to the matching rows. Because the entries are sorted, the same index also serves range conditions such as score BETWEEN 60 AND 80, and can deliver rows already in order for ORDER BY.

Indexes are not free. Each one takes storage, and every INSERT and DELETE must also update it. Which UPDATEs touch an index depends on the engine. Changing an indexed column always does. In PostgreSQL, an update writes a new row version, and unless it qualifies as a HOT (heap-only tuple) update, which needs no indexed column to change and room on the same page, every index on the table gets a new entry, even if no indexed column changed. A table with many indexes reads faster on those columns and writes slower. Primary keys and unique constraints are usually backed by an index automatically.

sections.title: When an index helps
sections.text:
An index helps most when a query asks for a small fraction of the rows by the indexed column: equality, ranges, or joins on that column. An index on enrollments(student_id) makes WHERE student_id = 7 and a join ON e.student_id = s.id cheap.

A composite index on several columns is sorted by the first column, then by the second within it, like a phone book sorted by surname and then first name. On courses(dept, year), the database can seek with WHERE dept = 'CS', and with WHERE dept = 'CS' AND year > 2. It generally cannot seek with WHERE year = 2 alone, just as a phone book does not help you find everyone named Ravi. This is the leftmost prefix rule. Some engines have a skip scan that softens it, but you should not count on that.

If an index contains every column a query needs, the database can answer from the index alone without visiting the table. This is a covering index: PostgreSQL shows Index Only Scan, SQLite shows USING COVERING INDEX and MySQL shows Using index. An index on enrollments(student_id, score) covers SELECT score FROM enrollments WHERE student_id = 7. PostgreSQL may still check the table for pages that VACUUM has not yet marked all-visible.

sections.title: When the index is ignored
sections.text:
Having an index does not mean it will be used. The most common reason is wrapping the column in a function or expression. An index on name stores name values, not UPPER(name) values, so WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ASHA' cannot seek through it. Many databases let you create an index on the expression itself; otherwise compare the bare column. Implicit type conversion applied to the column, such as comparing a text column with a number, can have the same effect.

A pattern with a leading wildcard, such as name LIKE '%son', cannot use a B-tree on name, because the sorted order is by the first characters, and those are unknown. A fixed prefix such as LIKE 'Ra%' can be turned into a range seek, but only when the index's ordering agrees with how LIKE compares text. MySQL usually manages it. PostgreSQL does with the C collation, or with an index built using text_pattern_ops under other collations. SQLite's LIKE ignores case by default, so an ordinary index on name is not used unless the index is declared COLLATE NOCASE or case_sensitive_like is switched on.

Finally, the optimizer may decide a scan is cheaper. If a query matches a large share of the table, such as status = 'active' when 95 percent of rows are active, jumping between index and table for each row costs more than reading the table straight through. The same is true of very small tables. That is a correct choice, not a failure.

sections.title: Reading a query plan
sections.text:
A query plan is the optimizer's chosen strategy for running a statement. You ask for it with EXPLAIN in PostgreSQL and MySQL, or EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in SQLite. PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports real row counts and times next to the estimates.

Start by finding how each table is accessed. A sequential scan, shown as Seq Scan in PostgreSQL or SCAN followed by the table name in SQLite, reads the whole table. Index Scan in PostgreSQL or SEARCH ... USING INDEX in SQLite means the index was used to seek. Then look at join methods, such as nested loop, hash join or merge join, and at any explicit sort step.

The optimizer is cost based: it estimates how many rows each step will produce from table statistics and picks the cheapest plan. When it chooses badly, the cause is often stale statistics, so the estimate and the real count are far apart. Refreshing them (ANALYZE in PostgreSQL and SQLite, ANALYZE TABLE in MySQL) is a reasonable first step before adding indexes or rewriting the query.

keyPoints: An index is a sorted structure, usually a B-tree, that finds rows in logarithmic time instead of a full scan.
Indexes speed up reads on their columns but cost storage and slow inserts, deletes and many updates.
A composite index helps only queries that constrain its leftmost columns.
A function on the column, a leading wildcard or a low-selectivity filter usually means no index seek.
A covering index answers a query from the index alone.
EXPLAIN shows the plan; compare estimated and actual rows to spot stale statistics.

challenges.title: Leftmost prefix
challenges.prompt: courses has a composite index on (dept, year). Which condition can the database use that index to seek on?
challenges.explanation: The index is sorted by dept first, then year within each dept, so fixing dept and taking a year range is a single contiguous slice. year = 2 alone does not fix the leading column, so the matches are scattered across every dept. The OR version must also return rows of any dept with year 2, so one seek on the index cannot cover it.
challenges.hint: Picture a phone book sorted by surname, then first name.

challenges.title: Function on an indexed column
challenges.prompt: students has an index on name. Why does WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ASHA' usually not seek through that index?
options: The index stores name values, not UPPER(name) values, so the sorted order cannot be used for this comparison
UPPER is not deterministic, so the optimizer refuses to use any index
Functions are not allowed in WHERE when an index exists
challenges.explanation: The index is ordered by the raw name, and the query asks about a computed value the index does not contain. The fix is an index on UPPER(name), where supported, or comparing the column directly. UPPER is deterministic, which is why an expression index on it works, and functions in WHERE are perfectly legal.
challenges.hint: Ask what values are actually stored in the index.

challenges.title: Low selectivity
challenges.prompt: orders has an index on status, and 95 percent of rows have status = 'active'. For SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'active', what is the optimizer most likely to do?
options: Always use the index, because one exists on the filtered column
Read the whole table with a sequential scan, because almost every row matches
Reject the query because the index has too few distinct values
challenges.explanation: When nearly every row qualifies, going through the index means an extra lookup per row in scattered order, which costs more than reading the table straight through. A cost-based optimizer chooses the scan. Having an index never forces its use, and low selectivity never makes a query invalid.
challenges.hint: Compare the work of one index lookup per row with one pass over the table.

challenges.title: Why not index everything
challenges.prompt: Why is adding an index on every column of a busy table usually a bad idea?
options: Indexes are only allowed on primary key columns
Too many indexes make SELECT queries return wrong results
Every index makes reads slower, even on columns that are not filtered
Each index costs storage and extra work on inserts, deletes and many updates
challenges.explanation: The cost of an index is paid on writes and in space, so many unused indexes slow down inserts and updates for no benefit. Every INSERT and DELETE maintains every index. An UPDATE that changes an indexed column maintains that index, and in PostgreSQL an update that is not HOT adds an entry to every index, even when no indexed column changed. Any column can be indexed, indexes never change query results, and an index a query does not use adds little to its cost.
challenges.hint: Think about what has to happen to each index when a row changes.

challenges.title: Covering index
challenges.prompt: enrollments has an index on (student_id, score). What can the database do for SELECT score FROM enrollments WHERE student_id = 7?
options: It must still read each matching table row to get score
It can answer the query from the index alone
It cannot use the index because score is not the first column
challenges.explanation: The index entries already contain student_id and score, so after seeking to student_id = 7 the database reads score straight from the index. This is a covering index; SQLite's plan shows SEARCH enrollments USING COVERING INDEX, and PostgreSQL's shows Index Only Scan, though it may still check the table for pages VACUUM has not marked all-visible. The filter is on the leading column, so the leftmost prefix rule is satisfied.
challenges.hint: List the columns the query touches and compare them with the index's columns.

guides.title: Handshakes at a meetup
guides.summary: Count every handshake in a room where everyone greets everyone else exactly once.
keyPoints: Count from one person's point of view, then fix the double counting.
Choosing 2 from n is n(n-1)/2.
Check a tiny case (3 or 4 people) by hand before trusting a formula.

puzzle.statement: Fourteen people arrive at a meetup. Before the talks start, every person shakes hands exactly once with every other person. Nobody shakes their own hand. How many handshakes take place in total?
hints: How many hands does one person shake? Now multiply by the number of people. Is anything counted twice?
The handshake between Asha and Ben gets counted once from Asha's side and once from Ben's side.
solution: Each of the 14 people shakes hands with the other 13.
Adding that up over everyone gives 14 x 13 = 182.
Every handshake involves two people, so each one was counted exactly twice in that total.
Divide by 2: 182 / 2 = 91 handshakes. This is the number of ways to choose 2 people from 14.

guides.title: The angle between the hands
guides.summary: Find the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at a given time.
keyPoints: Convert each hand to degrees measured from 12 before comparing.
The hour hand keeps moving between hours, half a degree per minute.
Take the smaller of the two angles the hands make.

puzzle.statement: An ordinary analog clock shows 4:36. Both hands move smoothly and continuously. What is the smaller angle, in degrees, between the hour hand and the minute hand?
hints: Work out how far each hand has turned from the 12 o'clock position, in degrees.
The minute hand moves 6 degrees per minute. The hour hand moves 30 degrees per hour plus 0.5 degrees per minute.
solution: Minute hand: 36 minutes x 6 degrees = 216 degrees from 12.
Hour hand: 4 hours x 30 degrees = 120 degrees, plus 36 minutes x 0.5 degrees = 18 degrees, so 138 degrees from 12.
The difference is 216 - 138 = 78 degrees.
The other way round the dial is 360 - 78 = 282 degrees, so the smaller angle is 78 degrees.

guides.title: Two trains and a restless bird
guides.summary: A bird shuttles between two approaching trains; find how far it flies in total.
keyPoints: Ask how long something lasts before asking where it goes.
An infinite sequence of small trips can still have a simple total.
Closing speed is the sum of two speeds toward each other.

puzzle.statement: Two trains are 150 km apart on the same straight track, heading toward each other. One travels at 40 km/h and the other at 35 km/h. At the moment they are 150 km apart, a bird leaves the front of the first train and flies at a constant 90 km/h toward the second. When it reaches the second train it turns instantly and flies back to the first, and keeps doing this until the trains meet. Turning takes no time. How many kilometres does the bird fly in total?
hints: Adding up each leg of the bird's trip is painful. Is there a quantity that is much easier to find?
The bird flies at a fixed speed for the whole time the trains are approaching. How long is that?
solution: The trains close the gap at 40 + 35 = 75 km/h.
A 150 km gap therefore disappears in 150 / 75 = 2 hours.
The bird flies non-stop at 90 km/h for exactly those 2 hours.
Total distance = 90 x 2 = 180 km. The back-and-forth legs form an infinite series, but it must sum to the same 180 km.

guides.title: Three switches, one bulb
guides.summary: Match three switches to one hidden bulb when you may look at the bulb only once.
keyPoints: A single observation can carry more than two outcomes if you use more than one property.
Time is a resource: what you do before looking can leave a trace.
Count outcomes: you need at least as many distinguishable results as possibilities.

puzzle.statement: In a hallway there are three ordinary on/off switches. Exactly one of them controls an incandescent bulb in a closed storeroom at the end of a long corridor; the other two do nothing. From the hallway you cannot see the bulb. You may flip the switches as often as you like, but you may walk to the storeroom and open the door only once, and after that you cannot touch the switches again. How can you be certain which switch controls the bulb?
hints: Looking at the bulb only tells you on or off, which separates two cases, not three. What else can you learn by being in the room?
An incandescent bulb that has been glowing for a while stays warm for some time after it goes dark.
solution: Call the switches A, B and C. Turn A on and leave it on for about ten minutes.
Turn A off, then turn B on, and walk straight to the storeroom.
If the bulb is lit, B controls it.
If the bulb is dark but warm to the touch, it was on recently, so A controls it.
If the bulb is dark and cold, it was never on, so C controls it.
The three outcomes (lit, dark and warm, dark and cold) are distinct, so one visit always settles the question.

guides.title: The 120 lockers
guides.summary: A crowd of students toggles a row of lockers in a pattern; count how many end up open.
keyPoints: Follow one item through the whole process instead of following the whole process.
Toggling an even number of times returns to the start.
Divisors come in pairs, except when a number is a perfect square.

puzzle.statement: A corridor has 120 lockers numbered 1 to 120, all closed. 120 students walk past one after another. Student 1 toggles every locker (opens it if closed, closes it if open). Student 2 toggles every 2nd locker (2, 4, 6, ...). Student 3 toggles every 3rd locker, and so on, until student 120 toggles only locker 120. After all 120 students have passed, how many lockers are open?
hints: Pick one locker, say number 12, and list exactly which students touch it.
Locker n is touched once for each divisor of n. Which numbers have an odd number of divisors?
solution: Student k touches locker n exactly when k divides n, so locker n is toggled once per divisor of n.
A locker ends up open only if it is toggled an odd number of times.
Divisors pair up as (d, n/d). The pairs are distinct unless d = n/d, which happens only when n is a perfect square.
So exactly the perfect-square lockers have an odd number of divisors and stay open.
The perfect squares up to 120 are 1, 4, 9, ..., 100 (10 squared); 11 squared is 121, which is too big.
Therefore 10 lockers are open.

guides.title: Nine coins, one heavy
guides.summary: Find the one heavier coin among nine using a balance scale as few times as possible.
keyPoints: A balance has three outcomes, not two, so split into three groups.
Each weighing can at most divide the possibilities by three.
Prove a lower bound by counting outcomes against cases.

puzzle.statement: You have nine coins that look identical. Eight weigh the same and one is slightly heavier. You have a two-pan balance scale with no weights; each use tells you only whether the left pan is heavier, the right pan is heavier, or they balance. What is the smallest number of weighings that is guaranteed to find the heavy coin, whatever happens?
hints: A weighing has three possible results. Can you make each result point to a different group of coins?
Put three coins on each pan and keep three aside. What does each outcome tell you?
solution: Weighing 1: put coins 1-3 on the left, 4-6 on the right, and keep 7-9 off the scale.
If one pan is heavier, the heavy coin is among its three. If they balance, it is among the three set aside.
Weighing 2: from the suspect three, put one coin on each pan and keep one aside. The heavier pan holds it; a balance means it is the coin set aside.
So 2 weighings always suffice.
One weighing cannot be enough: it has only 3 possible outcomes, but there are 9 possible heavy coins. Hence the minimum is 2.

guides.title: The ferry, the dog and the rabbit
guides.summary: Get a dog, a rabbit and a basket of carrots across a river without anything being eaten.
keyPoints: Model the puzzle as states and moves, then search for the shortest path.
Bringing something back can be a forward step.
Identify the item that conflicts with everything and handle it first.

puzzle.statement: A ferry operator must take a dog, a rabbit and a basket of carrots across a river. The boat holds the operator plus at most one of the three, and only the operator can row it. If the dog and the rabbit are left together on a bank without the operator, the dog chases the rabbit. If the rabbit and the carrots are left together without the operator, the rabbit eats the carrots. The dog ignores the carrots. Counting each trip across the river (in either direction) as one crossing, what is the fewest crossings needed to get all three safely to the far bank?
hints: Which item is in conflict with both of the others? It has to go first.
At some point the operator must carry something back to the starting bank.
solution: Crossing 1: take the rabbit over (the dog and carrots are safe together).
Crossing 2: return alone.
Crossing 3: take the dog over. Crossing 4: bring the rabbit back, so the dog is not left with it.
Crossing 5: take the carrots over and leave them with the dog. Crossing 6: return alone.
Crossing 7: take the rabbit over. Everything is across.

Fewer is impossible. The total is odd, since the operator ends on the far bank. If nothing is ever carried back, 5 crossings would mean three loaded trips over with empty returns: the first load must be the rabbit, and the second load would then be left with the rabbit while the operator returns. So something must be carried back and ferried again, which makes at least 7. A full search of all states agrees.

guides.title: Timing with two uneven ropes
guides.summary: Measure an awkward time interval using two ropes that burn at an uneven rate.
keyPoints: Lighting both ends halves the remaining time, however uneven the burn.
Use one event (a rope going out) as the trigger for the next action.
Track how much burn time is left on each rope, not how much length.

puzzle.statement: You have two ropes and a box of matches. Rope A takes exactly 10 minutes to burn from one end to the other, and rope B takes exactly 6 minutes. Both burn unevenly: some stretches burn fast and others slowly, so half the length does not mean half the time. You may light either end of either rope at any moment, and you can see when a rope burns out. Starting from the moment you first light something, how can you mark exactly 6.5 minutes?
hints: If you light a rope at both ends, it burns out in exactly half its remaining time, even though it burns unevenly.
Start A at one end and B at both ends together. What is left of A when B goes out?
solution: At time 0, light rope A at one end and rope B at both ends.
Burning from both ends, B goes out after 6 / 2 = 3 minutes.
At that moment A has burned for 3 minutes, so it has exactly 7 minutes of burn time left.
Immediately light the other end of A. Burning from both ends, the remaining 7 minutes takes 7 / 2 = 3.5 minutes.
A goes out at 3 + 3.5 = 6.5 minutes after the start, which is the moment you wanted.

guides.title: Six litres from a 4 and a 9
guides.summary: Use two unmarked jugs to measure an exact amount of water in as few steps as possible.
keyPoints: Every reachable state is a pair of amounts; search them breadth-first.
Pouring big into small repeatedly leaves remainders you can collect.
Try filling each jug first; one direction is often much shorter.

puzzle.statement: You have an unmarked 4-litre jug, an unmarked 9-litre jug, a tap and a drain. Both jugs start empty. One step is any one of: fill a jug to the brim from the tap; empty a jug completely into the drain; or pour from one jug into the other until the first is empty or the second is full. What is the fewest steps needed to have exactly 6 litres in one of the jugs?
hints: Only the 9-litre jug can hold 6 litres. Try starting by filling the big jug rather than the small one.
Filling the 9 and pouring off 4 twice leaves 1 litre. How can that 1 litre help you reach 6?
solution: Write states as (4-litre, 9-litre). Fill the 9: (0, 9). Pour into the 4: (4, 5).
Empty the 4: (0, 5). Pour again: (4, 1).
Empty the 4: (0, 1). Pour the 1 litre into the 4: (1, 0).
Fill the 9: (1, 9). Pour into the 4 until it is full, which takes 3 litres: (4, 6).
That is 8 steps. A breadth-first search over every reachable state finds no shorter route (starting by filling the 4-litre jug takes longer), so 8 is the minimum.

guides.title: The counterfeit bag
guides.summary: Identify a bag of fake coins with one reading of a digital scale, using as few coins as possible.
keyPoints: Give each candidate a unique signature in a single measurement.
The excess weight tells you how many fake coins are on the scale.
Zero is a valid label: one candidate can be left out entirely.

puzzle.statement: There are 8 bags, each holding plenty of coins. Every coin in seven of the bags weighs exactly 10 g. Every coin in the remaining bag is counterfeit and weighs exactly 11 g. You have an accurate digital scale that shows the total weight, and you may use it only once. You choose some number of coins from each bag (possibly zero) and weigh them all together. What is the fewest coins you can put on the scale and still be certain which bag is counterfeit?
hints: If you take a different number of coins from each bag, how does the scale reading reveal the fake bag?
The counts from the 8 bags must all be different. What is the smallest total of 8 different whole numbers that are zero or more?
solution: If N coins are on the scale and c of them came from the fake bag, the reading is 10 x N + c grams, so the excess over 10 x N equals c.
To tell the bags apart, each bag must give a different excess, so the 8 counts must all be different.
The smallest 8 different non-negative whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, ..., 7.
Take 0 coins from one bag, 1 from the next, and so on up to 7. That is 0 + 1 + ... + 7 = 28 coins.
The excess over 280 g names the bag directly; an excess of 0 means the bag you left out.
Any other set of 8 different counts has a larger sum, so 28 is the minimum.

guides.title: Dominoes on a trimmed board
guides.summary: Decide whether dominoes can cover a small chessboard that is missing two corners.
keyPoints: Look for an invariant: a quantity every move preserves.
Colouring is a powerful way to prove that something is impossible.
Counting squares is necessary but not sufficient.

puzzle.statement: A 6 x 6 board is coloured like a chessboard, in alternating black and white squares. Two diagonally opposite corner squares are cut away, leaving 34 squares. You have 17 dominoes, and each domino covers exactly two squares that share an edge. Can the 17 dominoes cover the 34 remaining squares with no overlaps and nothing hanging off the board? Explain why or why not.
hints: The square count works out, so the answer cannot come from counting alone. Think about the colours.
What colours are the two squares under any single domino? What colours were the two corners you removed?
solution: Any two squares that share an edge have different colours, so every domino covers one black and one white square.
17 dominoes would therefore cover exactly 17 black and 17 white squares.
The full 6 x 6 board has 18 black and 18 white squares.
Diagonally opposite corners always have the same colour, so removing them leaves 18 of one colour and 16 of the other.
17 and 17 can never match 18 and 16, so the covering is impossible, however the dominoes are arranged.

guides.title: Ants on a metre stick
guides.summary: Ants bounce off each other on a stick; find when the last one falls off.
keyPoints: Two identical objects bouncing apart look the same as passing through each other.
Ignore labels when only the collective outcome matters.
Replace a messy interaction with an equivalent simple one.

puzzle.statement: Five ants sit on a stick 100 cm long, at 10 cm, 25 cm, 40 cm, 70 cm and 85 cm from the left end. They all start walking at the same moment at 1 cm per second. The ants at 10 cm and 40 cm walk right; the ants at 25 cm, 70 cm and 85 cm walk left. Whenever two ants meet head-on, both instantly turn around and carry on at the same speed. An ant falls off as soon as it reaches either end of the stick. After how many seconds does the last ant fall off?
hints: Tracking every bounce is hard. If two ants meet and turn around, what would an observer who cannot tell ants apart see?
Pretend the ants walk straight through each other. Then each 'walker' just goes to the end it is facing.
solution: When two ants meet and both reverse, the picture is identical to them passing through each other with labels swapped.
So the moments at which ants fall off are the same as if every ant ignored the others and walked straight on.
Walking straight on, the ant at 10 cm heading right needs 90 s; at 25 cm heading left, 25 s; at 40 cm heading right, 60 s; at 70 cm heading left, 70 s; at 85 cm heading left, 85 s.
Ants fall off at 25, 60, 70, 85 and 90 seconds (a different ant may be the one falling each time).
The last ant falls off after 90 seconds.

guides.title: Four people, one torch, one bridge
guides.summary: Get four walkers of different speeds across a narrow bridge at night in the least time.
keyPoints: Send the two slowest together so their times overlap.
The fastest walkers should do the return trips.
Compare the two standard strategies; neither always wins.

puzzle.statement: Four people must cross a narrow bridge at night. They have one torch, and nobody may be on the bridge without it. At most two people can be on the bridge at once, and a pair walks at the pace of the slower person. The torch must be carried back and forth; it cannot be thrown. Alone, the four take 1, 3, 8 and 12 minutes to cross. What is the shortest total time, in minutes, to get all four across?
hints: Having the 1-minute person escort everyone wastes time, because the 8 and 12 each pay full price.
What if the 8 and 12 walk over together, and a fast person who is already on the far side brings the torch back?
solution: 1 and 3 cross (3 min). 1 returns with the torch (1 min). Running total 4.
8 and 12 cross together (12 min). 3 returns with the torch (3 min). Running total 19.
1 and 3 cross again (3 min). Total 22 minutes.
The alternative of 1 escorting each person takes 3 + 1 + 8 + 1 + 12 = 25 minutes, which is worse.
A full search of every possible sequence of crossings confirms 22 minutes is the minimum.

guides.title: The poisoned bottle
guides.summary: Find one poisoned bottle among hundreds using as few slow test strips as possible.
keyPoints: When tests run in parallel, give each item a unique pattern of tests.
k yes/no tests can tell apart at most 2 to the power k cases.
Binary numbering is a ready-made way to assign those patterns.

puzzle.statement: A cellar holds 500 bottles of wine, and exactly one is poisoned. A test strip changes colour if it touches even a drop of the poisoned wine, but only shows its result 24 hours later. You may put drops from as many bottles as you like on each strip, and every strip must be prepared at the start because you have only 24 hours. What is the fewest strips you need to be certain which bottle is poisoned?
hints: After 24 hours each strip is either changed or not. How many different overall results can k strips give?
Number the bottles and write each number in binary. Let each strip stand for one binary digit.
solution: Each strip ends in one of two states, so k strips give at most 2 to the power k different overall results.
To single out one of 500 bottles you need 2 to the power k to be at least 500. 2 to the 8 is 256, too few; 2 to the 9 is 512, enough.
Number the bottles 0 to 499 and write each in 9-bit binary. Strip i gets a drop from every bottle whose bit i is 1.
After 24 hours, read the changed strips as 1s and the others as 0s. That 9-bit number is the poisoned bottle.
So 9 strips suffice and 8 cannot, which makes 9 the minimum.

guides.title: One missing, one repeated
guides.summary: Spot the missing number and the repeated number in a long list using only a little memory.
keyPoints: Compare what you see with what you expected; the difference is information.
Two unknowns need two independent equations.
Running totals use constant memory, however long the list.

puzzle.statement: A list should contain each whole number from 1 to n exactly once, in some order. By mistake, one number was replaced by a copy of another, so one number is missing and one appears twice. The list is read to you once, one number at a time. You may keep only a few running totals, not the whole list or a checklist of n entries. How can you find both the missing number and the repeated number?
hints: Compare the sum you hear with the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n should have. What does the difference tell you?
One equation gives you missing minus repeated. Find a second equation from another running total, such as the sum of squares.
solution: While the list is read, keep two running totals: the sum S of the numbers and the sum Q of their squares.
The correct totals are n(n+1)/2 for the sum and n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 for the sum of squares.
Let m be the missing number and r the repeated one. Then n(n+1)/2 - S = m - r. Call this d.
Also n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 - Q = m squared - r squared = (m - r)(m + r), so m + r = (that difference) / d.
Solve the two equations: m = ((m + r) + d) / 2 and r = ((m + r) - d) / 2.
Example with n = 6 and list 3, 1, 4, 4, 6, 2: d = 21 - 20 = 1 and 91 - 82 = 9, so m + r = 9, giving m = 5 and r = 4.

guides.title: Shared birthdays in a group
guides.summary: Find how small a group can be while a shared birthday is still more likely than you might expect.
keyPoints: For "at least one" questions, compute the chance of "none" and subtract from 1.
The number of pairs grows much faster than the number of people.
Multiply the chances step by step as each new person joins.

puzzle.statement: Assume every year has 365 days, nobody is born on 29 February, and each person's birthday is equally likely to be any day, independently of everyone else. What is the smallest number of people in a group for which the chance that at least two share a birthday is 70% or more?
hints: It is easier to work out the chance that all birthdays are different, then take that away from 1.
Each new person must avoid all earlier birthdays: multiply 365/365 x 364/365 x 363/365 and so on until the product falls to 30% or below.
solution: With n people, the chance that all birthdays differ is (365/365) x (364/365) x ... x ((365 - n + 1)/365).
The chance of at least one shared birthday is 1 minus that product.
Multiplying the terms in turn, at 29 people the chance of a shared birthday is about 68.1%, still below 70%.
At 30 people it is about 70.6%, the first time it reaches 70%.
So the smallest group is 30 people. It is surprisingly small because 30 people form 435 different pairs.

guides.title: Hats in a line
guides.summary: A line of people must guess their own hat colours; plan a strategy that saves as many as possible.
keyPoints: One bit of shared information can be worth more than one guess.
Parity (odd or even) summarises a whole group in a single bit.
Agree the encoding in advance; then everyone can decode it.

puzzle.statement: Twelve people stand in a single-file line, all facing forward. Each wears a hat that is either black or white, chosen in any way at all; there may be any number of each colour. Each person can see every hat in front of them, but not their own or any behind them. Starting from the back of the line and moving forward, each person says aloud one word, 'black' or 'white', as a guess at their own hat colour, and everyone hears every guess. Nothing else may be communicated. The group may agree on a strategy beforehand. With the best strategy, how many people are guaranteed to guess correctly, however the hats are placed?
hints: The person at the back sees nothing about their own hat, so they can never be sure. Can they help everyone else instead?
The back person's word can carry one bit of information about the hats in front. Which single bit would let everyone else work out their own hat?
solution: Agree that the person at the back says 'black' if they see an odd number of black hats ahead, and 'white' if even.
The next person counts the black hats they can see. Comparing with the announced parity tells them their own hat colour.
Everyone further forward keeps track of the announced parity and every correct guess made since, plus the hats in front, and so deduces their own colour the same way.
So all 11 people in front of the back person are always right. The back person is right only by luck.
No strategy can guarantee 12: the back person's guess depends only on hats they can see, so for some placement their own hat is the other colour.
The guaranteed number is therefore 11.

guides.title: Two eggs, eighty floors
guides.summary: Find the highest safe floor with only two eggs and the fewest drops in the worst case.
keyPoints: Balance the worst case: each early step should cost the same total.
Shrink the jump size by one after each survival.
Turn "how many drops for n floors" into "how many floors for d drops".

puzzle.statement: A building has 80 floors. There is some unknown floor at or below which an egg dropped from a window survives, and above which it breaks; it is possible that eggs survive from every floor, or break from the 1st floor. You have exactly two identical eggs. A dropped egg that survives can be reused; a broken egg cannot. What is the fewest drops that guarantees you find the highest floor from which an egg survives, in the worst case?
hints: Once the first egg breaks, the second egg must check every floor in the remaining gap one at a time, from the bottom up.
If you allow d drops in total, the first drop can be at floor d, the next d - 1 floors higher, and so on. How many floors can d drops cover?
solution: With the second egg alone you must test floors one by one, so the first egg's job is to narrow down the range.
Suppose you allow d drops in total. Drop the first egg from floor d. If it breaks, the second egg checks floors 1 to d - 1: at most d drops in all.
If it survives, you have d - 1 drops left, so jump up d - 1 floors next, then d - 2, and so on.

This plan covers d + (d - 1) + ... + 1 = d(d + 1)/2 floors. No plan with d drops can cover more: the first drop can be no higher than floor d (if it breaks, every floor below needs its own drop), and if it survives you face the same problem with d - 1 drops.
With d = 12 that is 78 floors, not enough for 80. With d = 13 it is 91 floors, which is enough.
So the minimum worst-case number of drops is 13 (for example, first drops at floors 13, 25, 36, 46, ...).

guides.title: Seven pirates split the gold
guides.summary: Ruthless, logical pirates vote on how to split treasure; work out what the leader keeps.
keyPoints: Work backwards from the simplest end state.
A vote is cheap to buy from someone who would otherwise get nothing.
Pin down tie-break rules before reasoning about choices.

puzzle.statement: Seven pirates, ranked from most senior to most junior, must share 60 gold coins, which cannot be cut. The most senior pirate still on board proposes how to split the coins, and then every pirate on board, including the proposer, votes. If at least half the votes are yes, the split happens and the game ends. Otherwise the proposer is thrown overboard and the next most senior pirate proposes, and so on. Every pirate is perfectly logical and knows the others are. Each pirate wants, in order: first to stay alive, then to get as many coins as possible, and, if those are equal, to see someone thrown overboard. No promises or deals outside the vote are possible. How many coins does the most senior pirate keep?
hints: Start with just two pirates left, then three, and build upwards. What does each pirate get in each smaller game?
A pirate votes yes only for strictly more than they would get in the next smaller game. The cheapest votes come from pirates who would get nothing there.
solution: Number the pirates 1 (most junior) to 7 (most senior). With only pirate 2 and pirate 1, pirate 2's own vote is half, so pirate 2 takes all 60.
Three pirates: pirate 3 needs one more vote. Pirate 1 gets nothing in the two-pirate game, so 1 coin buys that vote: 3 gets 59, 2 gets 0, 1 gets 1.
Four pirates: pirate 4 needs one more vote; pirate 2 gets 0 in the three-pirate game, so give 2 one coin. Split for (4, 3, 2, 1): 59, 0, 1, 0.
Five pirates need 3 votes: the proposer plus pirates 3 and 1, who get 0 in the four-pirate game, at 1 coin each. Split for (5, 4, 3, 2, 1): 58, 0, 1, 0, 1.
Six pirates need 3 votes: the proposer plus pirates 4 and 2 at 1 coin each. Split for (6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1): 58, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0.
Seven pirates need 4 votes: the proposer plus pirates 5, 3 and 1, who get 0 in the six-pirate game, at 1 coin each.
So the most senior pirate keeps 60 - 3 = 57 coins. Buying votes any cheaper is impossible, since each bought vote must cost at least 1 coin.

guides.title: Thirty-six horses, six lanes
guides.summary: Find the three fastest horses using races with no stopwatch, in as few races as possible.
keyPoints: After each race, cross off everyone who can no longer make the top three.
A horse beaten by three known-faster horses is out.
Prove the lower bound by tracking which horses are still undefeated.

puzzle.statement: There are 36 horses and a track with 6 lanes, so at most 6 horses can run in one race. There is no stopwatch: a race only tells you the order in which its horses finished. Each horse always runs at exactly the same speed, and no two horses have the same speed. What is the fewest races that guarantees you can name the fastest, second fastest and third fastest horses in order?
hints: Every horse has to race at least once, and the heat winners then need to be compared with each other.
After the heats and a race of heat winners, list only the horses that could still finish in the top three. How many are left?
solution: Races 1-6: split the horses into six groups of 6 and race each group. Call the groups A to F.
Race 7: race the six group winners. Say the order is A1, B1, C1, D1, E1, F1. A1 is the fastest of all.
Groups D, E and F are out: their winners already trail A1, B1 and C1. C1 can be at best third, so C2 and below are out; B can supply at most B1 and B2; A at most A2 and A3.
Race 8: race the five remaining candidates A2, A3, B1, B2, C1. The top two finishers are second and third overall. So 8 races suffice.

Seven cannot be enough. Call a horse undefeated if it has never finished behind another horse. Any undefeated horse could still be the fastest, so you must get down to 1 undefeated horse: 35 must lose.

Imagine the results are as unhelpful as possible: whenever a race contains an undefeated horse, one of them wins (this never contradicts earlier results). Then a race with u undefeated horses defeats at most u - 1 of them, which is at most 5. Fewer than 7 races cannot defeat 35, and exactly 7 races only can if every race has 6 runners who are all undefeated.

In that case let W, the winner of race 6, also win race 7 (it is still undefeated, so it runs there). Its runner-up in race 6 and the runner-up in race 7 have each lost only to W, and they have never met: both were undefeated before race 6, and the second did not run in race 6. Either could be second fastest, so 7 races cannot guarantee the answer, and 8 is the minimum.

guides.title: Number series
guides.summary: Every number series hides one rule that turns each term into the next, and a fixed order of checks finds it quickly.

sections.title: Start with the differences
sections.text:
A number series hides one rule that turns each term into the next. Your first move is almost always to write the differences between neighbouring terms underneath the series. If the differences are all equal, the series is arithmetic: 7, 12, 17, 22 adds 5 each time, so the next term is 27.

If the differences are not equal, treat them as a new series. When the differences themselves grow by a fixed amount, you are looking at differences of differences. For 2, 3, 6, 11, 18 the differences are 1, 3, 5, 7, which rise by 2, so the next difference is 9 and the next term is 27.

If the terms grow fast and the differences roughly double or triple, try ratios instead. Dividing each term by the one before it reveals a geometric series: 3, 12, 48, 192 multiplies by 4 each time, so 768 comes next.

Work in a fixed order: differences, ratios, known squares and cubes, then alternating patterns. Most series give way at one of these steps in under a minute.

sections.title: Squares, cubes and a constant
sections.text:
Some series are built from perfect squares or cubes with a small number added or taken away. Knowing the squares up to 30 and the cubes up to 15 by heart lets you spot them on sight.

Take 3, 6, 11, 18, 27. The differences 3, 5, 7, 9 are consecutive odd numbers, which is the fingerprint of squares. Subtract 2 from each term and you get 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, so the rule is n squared plus 2 and the next term is 36 + 2 = 38.

For cubes, compare each term with 1, 8, 27, 64, 125. The series 4, 11, 30, 67, 128 is each cube plus 3, so 216 + 3 = 219 comes next.

Watch for multiply-then-add rules as well. In 2, 5, 11, 23, 47 every term is double the previous one plus 1. The differences 3, 6, 12, 24 double each time, and that doubling is the clue that a multiply step is involved, so the next term is 95.

sections.title: Alternating and interleaved series
sections.text:
When the differences jump up and down with no steady trend, suspect two rules taking turns. There are two common shapes.

In the first, one series uses two operations in turn. The series 6, 10, 9, 13, 12, 16 goes add 4, subtract 1, add 4, subtract 1, add 4, so the next step is subtract 1, giving 15.

In the second, two separate series are woven together. Read the odd positions and the even positions as two different lists. In 1, 20, 3, 17, 5, 14, 7 the odd positions 1, 3, 5, 7 climb by 2, while the even positions 20, 17, 14 fall by 3. The missing eighth term sits in an even position, so it is 14 - 3 = 11.

The tell-tale sign of interleaving is that terms two places apart look more related than neighbours do. Long series of seven or more terms often hide two lists. Before applying any rule, always check which position the missing term occupies.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. Find the next term: 5, 10, 8, 16, 14, 28, ?

Step 1: differences are +5, -2, +8, -2, +14. They do not settle, but every second step is -2, so suspect two alternating operations. Step 2: test multiply by 2 for the other steps: 5 x 2 = 10, 8 x 2 = 16, 14 x 2 = 28. All match. Step 3: the rule is x2, then -2, repeating. The last step was x2 (14 to 28), so the next is -2: 28 - 2 = 26. Answer: 26.

Example 2. Find the next term: 1, 3, 8, 18, 35, ?

Step 1: differences are 2, 5, 10, 17. Not constant. Step 2: differences of those are 3, 5, 7, rising by 2, so the next second difference is 9. Step 3: the next first difference is 17 + 9 = 26. Step 4: the next term is 35 + 26 = 61. Check another way: the differences 2, 5, 10, 17 are 1, 4, 9, 16 each plus 1, and the next square plus 1 is 25 + 1 = 26, which agrees. Answer: 61.

keyPoints: Write the differences first; equal differences mean an arithmetic series.
If the differences grow by a fixed amount, take differences of differences.
Fast growth suggests ratios or a multiply-then-add rule.
Consecutive odd differences are the fingerprint of squares; compare terms with known squares and cubes.
If terms two places apart look related, split the series into odd and even positions.

challenges.title: Growing gaps
challenges.prompt: What comes next? 4, 11, 25, 46, 74, ?
challenges.explanation: The differences are 7, 14, 21, 28, which are multiples of 7 rising by 7 each time. The next difference is 35, so 74 + 35 = 109. 102 comes from repeating the last difference of 28, which ignores that the gaps keep growing.
challenges.hint: Write the gaps between neighbouring terms and look at what they have in common.

challenges.title: Fast climber
challenges.prompt: What comes next? 7, 21, 63, 189, ?
challenges.explanation: Each term is three times the previous one: 7 x 3 = 21, 21 x 3 = 63, 63 x 3 = 189, so 189 x 3 = 567. 315 comes from adding the last difference again (189 + 126), which treats a geometric series as if it were arithmetic.
challenges.hint: The terms grow quickly. Try dividing instead of subtracting.

challenges.title: Hidden squares
challenges.prompt: What comes next? 6, 11, 18, 27, 38, ?
challenges.explanation: The differences 5, 7, 9, 11 are consecutive odd numbers, a sign of squares. Each term is a square plus 2: 4 + 2, 9 + 2, 16 + 2, 25 + 2, 36 + 2. The next is 49 + 2 = 51. Equally, the next difference is 13 and 38 + 13 = 51. Picking 49 means spotting the squares but forgetting the constant added to each.
challenges.hint: Compare each term with a perfect square close to it.

challenges.title: Two steps in turn
challenges.prompt: What comes next? 3, 8, 6, 11, 9, 14, ?
challenges.explanation: The steps go +5, -2, +5, -2, +5, so the next step is -2: 14 - 2 = 12. Reading odd positions (3, 6, 9, 12) confirms it. 17 comes from adding 3 to 14, which mixes up the two interleaved lists: the even positions 8, 11, 14 rise by 3, but the missing term is in an odd position.
challenges.hint: Look at the signs of the differences and at which position the missing term occupies.

challenges.title: Close to cubes
challenges.prompt: What comes next? 6, 25, 62, 123, 214, ?
challenges.explanation: Compare with the cubes 8, 27, 64, 125, 216: every term is two less, so the rule is n cubed minus 2, starting from n = 2. The next cube is 7 x 7 x 7 = 343, so the next term is 343 - 2 = 341. 343 is the cube itself with the constant forgotten, 345 adds 2 instead of taking it away, and 305 repeats the last difference of 91 instead of noticing the differences grow.
challenges.hint: Each term sits right next to a well-known power.

guides.title: Letter series
guides.summary: Turn letters into their alphabet positions, find the numeric rule, and wrap round from Z to A when a step runs off the end.

sections.title: Turn letters into numbers
sections.text:
Letter series become number series once you swap each letter for its position: A = 1, B = 2, and so on up to Z = 26. The whole skill is doing that conversion fast and without slips.

Learn a few anchors rather than counting from A every time. A handy set is E = 5, J = 10, O = 15, T = 20, Y = 25. To find R, start from T = 20 and step back two: R = 18. To find L, start from J = 10 and step forward two: L = 12.

Reverse positions count from the Z end, so Z is 1st from the right and A is 26th. A letter's forward position and reverse position always add up to 27. So the 6th letter from the right is the 27 - 6 = 21st letter from the left, which is U.

The same 27 rule pairs each letter with its opposite: A and Z, B and Y, C and X, through to M and N. These opposite pairs turn up constantly in series and in codes.

sections.title: Fixed steps and wrapping round
sections.text:
Once letters are numbers, look at the steps between them. A fixed step works just like an arithmetic number series. C, F, I, L adds 3 each time, so the next letter is position 15, which is O.

The twist is that the alphabet has only 26 letters. If a step takes you past Z, subtract 26 to wrap round to the start. W (23) plus 5 is 28, and 28 - 26 = 2, which is B. If a backward step takes you below A, add 26. C (3) minus 5 is -2, and -2 + 26 = 24, which is X.

Picture the alphabet as a circle rather than a line and wrap-around stops feeling like a special case.

Backward series work the same way with negative steps. Z, W, T, Q steps back by 3, so N comes next. If the steps are not fixed, apply every number-series idea you know to the list of steps: they may grow by 1 each time, alternate, or double.

sections.title: Changing gaps and paired letters
sections.text:
Many letter series use gaps that grow. A, C, F, J uses gaps of 2, 3, 4, so the next gap is 5 and the next letter is position 15, O. Writing the gaps under the series makes this obvious at a glance.

Series of letter groups, such as AZ, BY, CX, look harder but are really two or more simple series side by side. Treat the first letters as one list and the second letters as another. Here the first letters go A, B, C and the second letters go Z, Y, X, so the next group is DW.

Each position in a group can follow its own step. In KP, MN, OL, the first letters rise by 2 (K, M, O, Q) while the second letters fall by 2 (P, N, L, J), so QJ comes next.

Before settling on an answer, check whether the letters in each group are linked to each other as well, for example as opposite pairs. A second relationship that agrees is a good sign you have the rule right.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. Find the next letter: J, M, Q, V, ?

Step 1: convert to positions: J = 10, M = 13, Q = 17, V = 22. Step 2: gaps are 3, 4, 5, growing by 1, so the next gap is 6. Step 3: 22 + 6 = 28, which is past Z. Step 4: wrap round: 28 - 26 = 2, which is B. Answer: B.

Example 2. Find the next group: BY, DW, FU, HS, ?

Step 1: first letters B, D, F, H are positions 2, 4, 6, 8, rising by 2, so the next first letter is 10, which is J. Step 2: second letters Y, W, U, S are positions 25, 23, 21, 19, falling by 2, so the next second letter is 17, which is Q. Step 3: check with the 27 rule: 2 + 25, 4 + 23, 6 + 21 and 8 + 19 all make 27, so each pair is a letter and its opposite. The opposite of J (10) is 27 - 10 = 17, which is Q, so both routes agree. Answer: JQ.

keyPoints: Convert letters to positions A = 1 to Z = 26; anchors E, J, O, T, Y are 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
Forward and reverse positions of a letter add up to 27, and so do opposite letters such as A and Z.
Past Z, subtract 26; below A, add 26.
Write the gaps under the series and treat them like a number series.
Split letter groups into separate series, one per position.

challenges.title: From the far end
challenges.prompt: Which letter is 8th from the right end of the English alphabet?
challenges.explanation: A letter's position from the left and from the right add up to 27, so 8th from the right is 27 - 8 = 19th from the left, which is S. R comes from computing 26 - 8 = 18, which is off by one because Z itself is counted as 1st from the right.
challenges.hint: Counting from the right and counting from the left are linked by a fixed total.

challenges.title: Stepping back
challenges.prompt: What comes next? Y, U, Q, M, ?
challenges.explanation: Positions are 25, 21, 17, 13, falling by 4 each time. 13 - 4 = 9, which is I. J would be a fall of only 3, and H a fall of 5.
challenges.hint: Convert each letter to its position and look at the gaps.

challenges.title: Round the corner
challenges.prompt: What comes next? R, W, B, G, ?
challenges.explanation: R = 18 and W = 23 is a step of 5. 23 + 5 = 28, and wrapping round gives 28 - 26 = 2, which is B, so the series continues past Z. G = 7, and 7 + 5 = 12, which is L. K comes from miscounting the step as 4 after the wrap; the step stays 5 throughout.
challenges.hint: Think of the alphabet as a circle, not a line.

challenges.title: Pairs with different steps
challenges.prompt: What comes next? AC, BE, CG, DI, ?
challenges.explanation: First letters A, B, C, D rise by 1, so the next is E. Second letters C, E, G, I are 3, 5, 7, 9, rising by 2, so the next is 11, which is K. The answer is EK. EJ uses a step of 1 for the second letter too, but the second letters clearly skip one each time.
challenges.hint: Treat the first letters and the second letters as two separate series.

challenges.title: Widening gaps
challenges.prompt: What comes next? C, D, F, I, M, ?
challenges.explanation: Positions are 3, 4, 6, 9, 13, so the gaps are 1, 2, 3, 4. The next gap is 5, and 13 + 5 = 18, which is R. Q comes from repeating the last gap of 4 instead of letting it grow.
challenges.hint: Write down the gaps and see how they change.

guides.title: Coding and decoding
guides.summary: Work out the rule that turns a sample word into its code by comparing letter positions, then apply it forwards to code or backwards to decode.

sections.title: Find the rule from a known pair
sections.text:
A coding question gives you a word and its code, then asks you to code or decode something new. The method is always the same: write the positions of the plain word and the code word one above the other, and look at how each letter moved.

For each pair of letters, work out code position minus plain position. If every letter moved by the same amount, you have a shift code. A move that looks far out of line, such as Y to A giving -24, is usually a wrap round the alphabet: add or subtract 26, so -24 is really +2. If the amounts still differ, check whether each pair adds up to 27, which marks a reverse-alphabet code. If neither fits, look for a step that changes with the letter's place in the word, such as +1 for the first letter, +2 for the second and so on, or for a word that has simply been written backwards.

Test the rule on every letter of the example, not just the first one or two. A rule that fits two letters by luck will give a wrong answer.

When a question gives more than one example, use them all, because a second example often rules out a rival rule that fits the first.

sections.title: Shift codes forwards and backwards
sections.text:
In a shift code every letter moves the same number of places along the alphabet. A forward shift of 1 turns A into B and CAT into DBU. A backward shift of 3 turns F into C.

Wrap-around matters here exactly as in letter series. A forward shift of 2 turns Y (25) into 27, and 27 - 26 = 1, so Y becomes A. A backward shift of 3 turns B (2) into -1, and -1 + 26 = 25, so B becomes Y.

Decoding means running the rule in reverse. If the code was made by shifting forward 2, you get the original by shifting the code letters back 2. Students often apply the coding rule again instead of undoing it, which shifts the letters twice as far from the answer.

A quick sanity check: after decoding, the result should usually be a real word. If you get something unpronounceable, recheck the direction of the shift before anything else.

sections.title: Reverse-alphabet and number codes
sections.text:
In a reverse-alphabet code each letter is swapped for its opposite: A with Z, B with Y, C with X, and so on. Since a letter and its opposite always add up to 27, the code for a letter at position p is the letter at 27 - p. The code works the same in both directions, so coding and decoding are the same operation.

Number codes replace letters with numbers. The simplest writes each letter's position, so BAD becomes 2-1-4. Others combine the positions, for example by adding them: CAB would be 3 + 1 + 2 = 6.

With combined codes, be wary of rival rules. CAB gives 6 whether you add the positions or multiply them, so one example cannot tell the two apart. A second example settles it: FED gives 6 + 5 + 4 = 15 by adding but 120 by multiplying. Always check your chosen rule against every example the question provides, and pick the one that fits them all.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. If LAMP is coded as NCOR, how is DESK coded?

Step 1: positions of LAMP are 12, 1, 13, 16. Positions of NCOR are 14, 3, 15, 18. Step 2: each letter moved by +2, so this is a forward shift of 2. Step 3: DESK is 4, 5, 19, 11. Adding 2 gives 6, 7, 21, 13. Step 4: convert back: F, G, U, M. Answer: FGUM.

Example 2. If PEN is coded as KVM, how is INK coded?

Step 1: PEN is 16, 5, 14 and KVM is 11, 22, 13. Step 2: the moves are -5, +17, -1, which are not equal, so this is not a shift code. Step 3: try sums: 16 + 11 = 27, 5 + 22 = 27, 14 + 13 = 27. Every pair makes 27, so it is a reverse-alphabet code. Step 4: INK is 9, 14, 11. Opposites are 27 - 9 = 18, 27 - 14 = 13, 27 - 11 = 16. Step 5: convert back: R, M, P. Answer: RMP.

keyPoints: Write plain and code positions one above the other and compare every letter.
Equal moves mean a shift code; pairs adding up to 27 mean a reverse-alphabet code.
Wrap round past Z or below A when shifting.
Decode by undoing the rule, not by applying it again.
With number codes, use every example to rule out rival rules.

challenges.title: One step forward
challenges.prompt: If BOOK is coded as CPPL, how is DESK coded?
challenges.explanation: B to C, O to P, O to P and K to L are each a move of +1. Applying +1 to DESK gives D to E, E to F, S to T and K to L: EFTL. CDRJ shifts the wrong way (-1), and FGUM shifts by 2.
challenges.hint: Compare each letter of BOOK with the letter below it in CPPL.

challenges.title: Backwards with a wrap
challenges.prompt: If MILK is coded as KGJI, how is SOAP coded?
challenges.explanation: M to K, I to G, L to J and K to I are each a move of -2. For SOAP: S (19) to 17 = Q, O (15) to 13 = M, A (1) to -1, which wraps to -1 + 26 = 25 = Y, and P (16) to 14 = N. The code is QMYN. QMZN moves A back by only 1, and UQCR shifts forward instead of back.
challenges.hint: Work out the shift from MILK, then take extra care with the letter at the start of the alphabet.

challenges.title: Mirror alphabet
challenges.prompt: If GOLD is written as TLOW, how is SILVER written?
challenges.explanation: G (7) and T (20), O (15) and L (12), L (12) and O (15), D (4) and W (23) each add up to 27, so every letter is replaced by its opposite. SILVER is 19, 9, 12, 22, 5, 18, whose opposites are 8, 18, 15, 5, 22, 9: H, R, O, E, V, I, giving HROEVI. IVEORH has the right letters but reverses their order, which this code does not do.
challenges.hint: The moves from GOLD to TLOW are not all equal, so this is not a shift. Look for another fixed link between each pair of letters.

challenges.title: Letters to a number
challenges.prompt: In a code, CAB = 6 and FED = 15. What is the code for HIGH?
challenges.explanation: Adding positions fits both examples: C + A + B = 3 + 1 + 2 = 6 and F + E + D = 6 + 5 + 4 = 15. Multiplying also gives 6 for CAB but 120 for FED, so it is ruled out. HIGH is 8 + 9 + 7 + 8 = 32. 24 counts the repeated H only once (8 + 9 + 7); every letter in the word counts, including repeats.
challenges.hint: Find one rule that fits both examples, not just the first.

challenges.title: Undo the code
challenges.prompt: In a code, every letter is replaced by the letter two places after it in the alphabet. A word is coded as GCUA. What is the original word?
challenges.explanation: To decode, move each letter two places back: G to E, C to A, U to S, and A (1) to -1, which wraps to 25 = Y. The word is EASY. IEWC applies the coding rule again instead of undoing it, and EAST guesses a familiar word: A moved back two places wraps round to Y, not T.
challenges.hint: Decoding runs the rule in the opposite direction. Watch the last letter.

guides.title: Direction sense
guides.summary: Track a person's facing direction through each turn and their position on an x-y grid, then use Pythagoras for the straight-line distance.

sections.title: The compass and turning
sections.text:
Draw the compass the usual way: north at the top, south at the bottom, east to the right and west to the left. Halfway between them sit north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west.

A turn is always relative to the way the person is currently facing, not to the page. A right turn is 90 degrees clockwise and a left turn is 90 degrees anticlockwise. Turning right repeatedly cycles north, east, south, west and back to north. Turning left cycles the other way.

Shortcuts save time with long chains of turns. Two rights, or two lefts, make a U-turn. A right followed by a left cancels out. Four turns the same way bring you back to where you started facing. So count the rights, subtract the lefts, and only the remainder after dividing by 4 matters: a net of 3 rights is the same as 1 left, and a net of 2 either way is a U-turn.

Degree turns follow the same idea. Give each direction a bearing measured clockwise from north (north 0, east 90, south 180, west 270), add for clockwise turns and subtract for anticlockwise ones, then add or subtract 360 until the total lies between 0 and 359. Starting from the same direction, a turn of 270 degrees anticlockwise ends up facing the same way as a turn of 90 degrees clockwise, because 360 - 270 = 90.

sections.title: Tracking position with x and y
sections.text:
For any question about distance or position, put the starting point at (0, 0) on a grid. Moving east adds to x, west subtracts from x, north adds to y and south subtracts from y.

Go through the walk one leg at a time. For each leg, first update the facing direction if there was a turn, then add the distance in that direction. Keep a small table of direction, distance and running position so that nothing gets lost.

For example, walking 5 m north, then 7 m east, then 2 m south gives positions (0, 5), (7, 5) and (7, 3).

Only the final x and y matter for the answer. The total distance walked, which here is 5 + 7 + 2 = 14 m, is almost never what the question asks for, yet it often appears among the options as a trap. The x-y method also handles legs that cancel: walking 6 m east and later 6 m west leaves x unchanged, however far apart those legs are in the walk.

sections.title: Distance and direction from the start
sections.text:
Once you have the final position (x, y), the straight-line distance from the start is the square root of x squared plus y squared. This is Pythagoras: the east-west and north-south displacements are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle.

Setters like whole-number answers, so learn the common triples: 3, 4, 5; 6, 8, 10; 5, 12, 13; 9, 12, 15; and 8, 15, 17. If your x and y match the first two numbers of a triple, the distance is the third.

The direction of the final point from the start comes from the signs. Positive x and positive y is north-east, positive x and negative y is south-east, and so on. If x is 0, the point is due north or due south; if y is 0, it is due east or due west.

Read the question carefully: the direction of the start from the person is the exact opposite. If the person is north-east of the start, the start is south-west of the person.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.text:
Example 1. Asha faces north and walks 6 km, then turns left and walks 8 km. Where is she relative to the start, and which way does she face?

Step 1: start at (0, 0); 6 km north reaches (0, 6). Step 2: left from north is west; 8 km west reaches (-8, 6). Step 3: distance is the square root of 64 + 36 = 100, which is 10 km. Step 4: x is negative and y is positive, so she is north-west of the start, and she is facing west.

Example 2. Kabir faces east and walks 15 km, turns left for 2 km, turns left for 3 km, then turns right for 7 km. How far is he from the start, and which way does he face?

Step 1: east 15 km: (15, 0). Step 2: left from east is north; 2 km: (15, 2). Step 3: left from north is west; 3 km: (12, 2). Step 4: right from west is north; 7 km: (12, 9). Step 5: distance is the square root of 144 + 81 = 225, which is 15 km, from the 9, 12, 15 triple. He faces north, and he is north-east of the start.

keyPoints: Turns are relative to the current facing direction: right is clockwise, left is anticlockwise.
Two same-way turns make a U-turn; a right and a left cancel.
Put the start at (0, 0): east and north are positive, west and south negative.
Straight-line distance is the square root of x squared plus y squared; know the common triples.
The total path walked is rarely the answer.

challenges.title: Three turns
challenges.prompt: Meera faces south. She turns right, then right again, then left. Which direction is she facing now?
challenges.explanation: Right from south is west. Right from west is north. Left from north is west. She faces west. Equivalently, two rights and one left net to one right turn, and one right from south is west. East comes from turning the wrong way, treating right as anticlockwise.
challenges.hint: Remember that right means clockwise from the way she is facing at that moment.

challenges.title: As the crow flies
challenges.prompt: Dev walks 4 km north, turns left and walks 3 km. How far is he from his starting point in a straight line?
challenges.explanation: He ends at (-3, 4). The distance is the square root of 9 + 16 = 25, which is 5 km. 7 km is the total distance walked, not the straight-line distance.
challenges.hint: The two legs are at right angles to each other.

challenges.title: Where did she end up
challenges.prompt: Nisha walks 9 m east, turns right and walks 5 m, then turns right again and walks 13 m. In which direction is she from her starting point?
challenges.explanation: East 9 m gives (9, 0). Right from east is south, so 5 m gives (9, -5). Right from south is west, so 13 m gives (-4, -5). x is negative and y is negative, so she is south-west of the start. South-east would be right only if the last leg were shorter than 9 m, but it overshoots the start by 4 m.
challenges.hint: Track x and y separately, then look at their signs.

challenges.title: Net displacement
challenges.prompt: Arjun walks 10 m north, turns right and walks 6 m, turns right and walks 18 m, then turns left and walks 9 m. How far is he from the start?
challenges.explanation: North 10 m: (0, 10). Right from north is east, 6 m: (6, 10). Right from east is south, 18 m: (6, -8). Left from south is east, 9 m: (15, -8). The distance is the square root of 225 + 64 = 289, which is 17 m. 43 m is the total distance walked, and 15 m is only the east-west part.
challenges.hint: Combine all the east-west legs and all the north-south legs before using Pythagoras.

challenges.title: Turning by degrees
challenges.prompt: Ravi faces west. He turns 135 degrees clockwise, then 270 degrees anticlockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
challenges.explanation: Measuring clockwise from north, west is 270 degrees. Adding 135 gives 405, which is 45 degrees, north-east. Turning 270 degrees anticlockwise is the same as 90 degrees clockwise, so 45 + 90 = 135 degrees, which is south-east. North-east is where he faces after only the first turn.
challenges.hint: A large anticlockwise turn can be rewritten as a smaller clockwise one.

guides.title: Syllogisms
guides.summary: Draw the statements as Venn diagrams and accept a conclusion only if it holds in every diagram the statements allow.

sections.title: The four statement types
sections.text:
Syllogism questions use four kinds of statement, and each has a simple Venn picture.

All A are B: the A circle sits entirely inside the B circle. A and B could even be the same circle.

No A is B: the A and B circles are completely separate, with no overlap.
